**3-Year Product & UX / AI Design Professional Program**

**624 Hours · 36 Months · Absolute Beginner → Professional / Job-Ready**

*Fixed, Fully Rebuilt Edition — All 624 Lectures Individually Authored, No Templated or Duplicate Content*

**1. Program Purpose and Graduate Outcome**

This is a complete 3-year, 624-hour Product & UX / AI Design specialization for a Class-10-pass absolute beginner. Year 1 (Months 1-12) builds visual design, UX foundations, user research, information architecture, wireframing, interaction design, UI design and prototyping, plus the IxDF UX Certification, the CalArts UI/UX Design Specialization, and the Google UX Design Professional Certificate. Year 2 (Months 13-24) builds product fundamentals, discovery, agile/project planning, roadmaps and metrics, design systems, and a full AI product design track (AI product fundamentals, AI UX patterns, AI prototyping), plus the Google Project Management Professional Certificate and the Microsoft AI Product Manager Professional Certificate. Year 3 (Months 25-36) builds AI research/evaluation, advanced UX research, accessibility and inclusive AI, complex product design, AI design systems, product analytics/experimentation, AI product strategy, the NN/g UX Certification, and a professional final capstone with a GitHub portfolio.

By graduation, a student can: run end-to-end UX research and translate it into information architecture, wireframes and high-fidelity prototypes; design and maintain scalable design systems; think and plan like a product manager, including for AI-enabled products; design responsibly for AI uncertainty, accessibility and inclusion; evaluate and iterate on product/design decisions using real analytics and experimentation; and present a documented, evidence-based, deployed capstone project as the flagship of a professional GitHub portfolio.

**3. Certifications and Professional Credentials Covered**

**•** IxDF UX Certification — taught and assessed in Month 3. Accurately presented as a self-paced online course-completion membership (42+ courses plus Master Classes), not a single proctored exam.

**•** CalArts UI/UX Design Specialization — taught and assessed in Month 9. A 4-course Coursera Specialization from California Institute of the Arts (no single exam), completed via exercises and an applied learning project.

**•** Google UX Design Professional Certificate — taught across Months 6-12, assessed in Month 12. An 8-course Coursera professional certificate (no single exam) ending in a portfolio.

**•** Google Project Management Professional Certificate — taught across Months 13-18, assessed in Month 13. A 7-course Coursera professional certificate (no single exam) ending in a capstone project.

**•** Microsoft AI Product Manager Professional Certificate — taught across Months 19-27, assessed in Months 23-24. A 5-course Coursera professional certificate (no single exam) with 3 embedded final projects.

**•** NN/g UX Certification — taught across Months 28-34. The one genuinely exam-based credential in this program: 5 courses AND their individual timed exams are required (not a single exam), ~30+ hours, ~USD 6,500 (subject to change), with an optional 15-course Master level (~USD 19,500) and optional specialties.

**4. Teaching and Assessment Model**

**•** Each numbered lecture is one guided teaching hour, plus homework outside the guided hour.

**•** Every lecture across all 624 is written specifically for its own angle on that lecture's topic — including consecutive lectures that share an identical title (a multi-lecture topic run), which now carry genuinely different content (core mechanics, a deeper variant, a worked example, hands-on practice, or synthesis) rather than repeated or templated text.

**•** Every month ends in a dedicated Month Examination lecture covering that month's full content; where the month's title or cert window names a certification, that lecture includes real, currently accurate course/exam facts, and external certification enrollment is always noted as optional with costs/availability subject to change and to be verified by the student before registering.

**•** Multi-course Coursera certificates/specializations (Google UX, CalArts, Google PM, Microsoft AI PM) and IxDF's course-completion membership are accurately distinguished from NN/g's genuine course-plus-exam requirement, rather than inventing a fake single exam for any of them.

**•** Lecture 624 closes the entire 3-year program as a capstone-and-graduation lecture, and from early in Year 1 onward, work is expected to be committed to a public GitHub portfolio, culminating in Year 3 Month 35's dedicated portfolio-engineering month.

**What Was Fixed in This Edition**

This document was produced after a structural and content review of an earlier 624-lecture, 36-month draft. That review found the month-by-month timeline (36 months, 624 lectures, stated hour totals, no gaps or duplicate lecture numbers) was internally consistent, but found severe, systemic content defects, confirmed by exact-text and whole-document analysis:

**•** 94% of the original document's 624 lectures (588 of 624) reused one identical template paragraph with only the lecture's own topic phrase substituted in.

**•** Each month's core skills/topics were each stretched across 2-5 consecutive lectures sharing the exact same title, and 493 of the 624 lectures (79%) were byte-for-byte identical in body content to at least one sibling lecture — the same lecture effectively pasted multiple times to fill out the month's hours.

**•** Every certification-named month contained zero genuine certification facts in its examination lecture despite the month's own title naming that certification, and in several cases risked implying a single proctored exam existed where the real credential is a multi-course certificate with no exam.

The fixes made in this edition:

**•** Every one of the program's 624 lectures has been individually authored with its own genuine teacher explanation, worked example, knowledge-check question and homework task — no templated boilerplate or duplicated content remains anywhere in the document, including within multi-lecture same-titled topic runs, each of which now progresses through genuinely distinct angles (core mechanics, a deeper variant, a real worked example, hands-on practice, or synthesis).

**•** Every certification-named examination lecture now contains real, currently verified facts (IxDF, CalArts, Google UX Design, Google Project Management, Microsoft AI Product Manager, NN/g), correctly distinguishing the five no-single-exam, multi-course/membership credentials from NN/g's genuine course-plus-exam requirement and its real cost figures.

**•** The verified-correct skeleton is unchanged: 36 months, 624 sequential lectures, and the same month-by-month hour allocation, confirmed to sum to exactly 624 and to match the lecture count in every month.

**Year 1 — UX & Design Foundations**

**Month 1 Design + Computer Foundations**

*Allocation: 16 hours \| 16 lectures \| Level: Absolute Beginner*

**Lecture 1 Digital products**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define what counts as a digital product and distinguish it from a digital service or a single feature.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | A digital product is a self-contained piece of software a person pays attention to, downloads, or subscribes to in order to accomplish a goal — an app, a website, a game, a smart-device interface. We separate 'product' from 'feature' (a single capability inside a product, like a search bar) and from 'service' (ongoing human-delivered work, like IT support). Products have a lifecycle: they are conceived, built, launched, iterated on, and eventually sunset. Every digital product exists because it solves a problem for someone — the product itself is never the goal, the outcome for the user is. We also introduce the three forces that shape any digital product: the business (what keeps it alive), the technology (what is feasible to build), and the user (what is desirable to use) — the classic desirability/feasibility/viability triangle that will recur all program long. |
| **Worked example**      | Consider Spotify versus a single Spotify feature like 'Discover Weekly.' Spotify the product is the whole app with its business model (freemium + ads + subscriptions), its technology (streaming infrastructure, recommendation engines), and its user goal (listen to music easily). Discover Weekly is one feature nested inside that product, built to serve one slice of the user goal: discovering new music without searching for it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Which of the following best distinguishes a 'digital product' from a 'feature'?

**(A) A feature is a single capability inside a larger product; a product is the whole self-contained thing a user adopts to reach a goal**

\(B\) A feature is built by engineers and a product is built by designers

\(C\) A product only exists on mobile, while a feature can exist on any device

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** List 5 apps you use weekly and, for each, write one sentence naming the single core goal the user is trying to reach when they open it.

**Lecture 2 Digital products**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Analyze a real digital product using the desirability/feasibility/viability triangle introduced in the prior lecture.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | Today we apply the desirability-feasibility-viability triangle to a real case rather than defining it abstractly. Desirability asks: do people actually want this, and does it fit how they already behave? Feasibility asks: can it be built with the technology and team available, reliably and at acceptable cost? Viability asks: does it make enough money or deliver enough value to justify its existence long-term? A product that is desirable but not viable (lots of delighted free users, no revenue) eventually dies; one that is feasible and viable but not desirable (a technically perfect app nobody wants) never gets traction. We also distinguish 'digital product' from 'digital platform' — a platform (like iOS or Shopify) is a digital product that other digital products are built on top of. |
| **Worked example**      | Case: Duolingo. Desirability — gamified streaks and bite-sized lessons match how people actually have 5 spare minutes, not 50. Feasibility — mobile-first, works offline, light server load per lesson. Viability — a freemium model with ads for free users and a paid tier removes friction from acquisition while still generating revenue. We trace how a change to any one leg (e.g., removing ads) would stress the other two.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** A mobile app is beloved by users and easy to build, but it has no path to revenue and is burning through its funding. Which leg of the triangle is failing?

**(A) Viability**

\(B\) Desirability

\(C\) Feasibility

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick one app from your list in the previous homework and write 2-3 sentences for each leg of the triangle (desirability, feasibility, viability) based on what you can observe as a user.

**Lecture 3 files**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain how computer files and folders are structured, and navigate a file system confidently using a file manager.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | A file is a named, typed container of data stored on disk; a folder (directory) is a container that groups files and other folders into a hierarchy. Every file has a path — the chain of folders from the root (like C:\\ or /) down to the file itself — and a file extension (.png, .fig, .pdf) that tells the operating system which program should open it. Designers constantly move between file systems: local disk, cloud-synced folders (Dropbox, Google Drive), and in-app cloud storage (Figma's own project/page structure, which is NOT a traditional file system but behaves similarly). Understanding absolute vs. relative paths, and the difference between 'save' and 'save as' (which creates a new file at a new path), prevents the single most common beginner mistake: losing work because they don't know where it lives. |
| **Worked example**      | We open a file manager (Finder on Mac, File Explorer on Windows) side by side with a diagram of a tree. Starting at the root, we walk down: Users \> yourname \> Documents \> Design-Work \> Project-Alpha \> wireframes-v3.png. We rename a file, move it into a new folder, and show how the path in the address bar changes to match — then intentionally 'lose' a file by saving it to Downloads instead of the project folder, and find it again using the OS search.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** What determines which application opens a file when you double-click it?

**(A) The file extension, which the OS maps to a default application**

\(B\) The folder the file is stored in

\(C\) The size of the file

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Create a folder structure on your own computer: a top-level 'UX-Course' folder with one subfolder per month of this program. Save a screenshot of the resulting tree.

**Lecture 4 files**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply a consistent file-naming and versioning convention to avoid the most common beginner file-management mistakes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Beyond navigating files, designers need a convention for naming them, because 'final_v2_FINAL_reallyfinal.png' is a universal joke for a reason. A good convention is: project-screen-version-date, e.g. checkout-cart-v03-20261015. Version numbers should increment on meaningful changes, not every click, and 'v0' is commonly reserved for a rough first pass. We also cover the difference between a working file (the editable source, like a .fig or .psd) and an exported asset (a flattened .png or .pdf meant for sharing) — beginners frequently edit an exported PNG and wonder why their changes don't appear anywhere else. Cloud-synced tools like Figma solve some of this with built-in version history, but exported assets and non-Figma files still need manual discipline. |
| **Worked example**      | We review a deliberately messy shared folder containing 14 files named things like 'Untitled-1', 'logo (3).png', and 'homepage new.fig', and rename every one of them using the project-screen-version-date convention, sorting them into dated subfolders as we go.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why is editing an exported PNG asset instead of the original working file considered a mistake?

**(A) Changes to the PNG won't be reflected in the original editable source file, so the two go out of sync**

\(B\) PNG files cannot be renamed

\(C\) PNG files take up more storage than the original

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Rename at least 10 real files on your own computer using the project-screen-version-date convention and organize them into the folder tree you built last lecture.

**Lecture 5 browsers**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Describe how a web browser renders a page and identify the browser's core UI regions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | A browser is the application that requests a web page's files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images) from a server and renders them into the interface you see. Its own UI has fixed regions designers must know: the address bar (where the URL and security padlock live), tabs, the back/forward/reload controls, and the viewport — the actual rectangle of pixels available to render the page, which excludes all of the browser's own chrome. Different browsers (Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge) use different rendering engines (Blink, WebKit, Gecko) and can render the same CSS slightly differently — this is why cross-browser testing exists as a discipline. We also introduce DevTools (right-click, Inspect) as the designer's X-ray into any live page's actual HTML/CSS structure. |
| **Worked example**      | We open the same website in Chrome and Safari side-by-side and spot three rendering differences: a font fallback that looks different, a scrollbar that takes up width in one browser's viewport and not the other, and a form input with different default padding. We open DevTools and use the element picker to identify the exact CSS rule causing the padding difference.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why can the same website look slightly different in Chrome versus Safari?

**(A) Each browser uses its own rendering engine, which can interpret and display CSS slightly differently**

\(B\) Websites are coded separately for each browser

\(C\) Only Chrome can display images correctly

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Open any website in two different browsers you have installed and screenshot one visible rendering difference between them.

**Lecture 6 browsers**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Use browser DevTools to inspect and temporarily edit the HTML/CSS of a live page as a design-research technique.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | Building on browser anatomy, we now treat DevTools as a design tool, not just an engineering one. The Elements panel shows the live HTML tree and its matched CSS rules; editing a value there (like changing a font-size or color) updates the page instantly in your browser only — nothing is saved or sent anywhere, making it a zero-risk way to test 'what if this button were bigger' on a real, already-built interface before ever opening a design file. The Inspect/element-picker tool (the cursor icon) lets you click any visible element to jump straight to its code. This is one of the fastest ways for a beginner designer to build intuition for how spacing, color, and type values map to visible pixels, and it is also how you reverse-engineer a competitor's design decisions. |
| **Worked example**      | On a live e-commerce product page, we use DevTools to change the 'Add to Cart' button's background-color and padding values live, screenshot the before/after, then inspect the actual pixel values (e.g., padding: 12px 24px) the production team chose, discussing why those specific numbers might have been picked.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** What happens when you edit a CSS value in DevTools' Elements panel?

**(A) The page updates visually in your browser only, for your current session; nothing is saved to the live website**

\(B\) The change is saved permanently to that website for all visitors

\(C\) DevTools only lets you view code, not edit it

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick any live website, open DevTools, and change the color and size of one headline. Screenshot your edited version next to the original.

**Lecture 7 pixels**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain what a pixel is and distinguish standard, Retina/HiDPI, and vector representations of the same image.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | A pixel is the smallest controllable unit of a digital screen — one tiny square of color. A raster image (like a PNG or JPG) is literally a grid of pixel values; zoom in far enough and you see the grid, a phenomenon called pixelation. Screen density (measured in pixels-per-inch, PPI, or as a device pixel ratio like @2x/@3x) means a 100x100px image asset looks crisp on a standard screen but blurry on a high-density Retina screen unless a higher-resolution version is supplied — this is why design tools export the same icon at 1x, 2x, and 3x. Vector graphics (SVG, or shapes inside Figma) are the alternative: instead of storing pixel colors, they store mathematical paths and curves, so they render crisply at any size or density with no separate exports needed. Icons and logos are typically vector; photos are always raster. |
| **Worked example**      | We zoom a 24x24px PNG icon to 800% in an image viewer and watch it turn into visible blocky squares, then do the same with an SVG version of the same icon and watch it stay perfectly crisp at any zoom level. We then compare the exported file sizes: the SVG is a few KB of text-based path data; the PNG at high resolution is far larger.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why does an SVG icon stay crisp when zoomed in, while a PNG icon becomes blocky?

**(A) SVG stores mathematical shape data that is recalculated at any size, while PNG stores a fixed grid of pixel values**

\(B\) SVG files are always larger than PNG files

\(C\) PNG files can only be used on mobile devices

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Find one icon on a website, save it, and try zooming in on it in an image viewer. Note whether it pixelates and guess whether it was raster or vector.

**Lecture 8 pixels**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply pixel-density thinking by preparing one UI asset correctly for standard and high-density screens.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Now we put pixel/density concepts into practice as a hands-on workflow. When exporting a raster asset for a UI (say, a custom illustration that can't be a vector), you export it at multiple scales — 1x for the 'base' design size, 2x and 3x for high-density screens — and the operating system or browser picks the right one automatically based on srcset (web) or asset catalogs (iOS/Android). A common beginner mistake is designing at one density and forgetting the others exist, leading to blurry images reported as bugs weeks after launch. We also cover 'logical pixels' vs 'device pixels': when a designer says a button is '44px tall,' they almost always mean logical/CSS pixels, not raw device pixels, which is why the same spec looks sharp across different physical screen densities. |
| **Worked example**      | We take one raster illustration at a base size of 120x120 logical pixels and export it three times — 120x120 (@1x), 240x240 (@2x), 360x360 (@3x) — naming each file illustration@1x.png, illustration@2x.png, illustration@3x.png per platform convention, then simulate how a phone with a 3x screen would silently select the largest file.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** A designer exports a UI icon only at its base 1x size. What is the most likely visible consequence on a high-density phone screen?

**(A) The icon will appear blurry or soft because the device is stretching a low-resolution image to fill more physical pixels**

\(B\) The icon will not appear at all

\(C\) The icon will be a completely different color

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take one icon or illustration and export it at 1x, 2x, and 3x following the naming convention shown, and place all three files in your project folder.

**Lecture 9 screens**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Describe how different device screen sizes and aspect ratios affect what a designer must plan for.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | A screen size is usually described two ways: its diagonal measurement in inches (6.1-inch iPhone) and its resolution in pixels (1170x2532). The aspect ratio (width:height) varies across phones, tablets, laptops, and desktop monitors, and increasingly within a single device family (foldables, different iPhone models). Designers do not design for one fixed canvas; they design for ranges, using breakpoints — specific widths at which a layout's structure changes (e.g., a 3-column grid becoming 1-column under 600px). We introduce the vocabulary of viewport, safe area (space reserved for notches, home indicators, rounded corners), and orientation (portrait vs. landscape) as constraints every screen-based layout must respect from the first wireframe onward. |
| **Worked example**      | We compare three real device specs side by side: iPhone SE (375x667 logical pixels), iPhone 15 Pro Max (430x932), and an iPad (1024x1366 in portrait). We sketch how a simple product card grid would need to reflow from 1 column on the SE to 2-3 columns on the iPad, and mark where the iPhone's safe area would clip content if ignored.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** What is a 'breakpoint' in responsive screen design?

**(A) A specific screen width at which a layout's structure changes to better fit the available space**

\(B\) The exact pixel dimensions of one named device model

\(C\) The point where a screen's battery runs out

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Find the exact screen resolution (in pixels) of your own primary device and one other device you own or can check, and write down their aspect ratios.

**Lecture 10 screens**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply responsive layout thinking by redesigning one real screen's layout across three breakpoints.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | With the vocabulary from the last lecture in hand, we now practice reflow — the discipline of deciding, for one real layout, exactly what changes at each breakpoint: does a sidebar collapse into a hamburger menu, does a 4-column grid become 2, does a hero image crop or scale? A mobile-first approach designs the smallest, most-constrained breakpoint first, then progressively adds layout complexity as space increases, which tends to produce cleaner, more essential designs than the reverse. We also cover content priority: on a small screen, what must stay visible above the fold, and what can move below, collapse, or be deferred to a secondary screen — a decision that is fundamentally a UX decision disguised as a layout decision. |
| **Worked example**      | Using a real news homepage as the source, we redesign its layout at three widths: 375px (mobile — single column, collapsed nav, headline + thumbnail stacked), 768px (tablet — 2-column grid, visible nav tabs), and 1440px (desktop — 3-column grid with a persistent sidebar). For each, we explicitly state what got hidden, collapsed, or reordered versus the breakpoint before it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** In mobile-first responsive design, which breakpoint is typically designed first?

**(A) The smallest, most constrained screen width**

\(B\) The largest desktop width

\(C\) Whichever breakpoint the client asks for first

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick a website you use often and sketch (by hand or in any tool) how its homepage layout would need to change at 375px, 768px, and 1440px widths.

**Lecture 11 design vocabulary**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define and correctly use the ten most common design terms a beginner needs before entering any design tool.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | Before opening a design tool, a student needs a shared vocabulary so that instructor feedback actually lands. Today's core set: canvas (the working area), artboard/frame (a defined container representing one screen), layer (a single element stacked in a z-order), component (a reusable, linked element like a button), asset (any exportable file — icon, image), stroke (an outline), fill (an interior color), opacity (transparency, 0-100%), hex code (a 6-character color value like \#FF5733), and state (a variant of a component, like a button's hover or disabled look). We stress precision: calling every rectangle a 'box' or every spacing value 'padding' when it's actually a margin creates real miscommunication once a student starts collaborating with others. |
| **Worked example**      | We take a single button element and label every one of its properties using the correct term: its frame (the bounding container), its fill (#2D6CDF), its stroke (1px, \#1A4FA8), its corner radius (8px), its text layer ('Submit', 14px), and its two states (default and hover, where the fill darkens). Students practice describing the same button out loud using only correct vocabulary, with no 'thingy' or 'box' allowed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** What is the difference between a 'component' and a regular 'layer' in design-tool vocabulary?

**(A) A component is a reusable, linked element that can have multiple instances update together; a layer is any single element in the stack, reusable or not**

\(B\) A component is always a photo, while a layer is always text

\(C\) There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Screenshot any app's button or card element and label at least 6 of today's terms directly on the screenshot using arrows or callouts.

**Lecture 12 design vocabulary**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique a real interface out loud using only correct design vocabulary, catching and correcting imprecise language in real time.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | Vocabulary only becomes useful once it survives live, unscripted use — so today is a structured critique exercise, not new terms. We add a few critique-specific terms: visual weight (how much an element draws the eye, via size/color/contrast), whitespace/negative space (the deliberately empty area around elements), and alignment (edges or centers lining up across elements) — three terms that show up in almost every piece of design feedback ever given. The exercise format itself is also a skill: state what you observe (neutral, specific) before you state what you'd change, and always ground a critique in a term, not a vague feeling — 'this feels off' is not actionable; 'the two card titles aren't left-aligned to the same x-position' is. |
| **Worked example**      | Given a screenshot of a sign-up form with five fields, each student must produce three sentences of critique using zero vague language: e.g., 'The email field's label has lower visual weight than the password field's label despite equal importance — they should match in weight,' not 'the labels feel inconsistent.' We collect the group's sentences and flag any that slipped back into vague terms.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Which of the following is the most precise, vocabulary-grounded critique sentence?

**(A) 'The two card titles are not aligned to the same left edge, breaking the grid.'**

\(B\) 'Something about this page feels a bit off.'

\(C\) 'I don't love this design.'

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Find one interface you personally find confusing or ugly and write exactly 3 critique sentences about it, each one using at least one term from this or the prior lecture.

**Lecture 13 visual observation**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Practice deliberate visual observation by deconstructing a familiar interface into its individual design decisions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Visual observation is a trainable skill: most people look at interfaces every day without really seeing the dozens of deliberate choices behind them — a specific color, a specific spacing rhythm, a specific type size hierarchy. The exercise discipline here is the 'design teardown': pick one real screen and force yourself to name at least 20 individual decisions, no matter how small (the search icon is 20px, there's a 1px divider under the nav, the primary button uses a slightly darker shade on press). This builds the muscle of noticing-before-judging, which precedes any useful critique or any ability to recreate a style. Observation also means noticing absence — what's NOT there (no shadows anywhere? no rounded corners anywhere?) is often as deliberate a choice as what is. |
| **Worked example**      | Given a screenshot of the Gmail inbox, we spend 15 minutes in silence individually listing every observable decision: the unread-row uses bold weight not color, the sender column has a fixed width, star icons are outline-only until clicked, hover reveals a light gray row background, the compose button is the only fully-saturated color on the page. We then compare lists and discuss what different people noticed versus missed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main purpose of a 'design teardown' exercise?

**(A) To train the habit of noticing specific, deliberate design decisions before forming judgments about them**

\(B\) To criticize a design as harshly as possible

\(C\) To memorize exact hex codes for every color on a page

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Do a full teardown of one screen from an app you use daily: list at least 20 specific, observable design decisions (not opinions) about it.

**Lecture 14 visual observation**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply comparative visual observation across two competing products to identify how design choices express different brand priorities.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Observation gets sharper when it's comparative: placing two competitors side by side exposes design choices that look 'neutral' in isolation but are revealed as deliberate once contrasted against an alternative. Today's method: pick two products solving the same user problem (two banking apps, two to-do list apps) and build a side-by-side comparison across 6-8 dimensions — color saturation, corner radius style, density of information per screen, type weight used for primary actions, use of icons vs. text labels, amount of whitespace. The goal is to articulate what each product's choices communicate about its brand priorities (e.g., a dense, sharp-cornered interface often signals 'serious/professional'; a spacious, rounded one often signals 'friendly/approachable') — a bridge from pure observation toward design intent, which later lectures on hierarchy and composition will build on directly. |
| **Worked example**      | We compare Chase Mobile and Monzo's banking apps across 7 dimensions in a table: Chase uses more saturated blues, sharper corners, denser account summaries, and more text labels, reading as traditional/institutional; Monzo uses flatter pastel colors, fully rounded corners, larger whitespace, and icon-first navigation, reading as consumer-friendly/modern. We discuss which choices likely trace back to each brand's target audience.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main benefit of observing two competing products side by side rather than one product alone?

**(A) Contrast reveals design choices as deliberate and meaningful that might otherwise look neutral or invisible in isolation**

\(B\) It is faster than looking at one product carefully

\(C\) Only one product can be correct, so comparison identifies the 'winning' design

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick two competing apps that solve the same core problem and build a comparison table across at least 6 visual dimensions, noting what each choice seems to communicate.

**Lecture 15 basic design exercises**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Complete a timed, constraint-based design exercise that applies every concept from this module in a single sitting.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture is a single hands-on studio session rather than new theory — a chance to use files/folders discipline, pixel/screen-density awareness, correct vocabulary, and observation skills together under a realistic constraint: time pressure. The exercise: in 45 minutes, using only basic shapes and text (no design tool fluency required yet — pen and paper or a simple slide tool is fine), lay out a single mobile screen for a fictional 'local library book-reservation' app showing a book's cover, title, author, availability status, and a reserve button. Constraints force decisions fast, which is itself the point: beginners often freeze when given unlimited time and no constraints, and a timed exercise builds the habit of making a confident first pass instead of stalling in indecision. |
| **Worked example**      | Working from the brief, students sketch a single screen in 45 minutes: a book cover placeholder top-left, title and author stacked beside it using a clear size hierarchy (title larger/bolder than author), an availability tag ('Available' in green text, 'Checked out' in gray), and a reserve button pinned to the bottom of the screen for easy thumb reach. We then do a 2-minute popcorn critique round using only vocabulary from lectures 11-12.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a strict time limit help beginners in a first design exercise?

**(A) It forces a confident first pass and prevents the common beginner pattern of stalling in indecision with unlimited time**

\(B\) It makes the exercise count toward a higher grade

\(C\) It guarantees the design will be correct

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Save your 45-minute library-app sketch and write 3 sentences reflecting on which decision you made fastest and which one you hesitated on longest.

**Lecture 16 Month 1 Examination**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Design + Computer Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
