| **Learning outcome**    | Apply the user interview as a specific generative-qualitative method, practicing open-ended, non-leading questioning technique to avoid biasing a participant's answers.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | The user interview is the single most common entry-level qualitative research method, and its core skill is avoiding leading questions — questions that embed the answer you expect or want to hear. 'Don't you find this confusing?' leads a participant toward confirming confusion; 'Walk me through the last time you tried to do this' invites a neutral, concrete account instead. Open-ended questions ('tell me about...', 'walk me through...', 'what happened when...') consistently outperform closed yes/no questions for generative research, because they surface the participant's own framing and vocabulary rather than yours. We also cover the 'Why' follow-up as the single most useful interview habit, and the discipline of staying silent after asking a question rather than rescuing an awkward pause — pauses often precede a participant's most honest answer. |
| **Worked example**      | Comparing two interview scripts for the same study on grocery-app usage: Script A asks 'Don't you wish the app showed prices more clearly?' (leading, assumes the conclusion); Script B asks 'Walk me through the last time you looked up a price in the app — what happened?' (open, neutral) and follows any hesitation with a silent 3-second pause rather than jumping in, which in practice reliably surfaces the participant's own unprompted complaint if one exists, rather than planting it for them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why is 'Walk me through the last time you tried to do this' generally a better interview question than 'Don't you find this confusing?'

**(A) It is open-ended and non-leading, inviting the participant's own concrete account rather than planting an expected answer**

\(B\) It takes less time to answer

\(C\) It is the only question format allowed in formal usability research

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write 3 interview questions about any product you want to learn about, then rewrite each one to remove any leading or biased framing, explaining what you changed.

**Lecture 51 basic research**

*Year 1 · Month 3 · UX Foundations + IxDF · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply basic usability testing as a specific evaluative method, running a guided 5-participant think-aloud test on a simple prototype and synthesizing the resulting findings.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | Usability testing is the primary evaluative method: giving a participant a specific task on an actual (even low-fidelity) prototype and observing where they succeed, hesitate, or fail — directly operationalizing the usability components from lectures 37-40 with real users rather than expert review alone. The 'think-aloud' protocol asks participants to narrate their thoughts as they work, surfacing confusion in real time rather than only after the fact. Jakob Nielsen's well-known finding that roughly 5 participants surface about 85% of a design's usability problems (with diminishing returns after that) is why beginner researchers shouldn't feel they need 50 participants to learn something real and actionable — a point worth knowing before the certification review ahead revisits IxDF's own research-method coursework. |
| **Worked example**      | Running a think-aloud test on a 3-screen meal-planning app prototype with 5 participants, task: 'add tomorrow's dinner to your plan.' Participant 1 narrates 'I'm looking for an add button... oh, it's this plus icon, I wasn't sure' (minor hesitation, resolved); participants 2 and 4 both independently fail to find the plus icon at all within 30 seconds (same root cause, now a pattern, not a fluke); participants 3 and 5 succeed immediately. Synthesizing across all 5, the plus icon's visibility is the dominant, repeatable finding — not any one participant's individual reaction.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a finding that repeats across multiple participants in a usability test (like 2 of 5 failing to find the same icon) treated as more significant than a single participant's individual reaction?

**(A) A repeated pattern across independent participants suggests a real, generalizable design problem rather than one person's idiosyncratic reaction**

\(B\) More participants always means the study is statistically significant regardless of pattern

\(C\) Single-participant reactions should always be ignored entirely

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Run a simple 3-person think-aloud test (even informally, with friends or family) on any app doing one specific task, and write down one finding that repeated across at least 2 of the 3 participants.

**Lecture 52 Month 3 Examination**

*Year 1 · Month 3 · UX Foundations + IxDF · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Demonstrate integrated recall of Month 3's UX foundations by passing a comprehensive review assessment, and understand IxDF's real certification structure as an optional next step.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | This Examination reviews Month 3 in sequence: human-centered design's philosophy and double-diamond structure, grounded in a real case study and a personal mini-exercise (lectures 33-36); usability as Nielsen's five measurable components and 10 heuristics, applied diagnostically and hands-on (lectures 37-40); the stated-vs-latent need distinction and Jobs-to-be-Done theory, applied to a real pivot and a synthesis exercise (lectures 41-44); UX process as a looping research-define-design-test sequence, including the Lean UX variant, a failure-diagnosis case, and a constrained timeline mapping exercise (lectures 45-48); and basic research's generative/evaluative and qualitative/quantitative axes, applied through interviewing and think-aloud usability testing (lectures 49-51). As with Months 1 and 2, this program holds an 80% internal passing bar on module assessments — Month 4's user-research deep dive builds directly on fluency with lectures 49-51's method vocabulary in particular. |
| **Worked example**      | On certification: the Interaction Design Foundation (IxDF), named in this month's title, is a self-paced online learning membership — not a single proctored exam with domain weights. It offers 42+ courses across UX/UI/AI topics plus one-hour live Master Classes taught by industry practitioners, and each individual course ends in its own shareable IxDF Course Certificate (addable to LinkedIn/a resume), rather than one unified credential. Access is subscription-based with a money-back guarantee window. Enrollment is entirely optional and exists to deepen specific topics from this month (interviewing, usability testing, HCD process) at your own pace — verify current course offerings, pricing, and the guarantee window directly on IxDF's site before registering, since subscription terms can change.                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Which statement accurately describes the Interaction Design Foundation (IxDF) certification structure named in this month's title?

**(A) It is a self-paced membership with 42+ individual courses, each ending in its own course certificate, with no single proctored exam**

\(B\) It is a single 3-hour timed proctored exam covering all of UX design

\(C\) It requires passing 5 separate timed exams, similar to NN/g's certification

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write one sentence for each of Month 3's five topic groups (human-centered design, usability, user needs, UX process, basic research) naming the single lecture or exercise from this month you found most useful, as a personal review before Month 4.

**Month 4 User Research I**

*Allocation: 16 hours \| 16 lectures \| Level: Beginner*

**Lecture 53 Interview planning**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Write a discussion guide and recruiting screener for a semi-structured user interview study.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Interview planning starts with a clear research goal statement: are you exploring a problem space (generative) or checking a design decision (evaluative)? That goal drives everything downstream — who you recruit, what you ask, and how you analyze. A screener is a short questionnaire used to qualify or disqualify candidates against behavioral criteria (e.g., 'has booked a hotel online in the last 3 months'), not demographics alone, because behavior predicts relevant experience better than age or job title. A discussion guide lists your topics and key questions in a logical order but is not a verbatim script — it's a flexible skeleton the interviewer adapts in the moment. Planning also means deciding session length (45-60 minutes is typical), where it happens (remote video vs. in-context), and how many participants (5-8 per segment is a common starting rule for qualitative saturation). |
| **Worked example**      | A team researching why users abandon a meal-kit subscription after month two drafts a screener requiring 'subscribed to a meal-kit service, cancelled within the last 6 months' and excludes people who never subscribed. Their discussion guide opens with warm-up questions about cooking habits, moves to the subscription experience timeline, and ends with direct questions about the cancellation moment — ordered from broad to specific so early answers aren't primed by later ones.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why do screeners typically filter on behavior rather than demographics alone?

**(A) Behavior predicts relevant experience with the product; demographics alone often don't correlate with how someone actually uses it**

\(B\) Demographic quotas are illegal to collect in research studies

\(C\) Behavioral questions are faster for candidates to answer than demographic ones

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Draft a one-page discussion guide (5-7 topics) and a 4-question screener for a research study on a product of your choice.

**Lecture 54 Interview planning**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Choose and justify an interview structure (structured, semi-structured, or unstructured) for a given research goal.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Structured interviews ask every participant the identical set of questions in the identical order, which maximizes comparability across sessions but sacrifices the ability to follow an unexpected thread. Unstructured interviews use only a topic list and let the conversation unfold organically, surfacing rich, unanticipated insight but making cross-participant comparison harder and demanding a skilled, experienced interviewer. Semi-structured interviews — the default for most generative UX research — combine a consistent core question set with the freedom to probe deeper on interesting tangents, giving you both comparability and discovery. The choice depends on your goal: structured suits quick comparative studies or when multiple interviewers need consistency; unstructured suits deep ethnographic exploration; semi-structured suits most product research in between. |
| **Worked example**      | A researcher comparing how five different user segments manage household budgets chooses a structured format with identical questions ('Walk me through how you paid a bill last week') so segment answers can be tallied and compared side by side. A separate researcher exploring the emotional experience of filing a first tax return chooses an unstructured conversation, since the goal is to surface whatever anxieties or confusions arise naturally rather than to compare fixed data points.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Which interview structure best supports discovering unanticipated insights while still allowing some cross-participant comparison?

**(A) Semi-structured interviews**

\(B\) Structured interviews

\(C\) Unstructured interviews

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take your discussion guide from the previous lecture and mark each question as 'core' (ask everyone) or 'probe' (follow only if relevant).

**Lecture 55 Interview planning**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Produce a complete interview plan for a real product problem, including goal, screener, guide, and logistics.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture walks through planning an interview study end to end for a specific scenario: a food delivery app has a 40% checkout abandonment rate on first orders. The research goal is generative — understand why first-time users hesitate at checkout, not validate a specific fix. The screener recruits people who added items to a cart on a delivery app in the last 30 days but did not complete the order, split evenly across iOS and Android to catch platform-specific friction. The guide opens with general ordering habits, walks chronologically through their most recent abandoned attempt using a 'walk me through what you did' retrospective technique, and reserves direct questions about cost or trust concerns for later so they don't anchor the participant's earlier narrative. |
| **Worked example**      | The finalized plan recruits 8 participants (4 per platform), schedules 45-minute remote video sessions, and includes a consent-and-recording script at the start of the guide. Mid-session, the guide includes a planned probe: if a participant mentions 'delivery fee' unprompted, the interviewer has a prewritten follow-up ('tell me about the moment you saw that number') to dig into sticker-shock reactions without leading them there if they don't raise it themselves.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** In this checkout-abandonment study, why does the guide save direct cost/trust questions for later rather than asking them first?

**(A) Asking them early could anchor or lead the participant's account of their own experience before they describe it in their own words**

\(B\) Cost questions are considered too sensitive to ask at all in a first interview

\(C\) Participants forget cost details if asked too late in the session

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a full interview plan (goal, screener, 8-10 question guide, logistics) for a real abandonment or drop-off problem in an app you use.

**Lecture 56 questions**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Write open, non-leading interview questions and avoid common question-wording traps.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | Open questions ('tell me about the last time you...') invite narrative and reveal context the researcher didn't anticipate, while closed questions ('do you like this feature?') invite a one-word answer and shut the conversation down. Leading questions smuggle an assumption into the wording — 'how frustrating was the checkout?' presumes frustration exists — and should be rewritten as neutral prompts like 'how did the checkout feel?' Double-barreled questions ask two things at once ('was it fast and easy?') and produce ambiguous answers because the participant may feel differently about each half. The 'five whys' technique chains follow-up 'why' questions to move past a surface answer toward root motivation, but should be used gently in UX interviews — repeated 'why' can feel interrogative, so rephrasing as 'what made you feel that way?' softens it. |
| **Worked example**      | A researcher drafts the question 'Don't you find the sign-up form too long?' and rewrites it as 'Walk me through filling out the sign-up form — what stood out to you?' The rewrite removes the embedded judgment ('too long') and opens space for the participant to raise length, confusion, or something else entirely, which is exactly the kind of unanticipated finding the original leading version would have suppressed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main problem with the question 'Don't you find the sign-up form too long?'

**(A) It is leading — it embeds the researcher's assumption that the form is too long into the question**

\(B\) It is too short to be an effective interview question

\(C\) It cannot be answered with a yes or no

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take 5 questions from your own draft guide and rewrite any leading, closed, or double-barreled ones into open, neutral versions.

**Lecture 57 questions**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Sequence interview questions using funnel technique and plan probing follow-ups.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | The funnel technique starts each topic with a broad, open question and narrows gradually toward specifics, which lets the participant's own priorities surface before the interviewer imposes a frame — for example starting with 'tell me about how you track expenses' before narrowing to 'tell me about the last time you used this app for that.' Probing follow-ups are short, prewritten prompts ready to deploy when a participant says something notable but under-explained, such as 'you mentioned it felt risky — say more about that' or simply 'why is that?' Good sequencing also groups related topics together so the participant isn't jumping cognitively between unrelated memories, and places the most sensitive questions (money, failure, embarrassment) after rapport has been built, typically in the middle-to-late portion of the session. |
| **Worked example**      | In a guide about managing subscriptions, the funnel moves from 'tell me about the subscriptions you currently pay for' (broad) to 'tell me about the last time you tried to cancel one' (narrower) to 'walk me through exactly what happened when you clicked cancel on \[specific service\]' (most specific). A prewritten probe sits next to the middle question: 'if they mention a dark pattern or difficulty cancelling, ask: what did you expect to happen instead?'                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** What is the purpose of starting a topic with a broad question before narrowing it in the funnel technique?

**(A) It lets the participant's own priorities and framing surface before the interviewer narrows toward specifics**

\(B\) It shortens the overall length of the interview session

\(C\) It allows the interviewer to skip writing follow-up probes

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Reorder one topic section of your guide into funnel form (broad to narrow) and write two prewritten probes for likely notable answers.

**Lecture 58 questions**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique and rewrite a flawed interview script for a specific product study.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture takes a deliberately weak interview script for a fitness app onboarding study and fixes it question by question. The original script's opener, 'So, do you like working out?' is closed and irrelevant to onboarding; it's replaced with 'Tell me about the last time you started a new fitness routine.' A later question, 'Wasn't the goal-setting screen confusing?' is leading; it becomes 'Walk me through the goal-setting screen — what were you thinking as you went through it?' The script also lacked any transition cues, jumping abruptly from account creation to workout history, so transition phrases ('now let's talk about...') are added so participants aren't disoriented, and a missing closing question ('is there anything about getting started that we haven't covered?') is added to catch unanticipated feedback. |
| **Worked example**      | After the rewrite, the onboarding guide flows: warm-up on fitness habits, walkthrough of account creation with a prewritten probe on any hesitation at the goal-setting screen, questions about the first workout recommendation, and a closing catch-all question — each transition explicitly signposted so the participant always knows what phase of the conversation they're in.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** Why was 'Wasn't the goal-setting screen confusing?' flagged as a problem in the original script?

**(A) It is a leading question that presumes confusion rather than asking neutrally what the participant experienced**

\(B\) It is too long for participants to understand

\(C\) It does not relate to the onboarding flow at all

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Find or write a flawed 6-question interview script, mark each flaw (leading, closed, double-barreled, missing transition), and rewrite it clean.

**Lecture 59 observation**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Distinguish contextual inquiry from naturalistic observation and apply think-aloud protocol during a session.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Contextual inquiry is a semi-structured observation method where the researcher watches a participant perform real tasks in their actual environment and asks clarifying questions as the work happens, treating the participant as the expert and the researcher as an apprentice. Naturalistic observation, by contrast, minimizes researcher interference entirely — the observer watches silently and asks nothing during the session, saving all questions for afterward, which preserves more natural behavior but yields less in-the-moment explanation. Think-aloud protocol asks the participant to verbalize their thoughts continuously while working ('say what you're thinking as you go'), which externalizes reasoning that would otherwise stay invisible, though it can slow task completion and shouldn't be treated as a measure of real-world speed. Choosing between these depends on whether understanding the 'why' in real time (contextual inquiry, think-aloud) matters more than preserving undisturbed natural behavior (naturalistic observation). |
| **Worked example**      | A researcher studying how warehouse staff use a handheld scanner app uses contextual inquiry: as a worker scans a pallet, the researcher asks 'what made you check that screen before scanning?' right then, capturing reasoning that would be lost if asked an hour later. A separate study observing shoppers in a grocery store app uses naturalistic observation with no interruptions, because the goal is to see unprompted, undisturbed shopping behavior.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** What is the key difference between contextual inquiry and naturalistic observation?

**(A) Contextual inquiry allows the researcher to ask questions during the task; naturalistic observation does not interrupt the participant at all**

\(B\) Contextual inquiry only works for mobile apps; naturalistic observation only works for websites

\(C\) Naturalistic observation requires more participants than contextual inquiry

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Observe someone using an app for 10 minutes using naturalistic observation (no questions), then note 3 behaviors you couldn't have learned from an interview alone.

**Lecture 60 observation**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design a diary study as a longitudinal observation method and specify its logging cadence.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | A diary study asks participants to self-report their behavior, thoughts, or feelings at set intervals over an extended period (days to weeks), which is the main way to observe behavior that's too infrequent, private, or spread out to capture in a single session — things like monthly bill-paying habits or how a habit-tracking app gets used (or abandoned) over a month. Logging cadence matters: event-contingent diaries ask participants to log every time a specific thing happens (e.g., every time they open the app), while interval-contingent diaries ask for an entry at fixed times (e.g., every evening), and the choice depends on whether the behavior of interest is triggered by events or better captured as a daily reflection. Diary studies trade observational fidelity (you're not watching directly) for coverage over time that a single session can't provide, and are often followed by a debrief interview to clarify entries and probe standout moments. |
| **Worked example**      | Studying why users stop using a budgeting app after the first two weeks, a researcher runs a 21-day event-contingent diary study: participants log a short entry every time they open or intentionally avoid opening the app, capturing the actual moments of disengagement rather than relying on a single recalled interview weeks later, which is then followed by a 20-minute debrief call to unpack the most telling entries.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** When is an event-contingent diary study more appropriate than interval-contingent?

**(A) When the behavior of interest is triggered by specific occurrences rather than happening predictably at a fixed time each day**

\(B\) When the study needs to run for less than 24 hours

\(C\) When only one participant is available for the study

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Design a 1-week diary study plan (cadence, prompt text, and a debrief question list) for a habit you want to study in any app.

**Lecture 61 observation**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Plan and conduct a contextual inquiry session for a real workplace tool.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture walks through contextual inquiry applied to nurses using a hospital inventory app on the ward. Planning starts by identifying the real task context — the researcher must observe during an actual shift, not a simulated walkthrough in a conference room, because workarounds, interruptions, and environmental constraints (gloves, noise, multitasking) only appear in situ. The session follows the 'master-apprentice' model: the nurse narrates what she's doing as she restocks supplies and logs counts, and the researcher asks brief clarifying questions at natural pauses rather than interrupting mid-task, such as 'why did you check the shelf before the screen just now?' Afterward, the researcher writes an interpretation session summary immediately — within hours — since contextual detail (why a workaround happened, what else was happening in the room) fades fast from memory. |
| **Worked example**      | During the observed shift, a nurse is seen double-checking physical stock before trusting the app's count, which she explains afterward was because the app had shown incorrect counts before after a failed sync — a workaround and a trust problem that would never have surfaced in a lab-based usability test, only in situ.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why must contextual inquiry happen in the real work environment rather than a simulated lab setting?

**(A) Workarounds and environmental constraints that shape real usage typically only appear in the actual context of use**

\(B\) Lab settings are more expensive to rent than real workplaces

\(C\) Participants are legally required to be observed only at their workplace

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Identify a task you could observe someone doing in their real environment (not simulated) and write 3 contextual-inquiry questions you'd ask at natural pauses.

**Lecture 62 surveys**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Decide when a survey is the right research instrument versus an interview, and choose appropriate question types.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Surveys excel at answering 'how many' and 'how much' questions across a large sample — quantifying how widespread a behavior or opinion is — while interviews excel at answering 'why' and 'how' questions in depth with a small sample; using a survey to explore unknown motivations, or an interview to measure prevalence, mismatches the tool to the question. Core survey question types include closed-ended (multiple choice, for easy quantification), Likert scales (degree of agreement, e.g., 1-5 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree', for measuring attitude intensity), ranking questions (ordering options by preference), and a small number of open-text questions (for unanticipated detail, used sparingly since they're harder to analyze at scale). Sampling also matters: a survey's value depends on reaching a representative slice of the target population, not just whoever is easiest to recruit, or the results will mislead rather than validate. |
| **Worked example**      | A product team wants to know 'what percentage of our users have tried the new dark mode feature' — that's a prevalence question best answered by a survey sent to a representative sample of the user base, not by five in-depth interviews, which could tell them why a given user liked or disliked dark mode but not how common that reaction is across the whole population.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why would a 'what percentage of users have tried this feature' question be better answered by a survey than an interview?

**(A) Surveys can reach a large, representative sample to quantify prevalence, which a handful of interviews cannot do reliably**

\(B\) Interviews cannot ask yes/no questions

\(C\) Surveys always take less time to design than interviews

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write one research question that fits a survey (prevalence/quantity) and one that fits an interview (why/how) for the same product feature.

**Lecture 63 surveys**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Identify common survey biases and apply standardized instruments like SUS, NPS, and CSAT correctly.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | Survey bias creeps in through leading question wording (same risk as interviews), order effects (earlier questions can prime answers to later ones), and acquiescence bias (respondents tend to agree with statements regardless of content, which is why well-built scales mix positively and negatively worded items). Standardized instruments solve some of this by using validated, fixed wording that's been tested for reliability: the System Usability Scale (SUS) is a 10-item Likert questionnaire producing a 0-100 usability score comparable across studies; Net Promoter Score (NPS) asks a single 0-10 'how likely are you to recommend this to a friend' question and classifies respondents into detractors, passives, and promoters; Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT) asks a direct satisfaction rating right after a specific interaction. Because these instruments are standardized, you should not reword their items even slightly — doing so breaks comparability with established benchmarks and other studies that used the original wording. |
| **Worked example**      | A team wants to track usability improvement release over release, so they administer the unmodified 10-item SUS after every major usability test and plot the resulting scores over time; when a PM asks to 'simplify the SUS wording to be friendlier,' the researcher declines, explaining that any wording change invalidates the score's comparability to the published SUS benchmark norms.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why shouldn't the wording of a standardized instrument like the SUS be modified, even slightly?

**(A) Changing the wording breaks comparability with the instrument's validated norms and other studies that used the original wording**

\(B\) Standardized instruments are copyrighted and cannot legally be printed

\(C\) Modified wording takes longer for respondents to read

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Administer the unmodified 10-item SUS (or NPS question) to 3 people about an app you use, and calculate/record the resulting score.

**Lecture 64 surveys**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a complete post-purchase survey combining a standardized metric with targeted open-text follow-up.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture builds a real post-purchase survey for an e-commerce app step by step. It opens with the standard NPS question verbatim ('how likely are you to recommend this app to a friend or colleague, 0-10') to get a comparable benchmark metric, then adds one targeted open-text follow-up specifically for detractors (scores 0-6): 'what's the main reason for your score?' — routing the open-text question only to the segment most likely to reveal actionable friction, rather than asking everyone and drowning useful detail in noise. The survey then adds two or three closed questions about the specific checkout experience (shipping clarity, payment ease) using 5-point Likert scales with balanced wording, and ends with an optional open field for anything else, kept last and optional so it doesn't inflate abandonment of the whole survey. |
| **Worked example**      | The finished survey: Q1 NPS (0-10), Q2 (only shown to 0-6 scorers) 'what's the main reason for your score?', Q3-Q4 Likert on shipping clarity and payment ease, Q5 optional open text. Routing Q2 by score (skip logic) keeps the survey short for promoters while still capturing detailed complaint data from detractors.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why is the open-text 'main reason for your score' question routed only to detractors (scores 0-6) rather than shown to everyone?

**(A) It targets the segment most likely to reveal actionable friction, keeping the survey shorter for everyone else**

\(B\) Promoters are not legally allowed to answer open-text questions

\(C\) Open-text questions can only follow NPS questions, never Likert questions

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Draft a 5-question post-purchase survey (1 standardized metric + 1 conditional open-text + 2-3 closed questions) for an app of your choice.

**Lecture 65 qualitative notes**

*Year 1 · Month 4 · User Research I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
