| **Learning outcome**    | Build a consistency checklist and run a short style-guide audit against a set of screens, using design tokens to catch drift.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | A practical consistency checklist asks concrete, checkable questions per screen: do all headings use the defined type-scale levels (not a one-off size), do all spacing values trace back to the spacing scale, do all colors trace back to a named token (not a raw hex value picked fresh), and do repeated components (buttons, cards) match the component library exactly. Running this checklist across even 4-5 screens at once, rather than reviewing each screen in isolation, is what surfaces drift — a token system doesn't enforce itself; someone still has to check it's actually being used everywhere. |
| **Worked example**      | Auditing 5 screens of a shopping app against a checklist: Screen 2's heading uses 20px instead of the defined 22px heading-scale value (flag it), Screen 4 has a card component with 12px padding instead of the library's standard 16px (flag it), and Screen 5 uses a raw \#3366CC hex value instead of the color-primary token (flag it) — three separate drift instances caught only by checking across screens together.                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a consistency audit need to check multiple screens together rather than reviewing each screen fully in isolation?

**(A) Drift (a one-off size, spacing, or raw color value) is only visible by comparing a screen against the shared system and other screens, not by judging one screen alone**

\(B\) Multi-screen audits are required by every design tool's built-in linter

\(C\) Reviewing screens in isolation always catches more consistency issues than reviewing them together

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Run a 5-point consistency checklist (type scale, spacing scale, color tokens, component match, icon style) across at least 4 screens of your own project.

**Lecture 151 visual consistency**

*Year 1 · Month 9 · UI Design I + CalArts · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply a full consistency audit to a real competitor or reference app's screens, identifying specific drift the shipped product still has.                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Even shipped, polished products have consistency drift — auditing a real app (rather than only your own work) demonstrates that this is a universal maintenance problem, not a beginner mistake, and sharpens the critique skill by practicing it on material you didn't design yourself and have no attachment to defending.                         |
| **Worked example**      | Auditing a messaging app's screens: the chat-list screen's unread-count badge uses a slightly different red (#E53935) than the same badge on the notifications screen (#D32F2F) — a token drift that shipped anyway, likely because the two screens were built by different people or at different times without a shared color token being enforced. |

**Knowledge check:** What is the specific value of practicing a consistency audit on a real, shipped app rather than only on your own work?

**(A) It shows that consistency drift is a universal, ongoing maintenance problem even in polished products, and lets you critique without the bias of defending your own design**

\(B\) Shipped apps never actually contain any real consistency issues worth finding

\(C\) Auditing your own work is always more informative than auditing someone else's

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick 3-4 screens from a real app you use and run the lecture 150 consistency checklist against them, documenting at least 2 specific drift instances you find.

**Lecture 152 visual consistency**

*Year 1 · Month 9 · UI Design I + CalArts · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Audit your own earlier wireframe or UI screens against the 5-point consistency checklist and correct at least two drift instances.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | Turning the audit inward closes the loop on this topic: using the same checklist from lecture 150 on your own month's work (wireframes from Month 7, interaction states from Month 8, or the components built this month) surfaces whatever drift crept in while attention was on individual lectures rather than the whole body of work — this is also the most realistic rehearsal for maintaining a real design system over time, where drift accumulates lecture by lecture, or in practice, sprint by sprint. |
| **Worked example**      | Self-auditing a student's own 4 screens from this month: the 'components' lecture's button used 16px padding, but an earlier 'typography systems' screen had reused an old 14px button built before the token system was finalized (flag it, fix it to 16px) — exactly the kind of drift that accumulates when work spans several sessions.                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why is auditing your own accumulated work across several lectures a realistic rehearsal for maintaining a real design system?

**(A) Drift accumulates gradually across sessions exactly the way it does across sprints on a real product, so catching it in your own work mirrors real system maintenance**

\(B\) Self-audits are easier than auditing others' work because there is never any real drift to find

\(C\) This exercise only applies to typography, not to colors, spacing, or components

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Run the 5-point consistency checklist against at least 4 of your own screens from this month and correct at least 2 drift instances you find.

**Lecture 153 UI patterns**

*Year 1 · Month 9 · UI Design I + CalArts · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define what a UI pattern is (an established, recognizable solution to a recurring interface problem) and decide when to use one versus design something custom.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | A UI pattern — a card, a tab bar, a modal, a carousel, a bottom sheet — is a solution that's been tested across thousands of products, so using it means borrowing earned familiarity: users already know roughly how a tab bar behaves before they've touched your app specifically. The decision to use an established pattern versus inventing something custom should hinge on whether the interaction is common and well-solved (use the pattern — a settings list doesn't need reinvention) or genuinely novel to your product's core value (custom interaction may be warranted — but at real cost, since users have to learn it from zero). |
| **Worked example**      | Deciding pattern-vs-custom for a food-delivery app: the order-history screen uses a standard card list pattern (no reinvention needed, it's a solved problem), but the live-delivery-tracking map with an animated route is custom, because showing real-time courier movement relative to the user's location isn't a problem any standard pattern solves well.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main cost of choosing a fully custom interaction over an established UI pattern for a common problem?

**(A) Users have to learn the custom interaction from zero, instead of bringing familiarity they already have with the established pattern**

\(B\) Custom interactions are always technically slower to build than established patterns

\(C\) Established patterns cannot be customized with a product's own visual style at all

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** List 3 screens in your product and classify each interaction as 'use an established pattern' or 'custom is justified,' with a one-sentence reason for each.

**Lecture 154 UI patterns**

*Year 1 · Month 9 · UI Design I + CalArts · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Compare iOS Human Interface Guidelines and Material Design conventions for the same pattern category (navigation or pickers) and apply the correct one per platform.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | The same underlying pattern often has genuinely different platform-specific conventions: iOS HIG favors a bottom tab bar for primary navigation and an in-line date/time picker wheel; Material Design (Android) favors a navigation drawer or bottom nav bar with different iconography conventions, and a modal dialog-style date picker rather than an inline wheel. Following the platform's own convention rather than forcing one platform's pattern onto the other matters because platform-native users bring platform-native expectations — an iOS user expects iOS-style pickers even inside a cross-platform app. |
| **Worked example**      | Building a date-picker for a scheduling app on both platforms: the iOS version uses the native inline scrolling wheel picker (HIG convention), while the Android version uses a Material dialog-style calendar grid picker — two different components solving the identical underlying problem, each matching its platform's established expectation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why would a cross-platform app typically use two different date-picker components rather than one identical component on both iOS and Android?

**(A) Each platform's users bring established expectations from HIG or Material conventions, and matching those expectations reduces relearning**

\(B\) Material Design and HIG are actually identical specifications with different names

\(C\) Date pickers are the only component type that differs between the two platforms

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick one pattern (navigation, picker, or another) and describe its iOS HIG version and its Material Design version side by side, naming the actual differences.

**Lecture 155 UI patterns**

*Year 1 · Month 9 · UI Design I + CalArts · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Select and justify a specific combination of UI patterns for a real screen, such as a map-plus-stepper combination for an order-tracking screen.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | This worked example combines two established patterns deliberately rather than picking one as if the problem only needs one component: an order-tracking screen typically combines a map pattern (showing the courier's live position, a familiar pattern from navigation apps) with a stepper/progress-indicator pattern (showing discrete order stages — placed, preparing, out for delivery, delivered — a familiar pattern from checkout flows). Justifying the combination means stating what each pattern is doing that the other can't: the map shows continuous spatial progress, the stepper shows discrete status progress, and together they answer both 'where is it' and 'what stage is it at' without inventing a new pattern for either. This kind of deliberate, justified pattern selection — choosing conventional layout and interface solutions and explaining why — is exactly the kind of applied decision-making the CalArts UI/UX Design Specialization's project-based courses later this month assess, through its hands-on wireframe-to-prototype applied learning project rather than a proctored exam. |
| **Worked example**      | Designing a food-delivery order-tracking screen: a map pattern at the top shows the courier's live dot moving toward the user's pin (continuous spatial progress), and a horizontal stepper below it shows 4 discrete stages with the current one highlighted (placed → preparing → picked up → delivered) — justified because removing either pattern would leave a real question unanswered (removing the map loses 'how close are they,' removing the stepper loses 'what stage is this').                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** In the order-tracking example, what distinct question does the stepper pattern answer that the map pattern alone cannot?

**(A) What discrete stage the order is currently at, as opposed to its continuous spatial position**

\(B\) The stepper and the map both answer exactly the same question, making one of them redundant

\(C\) The stepper shows the courier's exact GPS coordinates, which the map cannot show

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Design one screen that deliberately combines two established UI patterns, and write one sentence justifying what each pattern contributes that the other doesn't.

**Lecture 156 Month 9 Examination**

*Year 1 · Month 9 · UI Design I + CalArts · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Demonstrate command of this month's UI design skills — typography, color, components, and consistency — and correctly describe the CalArts UI/UX Design Specialization's real structure, well enough to clear the course's 80% internal passing bar.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | This exam reviews the month's four UI design threads (typography systems and scales, color systems and accessible contrast, component anatomy and variants, visual consistency auditing) plus UI patterns, and covers the CalArts UI/UX Design Specialization named for this month. The CalArts specialization is a 4-course Coursera Specialization from California Institute of the Arts, roughly 72 hours total at up to 10 hours/week over about 16 weeks, with NO single proctored exam: Course 1, Visual Elements of User Interface Design (~13h), covers interface conventions, layout, color, and typography — directly mirroring this month's first two topics; Course 2, UX Design Fundamentals (~16h), covers app ideation, sitemaps, and functional prototypes; Course 3, Web Design: Strategy and Information Architecture (~15h), covers research and content structure; Course 4, Web Design: Wireframes to Prototypes (~28h), covers wireframes, high-fidelity mockups, responsive design, and clickable prototypes. Completion requires exercises plus an applied learning project — a mid-level digital prototype with a full website plan — not a timed test. As with every month, the program's internal passing bar for this exam is 80%; enrollment in the CalArts specialization itself is entirely optional, and its hours, cost, and availability should be verified directly on Coursera before registering, since certificate pricing and course details can change. |
| **Worked example**      | A review scenario: a student is asked to (1) explain why the CalArts specialization has no single final exam and instead uses an applied learning project, (2) name which of its 4 courses most closely overlaps with this month's typography and color lectures, and (3) audit a sample UI screen for type-scale, color-token, and component-consistency issues — connecting the month's hands-on skills to accurate certification facts in one pass.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Which statement about the CalArts UI/UX Design Specialization is accurate and should be used on this exam?

**(A) It is a 4-course Coursera Specialization (~72 hours total) completed through exercises and an applied learning project, with no single proctored exam**

\(B\) It is a single 3-hour timed proctored exam administered directly by CalArts with pass/fail domain-weighted scoring

\(C\) It requires passing 5 separate timed course exams, each with its own listed fee, similar to the NN/g certification

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Review your type scale, color tokens, component library, and consistency audits from this month, and look up the CalArts UI/UX Design Specialization's current page on Coursera to confirm its course list and hours before the exam.

**Month 10 UI Design II**

*Allocation: 16 hours \| 16 lectures \| Level: Beginner*

**Lecture 157 Responsive layouts**

*Year 1 · Month 10 · UI Design II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain what a responsive layout is and how fluid grids let a single design adapt to different screen widths.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | A responsive layout uses a fluid grid — usually 12 or 16 columns with percentage-based (or fr-unit) widths instead of fixed pixel widths — so content reflows as the viewport changes rather than staying a fixed size that overflows or leaves dead space. The core mechanic is the combination of a flexible grid, flexible images/media (max-width: 100%), and CSS media queries that swap layout rules at defined breakpoints. In Figma this is modeled with Auto Layout plus constraints (left/right/center/scale) on frames, so resizing a frame previews how the real layout will behave. The key principle is 'fluid first, breakpoints second' — you design the grid to flex naturally, and only add a breakpoint when the fluid behavior breaks down (text lines get too long, columns get too narrow to read). |
| **Worked example**      | Take a 3-column product-card grid on a shopping app's category page. At a 1440px desktop width the grid shows 4 cards per row with 24px gutters; as the frame narrows past 1024px the grid drops to 3 cards per row, then 2 at 768px, then 1 full-width card at 480px — all using the same 12-column fluid grid with the column span per card simply changing (3 cols at desktop, 4 cols at tablet, 6 cols at mobile, 12 cols at phone) rather than redesigning the card itself.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** In a fluid 12-column grid, what changes between breakpoints while the underlying grid system stays the same?

**(A) The number of columns a component spans**

\(B\) The total page width in pixels, which is fixed

\(C\) The font family used in body text

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Rebuild one existing wireframe (from Month 7) as a fluid 12-column Figma frame with Auto Layout, and resize it from 1440px down to 375px, screenshotting the layout at 1440, 1024, 768, and 375px.

**Lecture 158 Responsive layouts**

*Year 1 · Month 10 · UI Design II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define breakpoints and apply the standard device-class breakpoint ranges used in production UI design.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | A breakpoint is the specific viewport width at which a layout's structure changes rather than merely scaling. The industry-common ranges are roughly: mobile 320-479px, large mobile 480-767px, tablet 768-1023px, laptop/desktop 1024-1439px, and large desktop 1440px+ — though teams tune these to their actual traffic data rather than copying them blindly. Choosing breakpoints well means designing 'content-out': you shrink the canvas until something visibly breaks (a nav wraps badly, a table truncates, line length exceeds ~75 characters) and you place the breakpoint there, rather than designing to arbitrary device names like 'iPhone' or 'iPad' which change every year. |
| **Worked example**      | A SaaS dashboard's top navigation holds 7 menu items plus a search bar. Shrinking the frame shows the nav items start wrapping onto a second line at 900px — that becomes a breakpoint where the nav collapses into a hamburger/overflow menu, not at a round number like 1024px, because 900px is where the actual content broke first.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why do experienced UI designers set breakpoints by watching where content breaks, instead of hard-coding them to named devices like 'iPhone 14' or 'iPad'?

**(A) Device screen sizes and models change constantly, so content-based breakpoints stay valid regardless of which device ships next**

\(B\) Named devices are impossible to simulate in Figma

\(C\) Google requires content-based breakpoints for SEO ranking

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take the nav bar from the Month 9 UI kit and find its real breakpoint by narrowing the frame in 10px increments until it visually breaks; record the exact width.

**Lecture 159 Responsive layouts**

*Year 1 · Month 10 · UI Design II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply the mobile-first and desktop-first design strategies and explain the trade-offs between them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Mobile-first design starts the layout at the smallest supported width and progressively enhances upward, adding columns, secondary content, and hover-only affordances as space allows; desktop-first starts at the largest width and strips elements down as space shrinks. Mobile-first forces the designer to prioritize ruthlessly, since only the most essential content and actions fit on a 375px canvas first — this is why most consumer product teams (and CSS frameworks like Bootstrap and Tailwind) default to it. Desktop-first can be faster for internal tools or dashboards where the primary use case genuinely is a large screen and mobile is a secondary, reduced experience rather than an equal citizen. |
| **Worked example**      | A food-delivery app is designed mobile-first: the 375px view ships only the restaurant photo, name, rating, and an 'Order' button; at tablet width a cuisine-filter sidebar is added; at desktop width a map view is added alongside the list. A B2B analytics dashboard instead goes desktop-first: the 1440px view ships the full multi-panel chart layout, and the mobile view strips it down to a single KPI summary card with a link to 'view full dashboard on desktop'.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** Which product is the stronger candidate for a desktop-first (rather than mobile-first) design strategy?

**(A) An internal B2B analytics dashboard primarily used at a desk**

\(B\) A consumer food-delivery app used mostly while out and about

\(C\) A public marketing landing page for a mobile game

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick one screen from your own portfolio project and redesign it twice: once mobile-first (375px base, enhance upward) and once desktop-first (1440px base, strip downward). Note which was faster and why.

**Lecture 160 mobile patterns**

*Year 1 · Month 10 · UI Design II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Identify and apply the core native mobile navigation patterns: tab bars, bottom navigation, and the hamburger menu.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | Mobile navigation patterns each trade off discoverability against screen real estate. A bottom tab bar (iOS Human Interface Guidelines recommend 3-5 items) keeps top-level destinations always visible and reachable by thumb, which is why Instagram, Spotify, and most consumer apps use it for primary navigation. A hamburger menu hides navigation behind an icon, saving vertical space but reducing discoverability — research (including Nielsen Norman Group studies) has repeatedly shown hidden navigation lowers feature usage, so it's best reserved for secondary or rarely used items, not core flows. A top tab bar (segmented control) works well for switching between peer views of the same content, like 'Following' vs 'For You'. |
| **Worked example**      | A fitness app places Home, Workouts, Progress, and Profile in a 4-item bottom tab bar (primary, always-visible destinations) but tucks 'Settings,' 'Help,' and 'Invite a Friend' behind a hamburger menu reachable from the Profile tab, since those are low-frequency actions that don't need constant thumb-reach.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why do most consumer mobile apps avoid putting their 3-5 primary destinations behind a hamburger menu?

**(A) Hidden navigation measurably reduces how often users discover and use those features**

\(B\) Hamburger menus are not supported on iOS devices

\(C\) Apple's App Store rejects apps that use hamburger menus

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Audit three mobile apps you use daily and record which navigation pattern each uses for primary nav (tab bar, hamburger, or top tabs) and how many items are in it.

**Lecture 161 mobile patterns**

*Year 1 · Month 10 · UI Design II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply touch-target sizing standards and gesture-based interaction patterns (swipe, pull-to-refresh, long-press).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | Touch targets must meet minimum sizes because fingers are far less precise than a mouse cursor: Apple's HIG recommends a minimum of 44x44pt, Google's Material Design recommends 48x48dp, and both call for adequate spacing between adjacent targets to prevent mis-taps. Beyond tap, mobile UI relies on gesture vocabulary that has become standardized through repetition: swipe-to-delete (reveal a destructive action by swiping a list row left), pull-to-refresh (drag down past a threshold to reload content, popularized by Twitter/X), and long-press (hold to reveal a contextual menu, as with iOS app icons or message reactions). Designers must document both the gesture AND a visible fallback (an explicit button) for accessibility, since gestures aren't always discoverable or usable by everyone. |
| **Worked example**      | In an email app's inbox, swiping a message left reveals a red 'Delete' action and swiping right reveals a yellow 'Archive' action — but because pure gesture interactions fail discoverability and motor-accessibility checks, the design also keeps a three-dot overflow menu on each row exposing 'Delete' and 'Archive' as tappable text options.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** Why should a swipe-to-delete gesture always ship with a visible button alternative in the same screen?

\(A\) Swipe gestures are not reliably discoverable or usable by everyone, so an explicit control preserves accessibility

**(B) Swipe gestures are banned by the Google Play Store content policy**

\(C\) Visible buttons increase app store search ranking

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Design a swipe-to-delete row pattern for a to-do list app, including the required 44x44pt+ touch targets for both the swipe-revealed action and its button fallback.

**Lecture 162 mobile patterns**

*Year 1 · Month 10 · UI Design II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique a mobile screen for common pattern-selection and touch-target mistakes and apply fixes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | The most frequent mobile UI mistakes are: touch targets under the 44pt/48dp minimum (especially icon-only buttons placed too close together), putting primary actions inside a hamburger menu, using hover-dependent interactions that have no touch equivalent (mobile has no hover state), and ignoring thumb-reach zones — placing critical actions at the top of a tall screen where one-handed use can't reach them comfortably. A useful heuristic from mobile ergonomics research is the 'thumb zone' map: the bottom third of the screen is easy reach, the middle third requires a stretch, and the top third requires a grip shift — so primary actions belong low, and destructive or rare actions can live higher up. |
| **Worked example**      | A critique session on a food-ordering screen flags three issues: the 'Add to Cart' button sits at the very top of a 6-inch screen (poor thumb-reach for one-handed use), two icon buttons for 'favorite' and 'share' are only 32x32pt and 4px apart (both below minimum size and spacing), and a filter panel only opens on long-press with no visible trigger. The fix moves 'Add to Cart' to a sticky bottom bar, enlarges the icons to 44x44pt with 8px gaps, and adds a visible 'Filter' button alongside the long-press shortcut.                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Where should an app's single most frequent action (like 'Add to Cart') be placed on a tall phone screen for one-handed use?

**(A) In the bottom third of the screen, within easy thumb reach**

\(B\) In the top third, so it's the first thing seen

\(C\) Centered vertically in the middle of the screen

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Screenshot one mobile app screen you find awkward to use one-handed, annotate it against the thumb-zone map, and redesign it with primary actions moved into the bottom reach zone.

**Lecture 163 dashboards**

*Year 1 · Month 10 · UI Design II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define dashboard design fundamentals: information hierarchy, the five-second rule, and card-based layout.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | A dashboard's job is to let a user assess a situation and decide on action within seconds, so information hierarchy is the central design problem — not visual decoration. The 'five-second rule' for dashboards holds that a user should be able to identify the most important number or status within about five seconds of landing on the screen; this is achieved by sizing and positioning the single most critical metric (often called the 'hero metric') larger and higher than supporting data, then grouping related data into cards that each answer one question. Card-based layout — discrete bordered or shadowed containers, each holding one KPI, chart, or table — lets a dashboard be reorganized, resized, or made responsive without redesigning the whole page, and lets users mentally chunk information instead of parsing one dense table. |
| **Worked example**      | A sales dashboard places 'Monthly Revenue: \$482K (+12%)' as a large hero card top-left, with secondary cards below for 'New Customers,' 'Churn Rate,' and 'Top Product' — each card answers exactly one question and uses a consistent card template (label, number, trend arrow, sparkline) so a sales manager can scan the whole dashboard in under five seconds and know whether the month is on track.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** In the five-second rule for dashboard design, what determines which metric should be the largest and most prominent?

**(A) Whichever single metric the user most needs in order to judge the situation and decide on action**

\(B\) Whichever metric has the most decimal precision available

\(C\) Whichever metric was added most recently to the dataset

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick a dashboard you use at work or in an app, identify its actual hero metric, and redesign the layout so that metric is unmistakably the first thing seen.

**Lecture 164 dashboards**

*Year 1 · Month 10 · UI Design II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply data-visualization selection rules: when to use a line chart, bar chart, number card, or table within a dashboard.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | Chart-type selection in dashboard design follows the question being answered, not personal taste: line charts show a trend over continuous time (revenue over 12 months), bar charts compare discrete categories against each other (revenue by region), single number cards (often called KPI tiles) show a current state or single snapshot value, and tables show many data points across many attributes when users need to scan, sort, or compare specific rows rather than see an overall shape. A common mistake is defaulting to a table for everything because it 'shows all the data' — tables are the right choice specifically when the user's task is lookup or comparison of exact values, not pattern recognition, where a chart will always communicate faster. |
| **Worked example**      | A customer-support dashboard uses a line chart for 'Tickets Opened per Day' (trend over time), a horizontal bar chart for 'Tickets by Category' (comparing five discrete categories), a KPI number card for 'Current Open Tickets: 34' (single snapshot), and a sortable table for 'Agent Performance' (because a manager needs to look up and rank individual agents by name, not see an aggregate shape).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** A manager needs to compare exact ticket-resolution times across 12 named support agents by looking up individual values. Which visualization fits that task best?

**(A) A sortable table listing each agent by name with their resolution time**

\(B\) A single line chart showing the aggregate trend over the month

\(C\) One large KPI number card showing the team average

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take a dataset with at least three attributes (even sample data) and build one dashboard screen choosing a distinct chart type for each of: a trend, a category comparison, and an exact-value lookup.

**Lecture 165 dashboards**

*Year 1 · Month 10 · UI Design II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design a complete analytics dashboard for a real scenario, applying hierarchy, card layout, and chart selection together.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | Building a full dashboard requires sequencing these decisions rather than jumping straight to visuals: first identify the primary user and their top 1-3 questions (not every metric the stakeholder wants shown), then rank metrics by decision-relevance to pick the hero metric, then group remaining metrics into logical card clusters (e.g., 'acquisition,' 'engagement,' 'revenue'), then assign the right chart type to each card based on the question it answers, and only then apply visual grid and spacing rules. Skipping straight to layout produces the common failure mode of a dashboard that is visually polished but answers no question quickly — often called a 'vanity dashboard.' |
| **Worked example**      | For a podcast app's creator-analytics dashboard, the primary user is a podcast host who logs in weekly to ask 'is my show growing, and which episode is working?' The hero card becomes 'Total Listens This Week' with trend arrow; secondary cards cluster into 'Growth' (new vs. returning listeners, line chart), 'Episode Performance' (bar chart ranking episodes by listens), and 'Audience' (a table of listener demographics for deeper lookup) — three clusters, each matching one of the host's real recurring questions.                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** What is the first step in designing a dashboard, before choosing any chart types or layout grid?

**(A) Identify the primary user and the 1-3 questions they actually need answered**

\(B\) Pick the brand color palette for the cards

\(C\) List every metric available in the database

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Design one full dashboard screen (hero metric + at least two card clusters, each with an appropriate chart type) for a product/app of your choice, writing down the primary user's top question before you start.

**Lecture 166 tables**

*Year 1 · Month 10 · UI Design II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define data-table design fundamentals: row/column structure, alignment rules, and zebra striping.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Tables exist to let users compare many values across consistent attributes, so the design rules center on scannability: numeric columns are right-aligned (so digits of different magnitude line up for easy comparison), text columns are left-aligned, and column headers stay visually distinct (bold, different background, or a top border) so the eye always knows what it's scanning. Zebra striping — alternating row background colors, usually a very subtle tint — helps the eye track across a wide row without losing its place, but should be used sparingly since heavy striping can itself create visual noise; many modern tables instead use thin row-dividing lines alone. Row height and horizontal padding need enough breathing room (commonly 12-16px vertical padding) that dense data doesn't feel cramped, since cramped tables are one of the most common usability complaints in UI critiques. |
| **Worked example**      | An inventory table lists Product Name (left-aligned text), SKU (left-aligned, monospace for even character width), Quantity (right-aligned numbers so '8' and '1,240' both line up by their last digit), and Price (right-aligned, currency-formatted). Subtle zebra striping (alternating \#FFFFFF and \#F7F8FA rows) helps a warehouse manager track a row across 8 columns without losing their place.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** Why are numeric columns in a well-designed table right-aligned rather than left-aligned?

**(A) Right alignment lines up digits by magnitude, making numbers easier to compare at a glance**

\(B\) Right alignment is required by WCAG accessibility guidelines

\(C\) Right alignment makes the table narrower

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Redesign one poorly aligned table you've encountered (screenshot or recreate it) applying correct left/right alignment rules and appropriate row padding.

**Lecture 167 tables**

*Year 1 · Month 10 · UI Design II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
