Horizontal (bad) split: 'build export backend API' then 'build export UI' then 'wire them together' — nothing works until all three are done. Vertical (good) split: 'export to CSV, happy path only' (complete end-to-end for the simplest case), then 'export to PDF' (same workflow, different format), then 'handle exports over 10,000 rows' (same workflow, edge case) — each slice is independently shippable and testable on its own.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main problem with splitting a large story horizontally (by technical layer) instead of vertically?

**(A) Nothing is end-to-end testable or usable until every layer is complete, which hides integration problems until late**

\(B\) Horizontal splitting is against Scrum Guide licensing terms

\(C\) It requires twice as many story points as vertical splitting

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take an epic-sized feature idea and split it into 3 smaller, vertically-sliced stories, each independently shippable and each delivering some end-to-end value on its own.

**Lecture 247 user stories**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply the INVEST criteria to evaluate whether a user story is actually ready to be worked on.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | INVEST is a checklist for story quality: Independent (can be built/shipped without requiring another unfinished story first), Negotiable (describes intent, not a locked implementation spec engineering has zero input on), Valuable (delivers something a user or the business actually cares about, not just an internal technical task dressed as a story), Estimable (the team has enough information to size it), Small (fits within a sprint), and Testable (has clear enough acceptance criteria that someone can verify it's done). A story that fails even one of these criteria usually causes a specific, predictable problem during the sprint — a non-Independent story blocks other work, a non-Testable story causes review disputes, a non-Small story risks spilling past sprint end. Running new stories through INVEST before sprint planning catches these problems while they're still cheap to fix. |
| **Worked example**      | A story 'As a user, I want the entire settings page redesigned' fails 'Small' (too big for one sprint) and partly fails 'Testable' (no specific acceptance criteria for what 'redesigned' means). Running it through INVEST catches this before sprint planning, prompting a split into smaller, independently testable stories like 'reorganize settings into collapsible sections' and 'add a settings search bar.'                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** A story turns out not to be 'Independent' per the INVEST checklist. What practical problem does this typically cause during a sprint?

**(A) It blocks or is blocked by other unfinished work, making it hard to complete on its own within the sprint**

\(B\) It cannot be assigned story points at all

\(C\) It automatically becomes the highest-priority item in the backlog

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take 2 user stories you've written in this run of lectures and check each against all 6 INVEST letters, noting any that fail and how you'd fix them.

**Lecture 248 user stories**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Facilitate a story-writing workshop where a cross-functional team collaboratively drafts and critiques stories together.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | Writing stories in isolation (just the PM, alone, at a desk) misses input that design and engineering could have caught immediately — a story-writing workshop brings the PM, a designer, and an engineer together to draft stories collaboratively, with each role catching different blind spots in real time: engineering flags technical dependencies or sizing concerns the PM wouldn't know to ask about, design flags missing states (empty, error, loading) that change what 'done' means, and the PM keeps everyone anchored to the actual user benefit instead of drifting into solutioning too early. The workshop format also naturally produces the INVEST and vertical-slicing checks from earlier lectures as a live conversation instead of a solo checklist exercise, since disagreement during drafting is exactly where those criteria get tested. |
| **Worked example**      | In a workshop drafting the story 'As a user, I want to see my order status,' the engineer flags that 'status' depends on a third-party shipping API with occasional downtime (a dependency the PM hadn't considered), and the designer flags that the story as written doesn't account for what the user sees when the API is down (a missing state) — both catches happen live, in minutes, instead of surfacing mid-sprint as a surprise.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main advantage of drafting user stories in a cross-functional workshop rather than having the PM write them alone?

**(A) Design and engineering catch missing states, dependencies, and sizing issues in real time that a PM working alone wouldn't know to ask about**

\(B\) It eliminates the need for acceptance criteria entirely

\(C\) It guarantees the story will require zero story points

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Describe how you'd run a 30-minute story-writing workshop for one feature idea, including which roles you'd include and one specific thing you'd expect each role to catch.

**Lecture 249 acceptance criteria**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Write acceptance criteria for a user story using the Given/When/Then format.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Acceptance criteria define the specific, testable conditions a story must satisfy to be considered done, and the Given/When/Then format (borrowed from behavior-driven development) structures each criterion as a precondition (Given), an action (When), and an expected result (Then) — turning a fuzzy 'make sure it works' into something QA, engineering, and the PM can check identically without interpretation. Writing acceptance criteria is also where edge cases get caught before development starts rather than during review: a story that only has a happy-path criterion will get built to only handle the happy path, and the gap surfaces as a bug report instead of a planning conversation. Good acceptance criteria are written collaboratively, often in the same workshop as the story itself, since engineering often spots edge cases the PM wouldn't think to specify. |
| **Worked example**      | Story: 'As a user, I want to reset my password via email.' Acceptance criteria: 'Given a user enters a valid registered email, When they submit the reset request, Then a reset link is sent within 60 seconds.' Plus an edge case: 'Given a user enters an email not in the system, When they submit the reset request, Then the system shows the same generic confirmation message (not an error) to avoid revealing which emails are registered.' That second criterion is a security consideration that would likely be missed without explicit Given/When/Then coverage.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** Why does writing acceptance criteria often surface edge cases before development begins?

**(A) Each Given/When/Then condition forces explicit consideration of a specific scenario, including non-happy-path cases that a vague description would skip**

\(B\) Acceptance criteria are reviewed by a legal team before any coding starts

\(C\) Given/When/Then format automatically generates unit test code

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write 2 acceptance criteria in Given/When/Then format for one of the user stories you wrote in lecture 245 or 246, including at least one non-happy-path case.

**Lecture 250 acceptance criteria**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Distinguish acceptance criteria from a Definition of Done, and explain why conflating them causes scope disputes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | Acceptance criteria are specific to one story and describe what that particular piece of work must do; Definition of Done (DoD) is a team-wide, story-independent checklist applied to every single item regardless of content — things like 'code reviewed by one other engineer,' 'unit tests written and passing,' 'no new accessibility violations introduced,' 'documentation updated.' Conflating the two causes disputes: if 'passes accessibility check' is only written into some stories' acceptance criteria and not others, it becomes optional in practice for whichever stories happened to omit it, when it should be a non-negotiable team-wide bar applied uniformly. Separating them means acceptance criteria stay focused on describing this story's specific behavior, while the DoD silently and consistently enforces quality bars across everything the team ships, without needing to be rewritten into every single story. |
| **Worked example**      | A team's DoD includes 'all new UI components pass a contrast-ratio accessibility check' as a standing rule applied to every story — so a story for 'add a new filter dropdown' doesn't need to explicitly re-state the accessibility requirement in its acceptance criteria; it's covered automatically by the DoD, while the story's own acceptance criteria focus narrowly on what the filter actually does.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** Why might a team keep an accessibility standard in the Definition of Done rather than writing it into every story's acceptance criteria?

**(A) The DoD applies uniformly and automatically to every story, so a standing quality bar doesn't depend on someone remembering to re-state it each time**

\(B\) Acceptance criteria cannot technically contain any non-functional requirements

\(C\) Definition of Done is set once by legal and can never be edited by the team

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a 4-item Definition of Done for a team (real or hypothetical) and explain why each item belongs there rather than being repeated in every story's acceptance criteria.

**Lecture 251 acceptance criteria**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a real acceptance-criteria dispute at story review and resolve it by tightening the written criteria.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Acceptance-criteria disputes at review time are common and almost always trace back to a criterion that was written ambiguously enough to support two honest readings — the fix isn't to argue about who's 'right' in the moment, it's to recognize the criterion itself was underspecified and rewrite it more precisely for next time. A frequent ambiguity trap is relative or subjective language ('loads quickly,' 'looks clean,' 'works well') that sounds concrete when written but turns out to mean different things to different reviewers. Treating every dispute as a signal to improve the next story's criteria-writing, rather than as a one-off disagreement to argue through, is what actually improves a team's review process over sprints. |
| **Worked example**      | A story's criterion says 'the page should load quickly.' At review, the PM thinks 3 seconds is acceptable; engineering thought under 1 second was the bar, since that's their internal performance budget. Rather than arguing about whose definition of 'quickly' wins, the team rewrites the criterion for future stories to always specify a number: 'page loads in under 1.5 seconds on a throttled 4G connection,' eliminating the ambiguity for every future story that touches load time.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** When a review dispute arises from an ambiguous acceptance criterion like 'should look clean,' what is the recommended fix?

**(A) Rewrite the criterion with specific, measurable language for future stories, rather than just arguing over the current one's interpretation**

\(B\) Escalate the disagreement to the CTO for a binding ruling

\(C\) Mark the story as done anyway, since disputes at review don't affect the sprint burndown

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Find or imagine an acceptance criterion written with vague/subjective language, and rewrite it to be specific and measurable enough to prevent a review dispute.

**Lecture 252 acceptance criteria**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Audit a sprint's worth of stories for acceptance-criteria quality and identify systemic gaps before they reach QA.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | Running a quality audit across a whole sprint's acceptance criteria — rather than checking them one at a time as they come up — surfaces systemic patterns that individual story review misses: maybe every story this sprint covers the happy path but none specify error states, or maybe accessibility is inconsistently covered across stories that should all be bound by the same DoD. This audit step closes the loop on everything taught in this run: Given/When/Then structure, the DoD/acceptance-criteria distinction, and precise non-subjective language all get checked systematically rather than story-by-story. Catching a systemic gap (like 'nobody on this team writes error-state criteria') before QA finds it story-by-story saves far more time than fixing each instance individually after the fact. |
| **Worked example**      | Auditing 8 stories in a sprint, a PM notices none of them specify what happens on a network failure during form submission — a systemic gap, not a one-off oversight. Rather than fixing each story individually, the PM adds 'handle network/API failure gracefully' to the team's Definition of Done going forward, closing the gap for every future story at once instead of patching it story-by-story.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main benefit of auditing acceptance criteria across a whole sprint's worth of stories at once, rather than reviewing each story individually?

**(A) It surfaces systemic, repeated gaps (like missing error-state coverage) that can be fixed once at the process level instead of story-by-story**

\(B\) It eliminates the need for a sprint retrospective

\(C\) It automatically recalculates story points for the whole sprint

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick (or imagine) 4-5 stories from one sprint and audit their acceptance criteria for one systemic gap (e.g., missing error states, vague language), then propose one process-level fix.

**Lecture 253 sprint planning**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Run a sprint-planning meeting that sets a sprint goal and pulls a realistically sized set of stories against team capacity.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Sprint planning has two distinct outputs that are easy to conflate: a sprint goal (a short, qualitative statement of what this sprint is meant to achieve, giving the team a shared sense of purpose beyond just 'complete these tickets') and the actual set of stories pulled from the backlog to achieve it, sized against the team's realistic capacity (accounting for known time off, meetings, and support work, not just raw headcount times five days). A team that skips the sprint goal and just pulls stories top-down from the backlog loses the ability to make in-sprint tradeoffs — if something unexpected comes up mid-sprint, a team with a clear goal can judge 'does dropping this item still let us hit the goal,' while a team with no goal has no principled way to decide what to cut. |
| **Worked example**      | Sprint goal: 'Make checkout reliable for mobile users.' Pulled stories: fix a mobile-specific payment-form bug, add retry logic for flaky connections, improve error messaging on failed payments — all stories support that one goal, sized against the team's actual capacity of 32 person-hours after accounting for one engineer's planned day off. Mid-sprint, when an urgent unrelated request comes in, the team can clearly say 'that doesn't serve this sprint's goal' and defer it instead.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a sprint goal matter beyond just the list of stories pulled into the sprint?

**(A) It gives the team a shared purpose that lets them make principled tradeoffs if something unexpected comes up mid-sprint**

\(B\) It replaces the need to size stories against team capacity

\(C\) It is required paperwork for Scrum.org certification, with no team-level benefit

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a one-sentence sprint goal for a hypothetical 2-week sprint, and list 3 stories that would directly serve that goal (and one you'd leave out because it doesn't).

**Lecture 254 sprint planning**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply story-point estimation (via Planning Poker or T-shirt sizing) and explain why relative sizing works better than absolute time estimates.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Story points estimate relative size/complexity/uncertainty rather than absolute hours, which sounds like a small distinction but solves a real problem: different engineers take different absolute time on the same task, but a team usually agrees reasonably well on relative comparisons ('this is about twice as complex as that other story we did last sprint'). Planning Poker formalizes this by having each team member privately estimate a story on a Fibonacci-like scale (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13...) and reveal simultaneously, which prevents anchoring (the first person to say a number out loud otherwise biases everyone else) and surfaces hidden disagreement — if estimates range from 2 to 13 for the same story, that gap itself is valuable information revealing the team doesn't share an understanding of the work, which needs a conversation before planning proceeds, not an average taken and moved past. |
| **Worked example**      | In a Planning Poker round, four engineers privately estimate a story and reveal 2, 3, 13, and 2. The outlier isn't just averaged away — discussion reveals the engineer who said 13 knows about a legacy data-migration complication the others didn't factor in. That conversation, triggered by the estimate spread itself, surfaces real information the team needed before committing to the sprint.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a wide spread of individual estimates in Planning Poker (e.g., 2, 3, 13, 2) matter more than just averaging them?

**(A) The spread itself signals a disagreement in understanding of the work that needs to be discussed, often surfacing hidden complexity**

\(B\) A spread that wide means the story must be removed from the sprint entirely

\(C\) Fibonacci-scale estimates are only valid when every team member agrees before any discussion

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Run a mini Planning Poker exercise (even solo, imagining 3 different team perspectives) on 2 stories using a 1/2/3/5/8/13 scale, and note any estimate disagreement and what it might reveal.

**Lecture 255 sprint planning**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Diagnose and recover from a sprint going off-track mid-sprint, using the daily standup as the detection mechanism.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | A sprint going off-track is normal, not a failure in itself — what matters is detecting it early, and the daily standup exists specifically for this: each team member briefly states what they did, what they're doing next, and critically, what's blocking them, which surfaces problems while there's still time to adjust rather than discovering at sprint review that half the sprint didn't ship. A standup that turns into a status report to the PM (rather than a quick peer-to-peer sync) misses blockers, because people under-report problems to someone evaluating them but surface them readily to peers who might help solve it. Mid-sprint recovery options once a blocker surfaces include re-negotiating sprint scope against the sprint goal (dropping a lower-priority story to protect the goal), swarming (temporarily reassigning people to unblock the critical item), or escalating a cross-team dependency immediately rather than waiting for it to resolve itself. |
| **Worked example**      | On day 3 of a 2-week sprint, a standup surfaces that a story is blocked on an external API team's untested endpoint. Instead of waiting and hoping, the PM escalates to the external team immediately, and the engineer temporarily swarms onto another in-sprint story so the days aren't wasted — by day 5, if the blocker still isn't resolved, the team makes an explicit call to drop that story and protect the sprint goal with the remaining stories instead.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Why might a daily standup that functions as a 'status report to the PM' fail to surface real blockers?

**(A) People tend to under-report problems to someone evaluating them, while they'd surface the same blocker readily to peers who could help**

\(B\) Standups are legally required to be silent unless the PM asks a direct question

\(C\) Status-report-style standups take longer than 15 minutes on average

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Describe a real or hypothetical mid-sprint blocker and walk through which recovery option (scope renegotiation, swarming, or escalation) you'd use and why.

**Lecture 256 sprint planning**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Run a sprint review and retrospective, distinguishing what each ceremony is actually for.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | Sprint review and sprint retrospective are both end-of-sprint ceremonies but serve entirely different purposes, and conflating them wastes both: sprint review is about the product — demoing completed work to stakeholders, gathering their feedback, and deciding what that feedback means for the backlog — it's externally facing and focused on what was built. Sprint retrospective is about the process — the team alone (no outside stakeholders) reflecting on how the sprint went, what worked, what didn't, and committing to one or two specific process changes for next sprint. A retro that turns into another product demo wastes the one regular opportunity a team has to actually improve how it works, and a review cluttered with internal process complaints wastes stakeholders' time on something that isn't their concern. |
| **Worked example**      | At sprint review, stakeholders see a demo of the new checkout retry logic and raise a new edge case the PM adds to the backlog. At the separate retrospective immediately after (stakeholders not present), the team identifies that daily standups ran long all sprint because of unrelated tangents, and commits to a specific process fix: a visible 2-minute timer per person starting next sprint. Mixing these two conversations into one meeting would have buried the process fix under product feedback.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** What is the key difference in purpose between sprint review and sprint retrospective?

**(A) Review is externally-facing, focused on product feedback from stakeholders; retrospective is internal, focused on improving team process**

\(B\) Review happens before the sprint starts; retrospective happens after

\(C\) Retrospective is optional while review is mandatory under the Scrum Guide

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write one sprint-review talking point (product feedback to gather) and one separate sprint-retrospective commitment (a specific process change) for a hypothetical sprint.

**Lecture 257 delivery tracking**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Read a burndown chart to assess whether a sprint is on track, ahead, or at risk.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | A burndown chart plots remaining work (in story points or hours) against time remaining in the sprint, with an ideal line showing steady, even progress — the value of the chart is in how the actual line deviates from that ideal, not the ideal line itself. A line tracking close to ideal suggests the sprint is on track; a line that's flat for several days then drops sharply right before sprint end is a red flag even if the sprint technically 'finished on time,' because it usually means work was rushed or under-tested at the end rather than steadily verified throughout; a line trending consistently above ideal (work not being completed as fast as planned) signals a risk that should trigger a mid-sprint conversation, not just be noted after the fact at review. A PM's job with a burndown chart is pattern-reading, not just checking if the line eventually reaches zero. |
| **Worked example**      | A sprint's burndown shows almost no movement for the first 7 of 10 days, then a steep drop to zero on the last day. Even though the sprint technically 'burned down to zero,' the PM flags this pattern at retro — it likely means work was marked done in a rush at the end rather than genuinely completed and tested throughout, which is a quality risk worth investigating even though the chart superficially looks successful.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** A burndown chart stays nearly flat for most of the sprint, then drops sharply to zero on the final day. What should this pattern raise as a concern?

**(A) Work was likely rushed and under-tested near the end rather than completed steadily, even though the sprint nominally finished on time**

\(B\) The sprint goal was set too easily and should be made harder next time

\(C\) The chart indicates a tooling bug and should be ignored

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Sketch (describe in words or draw) a burndown pattern for a sprint that technically finished but had a concerning shape, and explain what risk that shape would signal.

**Lecture 258 delivery tracking**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Track flow metrics (cycle time and throughput) across multiple sprints to diagnose a team's delivery health beyond any single sprint's burndown.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | While a burndown chart tracks one sprint in isolation, cycle time (how long an item takes from start-of-work to done) and throughput (how many items complete per sprint) tracked across many sprints reveal trends a single sprint's chart can't show — a gradually lengthening average cycle time across six sprints might indicate growing technical debt or unaddressed process friction, even if every individual sprint's burndown looked fine in isolation. These flow metrics also help answer a question stakeholders constantly ask ('when will X be done') with actual historical evidence instead of optimistic guessing — if the team's items have historically averaged a 6-day cycle time, that's a far more defensible estimate than a fresh guess with no track record behind it. |
| **Worked example**      | A team's burndown charts have looked fine for six straight sprints, but tracking cycle time across those same sprints shows average time-to-complete creeping from 3 days to 7 days. That trend, invisible in any single sprint's burndown, prompts the PM to investigate and finds a code-review bottleneck building up as the only two senior reviewers got pulled onto unrelated urgent work — a problem no single sprint's chart would have surfaced on its own.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why might cycle time tracked across multiple sprints reveal a problem that individual sprint burndown charts miss?

**(A) A burndown resets each sprint and can't show a slow, cumulative trend like steadily lengthening completion time across many sprints**

\(B\) Cycle time can only be measured using proprietary enterprise software

\(C\) Burndown charts and cycle time measure the exact same thing, just with different units

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** If you have access to real sprint data, calculate average cycle time for 2-3 recent items; if not, describe what a lengthening cycle-time trend across sprints would suggest is happening on a team.

**Lecture 259 delivery tracking**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a simple stakeholder delivery-status report that communicates progress and risk honestly without burying it in jargon.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Translating sprint-level tracking data (burndown, cycle time, blockers) into a stakeholder-facing status update requires a different register than the team's internal ceremonies — stakeholders generally need three things stated plainly: what shipped or is on track to ship, what's at risk and why (in plain terms, not 'velocity variance'), and what decision, if any, is needed from them. A common failure mode is a status report that's either so technical it obscures real risk behind jargon, or so vague and upbeat ('things are going well!') that a genuine problem doesn't surface until it's too late for stakeholders to help or adjust expectations. Honest, plain-language risk communication, even when the news is bad, builds more stakeholder trust over time than consistently optimistic reports that later turn out to have hidden a slip. |
| **Worked example**      | A status update reads: 'Checkout reliability fixes: 3 of 4 stories shipped on schedule. The 4th (retry logic for international payments) is delayed because we discovered the third-party processor's test environment doesn't match production behavior — we need 3 extra days and are not asking for scope cuts elsewhere.' That's plain, specific, names the real cause, and states exactly what's needed — not 'things are progressing' and not a jargon-dense velocity report.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main risk of a stakeholder status report that's vague and uniformly upbeat even when a real problem exists?

**(A) A genuine problem won't surface until it's too late for stakeholders to help, adjust expectations, or make a needed decision**

\(B\) It violates data-privacy regulations around sprint metrics

\(C\) It causes the burndown chart to recalculate incorrectly

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a short (3-4 sentence) stakeholder status update for a hypothetical delayed deliverable, stating plainly what shipped, what's at risk and why, and what decision (if any) you need from them.

**Lecture 260 Month 15 Examination**

*Year 2 · Month 15 · Agile + Project Planning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Demonstrate command of this month's agile and project-planning concepts across the full backlog-to-delivery workflow.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | This month covered the operational core of agile product delivery: maintaining a healthy, groomed, DEEP backlog distinct from a roadmap and sprint backlog (241-244), writing user stories with INVEST-quality and vertical slicing (245-248), writing precise Given/When/Then acceptance criteria distinct from a team's Definition of Done (249-252), running sprint planning with a real sprint goal and relative story-point estimation (253-256), and tracking delivery health through burndown charts, multi-sprint flow metrics, and honest stakeholder status reporting (257-259). The throughline is that agile ceremonies and artifacts aren't bureaucratic overhead for its own sake — each one (grooming, INVEST, Given/When/Then, sprint goals, burndown, retro) exists to catch a specific, predictable failure mode (stale backlogs, oversized stories, ambiguous 'done,' scope drift, rushed late-sprint work, repeated hidden problems) before it becomes expensive. As with every month, the internal passing bar for this course's own assessment is 80%. |
| **Worked example**      | A student reviewing the month traces one feature from backlog to delivery: it starts as a groomed backlog item (241-244), becomes an INVEST-checked, vertically-sliced user story with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria (245-252), gets pulled into a sprint with a clear sprint goal and a Planning-Poker point estimate (253-256), and its progress is tracked via burndown during the sprint and reported honestly to stakeholders if it's at risk (257-259) — the same evidence-and-process discipline from Month 14's discovery work, now applied to delivery instead of discovery.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** What is the common thread connecting backlog grooming, INVEST stories, Given/When/Then criteria, sprint goals, and burndown tracking as taught this month?

**(A) Each one exists to catch a specific, predictable delivery failure mode early, before it becomes expensive to fix**

\(B\) Each one is a legal requirement under the Scrum Guide's certification body

\(C\) Each one applies only to teams larger than 20 engineers

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Trace one real or hypothetical feature through the full backlog-to-delivery pipeline from this month (backlog item, user story, acceptance criteria, sprint goal, tracking), writing one line per stage.

**Month 16 Roadmaps + Metrics**

*Allocation: 16 hours \| 16 lectures \| Level: Intermediate*

**Lecture 261 Roadmaps**

*Year 2 · Month 16 · Roadmaps + Metrics · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain what a product roadmap is and why it communicates direction rather than a fixed delivery date.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | A product roadmap is a living plan that shows where a product is headed and why, not a shipping schedule with guaranteed dates. The now/next/later format is the standard beginner structure: 'Now' holds what the team is actively building, validated and scoped; 'Next' holds what is likely up after that, still being shaped; 'Later' holds directional bets that may change as you learn more. This format deliberately avoids hard dates for Next and Later because committing to dates before discovery is done creates false certainty and erodes stakeholder trust when reality shifts. A roadmap earns its place by answering three questions for any reader: what are we solving, in roughly what order, and why — the 'why' tied to a problem or outcome, not a feature name. |
| **Worked example**      | A fintech startup building a budgeting app puts 'Bank account linking (Plaid integration)' in Now because it is scoped and in development. 'Shared household budgets' sits in Next because the team has early signal from support tickets but hasn't scoped it. 'AI spending insights' sits in Later as a directional bet tied to the outcome 'help users feel in control of spending,' with no committed timeline. The roadmap itself is a single horizontal document the whole company can read in two minutes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the now/next/later format intentionally avoid assigning fixed calendar dates to the 'Next' and 'Later' columns?

**(A) Because dates that far out are almost always wrong once discovery and scoping happen, and stating them as fact damages trust when they slip**

\(B\) Because engineering teams refuse to work without a Gantt chart

\(C\) Because only paid roadmapping software can display real dates

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick a product you use daily and sort five features you'd want built into Now, Next, and Later, writing one sentence of justification for each placement.

**Lecture 262 Roadmaps**

*Year 2 · Month 16 · Roadmaps + Metrics · 1 guided hour + homework*
