| **Worked example**      | A travel-booking app defines the token color-brand-primary = \#1A73E8 once in its token file. Every 'Book now' button, every active tab indicator, and every link color references that token instead of the literal hex value. When the brand team updates the color to \#0F5FD1 for a rebrand, one token change propagates instantly across every button, tab, and link in both the Figma library and the production codebase.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** What specific problem does replacing hard-coded hex values with a single named color token solve?

**(A) It eliminates the need to hunt down and manually update every place that color was typed literally when the brand color changes, preventing missed instances and visual drift**

\(B\) It makes the color impossible to ever change again once it's set

\(C\) It allows designers to skip choosing colors altogether

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Open a product you use, pick one color and one spacing value you see repeated across several screens, and write what you'd name each as a token (e.g. color-brand-primary, space-16).

**Lecture 278 Tokens**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain token tiers (global, alias/semantic, component-specific) and when to use each.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | Mature token systems organize tokens into tiers rather than one flat list. Global tokens (sometimes called 'core' or 'option' tokens) are raw values with no meaning attached — blue-500 = \#1A73E8, space-4 = 4px — just a palette and scale. Alias (semantic) tokens map a global token to a purpose — color-text-link = blue-500, color-background-danger = red-600 — so the name describes what the value is used for, not what it literally is. Component-specific tokens go one level deeper, scoping a semantic token to one component — button-primary-background = color-background-brand — which lets you change a single component's styling without touching the semantic layer everyone else depends on. The payoff of this layering is that a rebrand only touches global tokens, a light/dark theme swap only touches semantic tokens, and a one-off component tweak only touches component tokens — each layer of change is contained to its own blast radius. |
| **Worked example**      | A dark-mode rollout for a news app doesn't touch any global token (blue-500 stays blue-500) or any component token. It only remaps the semantic layer: color-background-page flips from referencing gray-50 to referencing gray-900, and color-text-primary flips from gray-900 to gray-50. Every component built on semantic tokens re-themes automatically, with zero changes to the components themselves.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** In a three-tier token system, which tier would you change to implement a dark theme without touching individual components?

**(A) The semantic (alias) tier, by remapping tokens like color-background-page and color-text-primary to different global values**

\(B\) The global tier, by deleting and recreating every raw color value

\(C\) The component tier, by manually re-styling every single component one at a time

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take the token you named last lecture and write its three-tier version: a global value, a semantic alias that names its purpose, and one component-specific token that uses the semantic alias.

**Lecture 279 Tokens**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a starter token set for a specific product and justify each naming and tier decision.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Building a token set from scratch starts with an audit: screenshot or list every distinct color, spacing value, font size, and corner radius actually in use across the existing product, because an un-audited token system just invents a new mess from nothing. From that audit, you collapse near-duplicate values into a smaller deliberate scale (most products need far fewer unique spacing or color values than they currently have scattered across screens), assign global tokens to the surviving values, then layer semantic tokens over the globals for every purpose the product actually needs (text, background, border, status colors like success/warning/danger). The discipline here is restraint — a token set with 200 color tokens defeats the purpose of having a system at all, and a well-scoped product usually needs a spacing scale of 6-10 steps and a color palette of a few dozen tokens across all tiers combined. |
| **Worked example**      | Auditing a food-delivery app turns up 14 different shades of gray used for text across the app, most of them accidental near-duplicates from different designers. The token-building exercise collapses these into 4 deliberate global grays (gray-100 through gray-900 by steps), then defines semantic tokens color-text-primary, color-text-secondary, color-text-disabled, and color-text-inverse mapped onto those four globals — reducing 14 inconsistent values to 4 globals and 4 clear semantic purposes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why does auditing existing screens for actual color and spacing values matter before defining a new token set?

**(A) It reveals how many near-duplicate values are already in use so they can be deliberately collapsed into a smaller, intentional scale instead of the token system inheriting the same inconsistency**

\(B\) Auditing is only useful for accessibility compliance, not for token design

\(C\) It is unnecessary because every product needs exactly the same token set regardless of its current state

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Audit five screens of a real app for their color values (using a screenshot and color picker, or browser dev tools) and propose a collapsed set of 4-6 global color tokens that could replace what you found.

**Lecture 280 components**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define a design-system component and explain the atomic-design hierarchy it typically sits within.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | A design-system component is a reusable, documented UI building block — a button, an input field, a card — built once in a shared library and then instanced everywhere it's needed, rather than redrawn from scratch on every screen. Components are commonly organized by atomic design's hierarchy: atoms are the smallest indivisible pieces (a single button, an icon, a label), molecules combine a few atoms into a small functional unit (a search bar is an input atom plus a button atom), and organisms combine molecules and atoms into a larger, self-contained section (a full navigation bar, a product card with image, title, price, and a button). This hierarchy matters practically because it tells a team where to intervene: fixing a button's corner radius at the atom level fixes it everywhere that atom is used, while a layout problem in a product listing page is an organism-level concern. |
| **Worked example**      | An e-commerce design system defines the atom Button (primary/secondary/text variants), the molecule Quantity Stepper (a minus button atom + a number input atom + a plus button atom), and the organism Product Card (a product image, the stepper molecule, a price label atom, and an 'Add to cart' button atom all composed together). Updating the base Button atom's hover state instantly updates it inside the stepper, inside the product card, and everywhere else a button appears.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a 'search bar' typically classified as a molecule rather than an atom in atomic design?

**(A) It is composed of two or more smaller atomic pieces (an input field and a button) working together, rather than being an indivisible single element**

\(B\) Molecules are simply components that use the color blue

\(C\) The classification is arbitrary and has no bearing on how the design system is maintained

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick an app and classify five of its UI pieces into atoms, molecules, or organisms, explaining your reasoning for one borderline case.

**Lecture 281 components**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain component anatomy — props, instances, and the master/instance relationship.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | A component in a design tool or codebase has a 'master' or 'main component' definition and any number of 'instances' placed across different screens, where every instance inherits the master's structure and styling but can override specific properties exposed as props (in Figma, these are usually called component properties; in code, they're function/class props). This master/instance relationship is what makes systemic updates possible: editing the master's padding updates every instance across every file simultaneously, while an instance-level override (swapping an icon, changing text) stays local to that one instance and doesn't affect siblings. Understanding which properties a component exposes as overridable props versus which are locked at the master level is a key design decision — expose too little and the component can't flex to real use cases; expose too much and the component loses its consistency guarantees. |
| **Worked example**      | A Card component's master defines fixed structure (image slot, title slot, consistent padding and corner radius) but exposes three props: hasBadge (boolean), ctaLabel (text), and size (variant: compact/default). A product team places forty instances of this Card across the app, each instance locally overriding the text and badge visibility, but none of them can override the padding or corner radius because those aren't exposed as props — keeping every card visually consistent even as its content varies.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** If a component's padding is locked at the master level and not exposed as a prop, what happens when a designer tries to change the padding on one specific instance?

**(A) They cannot change it on that instance alone — padding stays consistent across every instance, since only properties exposed as props can be overridden per instance**

\(B\) The padding changes for that instance only, with no effect on the master

\(C\) The entire component library breaks and must be rebuilt

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take a component from your earlier atomic-design classification and list which of its properties should be locked at the master level versus exposed as overridable props, with a one-line reason for each.

**Lecture 282 components**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a simple component (a button or card) following master/instance and prop-exposure principles.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | Building a well-formed component starts with defining its fixed structure — the parts that never change regardless of context, like a button's padding, corner radius, and font — then deciding the minimum set of props needed to cover real use cases without over-exposing control. A good process is to look at every actual instance the component needs to support across the real product first (primary action, destructive action, disabled state, icon-only variant) and derive the prop list from that survey, rather than guessing at props in the abstract. Once built, the component should be tested by creating several instances with different prop combinations and checking that every combination still looks and behaves correctly — a component that breaks visually when two props are combined in an untested way isn't finished yet. |
| **Worked example**      | Building a Button component: survey of real use cases across the app reveals primary, secondary, and destructive variants; a disabled state; and an optional leading icon. The resulting component exposes props variant (primary/secondary/destructive), disabled (boolean), and icon (optional slot) — four props total, derived directly from the survey, not invented in isolation. Testing all combinations catches that the destructive variant's text was unreadable when disabled was also true, which gets fixed before the component ships to the library.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why does surveying real use cases across the actual product come before deciding a new component's prop list?

**(A) It grounds the prop list in what the product genuinely needs, rather than guessing at hypothetical options that may not match real use cases or may miss ones that matter**

\(B\) Surveying is a formality with no effect on which props end up being useful

\(C\) Props should always be decided before any use cases are reviewed, never after

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Design and document one component's full prop list (name each prop, its possible values, and the real use case each one supports) for a component you identified earlier in the month.

**Lecture 283 variants**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define component variants and explain the difference between a boolean prop and a variant prop.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | A variant is a predefined set of mutually exclusive versions of a component — a button's variant prop might be primary/secondary/text, where exactly one option applies at a time — distinct from a boolean prop, which is simply on/off (disabled: true/false) and can combine freely with any variant. Variants exist because many real differences between component versions aren't just a style toggle but a meaningfully different combination of structure and styling together, and grouping those combinations as named variants (rather than as several independent boolean toggles that the designer has to combine correctly every time) prevents invalid or nonsensical combinations from being assembled by accident. The design decision of whether something should be a variant or a separate boolean usually comes down to whether the options are mutually exclusive (variant) or independently toggleable (boolean). |
| **Worked example**      | A Badge component uses a variant prop status (success/warning/danger/neutral) because exactly one status applies at a time and each status carries a different background color, icon, and text color together as a bundle. It separately uses a boolean prop hasIcon, because showing or hiding the icon is independent of which status color is chosen — any status can combine with hasIcon true or false.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Why would a design system use a variant prop instead of three separate boolean props for a badge's success/warning/danger states?

**(A) The states are mutually exclusive — only one should ever be true at once — and a variant prevents the invalid combination of, say, both success and danger booleans being true simultaneously**

\(B\) Variants and boolean props are functionally identical with no practical difference

\(C\) Variant props are only used for components that have no color

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For a component you've already documented, identify one property that should be a variant (mutually exclusive options) and one that should be a boolean (independent toggle), explaining why each belongs in its category.

**Lecture 284 variants**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explore variant properties more deeply, including nested variants and variant combination explosion.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | As components grow more capable, their variant sets can multiply combinatorially — a button with a 3-option style variant, a 3-option size variant, and a 2-option state (default/disabled) produces 18 total combinations that all need to look correct, and adding one more 3-option variant triples that to 54. This 'combination explosion' is a real design-system risk: it becomes impractical to manually check every combination, and some tools (like Figma's variant grid) visually degrade past a few dozen combinations. The practical mitigation is to separate truly independent properties into separate props (as covered last lecture) so the tool can compute combinations systematically, to intentionally restrict a variant's option count to what's genuinely needed rather than every theoretically possible value, and to spot-check combinations programmatically or via a documented test matrix rather than eyeballing a giant grid. |
| **Worked example**      | A design system's Input component has variant properties for state (default/focus/error/disabled — 4 options), size (small/medium/large — 3 options), and hasLabel (boolean — 2 options), producing 24 total combinations. Rather than manually building and checking 24 separate layouts, the team builds the component so state, size, and hasLabel are structurally independent (each affects a different visual property with no interaction effects), then spot-checks only the combinations most likely to interact badly, like error state combined with small size, where the error message text might overflow.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** What is 'combination explosion' in the context of component variants?

**(A) The rapid multiplication of total variant combinations as more independent variant properties are added, making full manual verification impractical**

\(B\) A bug that occurs only when a component has zero variants defined

\(C\) A feature that automatically deletes unused variants from the library

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Calculate the total variant combinations for a component with three variant properties of your own design (state your option counts for each), and identify which two or three combinations you'd prioritize for manual testing.

**Lecture 285 variants**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a variant set for a real component and document the rationale for each option.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | Building a variant set well means starting from the smallest number of options that cover genuine product needs, documenting why each option exists (not just what it looks like), and explicitly marking which combinations are unsupported or discouraged if the component doesn't structurally prevent them. A variant set without stated rationale tends to accumulate options nobody can justify years later — someone adds a 'large-compact' size variant for one one-off screen, and it quietly becomes tech debt nobody dares delete because nobody knows who depends on it. Documenting rationale alongside each variant (even briefly, like 'small: used in dense data tables only') gives future maintainers the context to safely prune or extend the set later. |
| **Worked example**      | Building a Tag component's variant set: size (small — 'used only inside data table cells where vertical space is tight'; default — 'used everywhere else'), and color (neutral, info, success, warning, danger — 'maps to the same five-state system used by Badge and Alert components for visual consistency across the library'). The documentation explicitly notes that color and size combine freely with no unsupported pairs, because both properties are visually independent by design.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Why is it useful to document the rationale behind each variant option rather than just its visual appearance?

**(A) It gives future maintainers the context needed to safely prune, extend, or justify keeping an option, preventing unexplained variants from accumulating as unremovable tech debt**

\(B\) Rationale documentation has no practical use once a component ships

\(C\) Design tools automatically generate rationale, so writing it manually is redundant

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write the full variant documentation (each option plus a one-sentence rationale) for a component you've built this month, and flag any combination of its variants that should be considered unsupported.

**Lecture 286 states**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define the standard interactive states a component must support and why each exists.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | Interactive components need to visually communicate a consistent set of states regardless of what the component is: default (resting appearance), hover (pointer is over it, desktop only), focus (keyboard or assistive-tech focus has landed on it — critical for accessibility, not optional), active/pressed (currently being clicked or tapped), disabled (not currently interactive, visually de-emphasized), and often error or loading for form-related components. Each state exists to answer a different question for the user: hover and focus both signal 'this is interactive and currently targeted,' but through different input modalities, while disabled communicates 'this exists but isn't available right now' as opposed to being hidden entirely, which would remove context about why an action isn't available. Skipping the focus state is a common and serious accessibility failure, because keyboard and screen-reader users have no other way to see where they currently are on the page. |
| **Worked example**      | A design system's Button component defines all six states explicitly: default (base styling), hover (slightly darker background, desktop only), focus (a visible 2px outline ring, meeting WCAG's focus-visible requirement), active (background darkens further and the button scales down 2% to feel 'pressed'), disabled (50% opacity, cursor shows not-allowed, no hover/active behavior triggers), and loading (spinner replaces label, button temporarily non-interactive). Each state is a distinct documented artboard in the library, not an afterthought bolted on at implementation time.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a visible focus state considered a non-optional accessibility requirement rather than a nice-to-have, unlike hover?

**(A) Keyboard and screen-reader users have no mouse to produce a hover effect, so focus is their only visual way to know which element on the page is currently selected**

\(B\) Focus states are purely decorative and exist only for visual variety

\(C\) Hover states are required by accessibility standards while focus states are optional

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Audit a component in an app you use for all six states (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading/error if applicable) using keyboard Tab navigation to check focus specifically, and note any state that's missing or broken.

**Lecture 287 states**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply state design to a real component and critique common state-design mistakes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | A common state-design mistake is defining hover and active states but skipping focus entirely, which works fine for mouse users and silently breaks the experience for keyboard and screen-reader users — this is the single most frequent accessibility gap found in component audits. A second mistake is making the disabled state visually too similar to the default state (a tiny opacity change that's easy to miss), which leaves users unsure why a button isn't responding to clicks. A third mistake is state-styling that only changes color, which fails users with color-vision deficiencies — a good state design changes at least one non-color property (border, icon, text) alongside any color shift, consistent with WCAG's guidance that color alone should never be the only signal of state. |
| **Worked example**      | An audit of a checkout form's 'Place order' button finds three mistakes: no visible focus ring at all (keyboard users can't tell the button is selected before pressing Enter), the disabled state only drops opacity from 100% to 90% (barely perceptible), and the error state on the adjacent card-number field is signaled only by the border turning red (invisible to users with red-green color blindness). The fix adds a 2px focus outline, drops disabled opacity to 50% with a not-allowed cursor, and adds an error icon plus text message alongside the red border.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why is color-only error signaling (a red border with no icon or text) considered a design-states mistake?

**(A) Users with color-vision deficiencies may not perceive the color change at all, so the error has no way to communicate itself to them without an additional non-color cue**

\(B\) Red is universally recognized by all users as positive feedback

\(C\) Color-only signaling is a mistake only on mobile devices, never on desktop

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Find a component with a state-design flaw (missing focus, weak disabled contrast, or color-only error signaling) in a real product, screenshot or describe it, and specify the exact fix you'd make.

**Lecture 288 naming**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Establish naming conventions for tokens and components and explain why consistency matters.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | A naming convention is a consistent, predictable pattern for naming tokens and components so that anyone browsing the library — designer or engineer — can guess an item's name correctly before searching for it, and can tell at a glance what category something belongs to. A common token naming pattern follows category-purpose-variant-state, such as color-text-primary or color-background-danger-hover, read left to right from broadest to most specific. Component names typically follow a category/name/variant hierarchy in file or folder structure, like Button/Primary or Form/Input/Error. The payoff of a disciplined convention isn't aesthetic — it directly reduces duplicate token creation (someone who can't find color-text-primary because it's actually named TextColor1 will just make a new, redundant token), and it keeps design and code vocabularies aligned so a developer reading a Figma spec and a codebase variable name recognize them as the same thing. |
| **Worked example**      | A library renames inconsistent legacy tokens — TextColor1, textGray, color_dark — into a single pattern: color-text-primary, color-text-secondary, color-text-disabled. A developer who previously had to ask a designer 'which gray is this supposed to be' can now infer the correct token name directly from the design file label, matching the corresponding CSS variable --color-text-primary without a lookup.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main practical cost of an inconsistent token naming convention like mixing TextColor1, textGray, and color_dark in the same library?

**(A) People can't reliably guess or find the right existing token, so they end up creating redundant duplicate tokens instead of reusing what already exists**

\(B\) Inconsistent naming has no real cost as long as every token still has some name

\(C\) It only affects how the library looks when sorted alphabetically

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Rename five inconsistently-named tokens or components you can find in a real design file or codebase into one consistent category-purpose-variant pattern.

**Lecture 289 naming**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Run a naming audit and critique session on a shared component library.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | A naming audit is a deliberate pass through an existing library looking specifically for naming problems: synonyms used inconsistently for the same concept (primary vs. main vs. brand all referring to the same color), ambiguous names that don't reveal purpose (Color1, Blue2), and names that leak implementation detail that will become wrong later (color-blue-button, which breaks the moment that button becomes green). The fix for each category differs — synonyms get consolidated to one chosen term used everywhere going forward, ambiguous names get renamed to state their purpose, and implementation-leaking names get renamed to describe function instead of current appearance, because a name describing what something looks like today becomes a lie the first time that appearance changes. |
| **Worked example**      | A naming audit of a library finds the token color-blue-link used for every hyperlink color — a name that leaks today's color into the name itself. When the brand later shifts link color to purple, every use of color-blue-link is now a lie nobody wants to touch. The audit renames it to color-text-link (describing function: 'the color of link text') before the rebrand happens, so the rebrand only requires changing the token's value, not hunting down and renaming every reference.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a token named color-blue-link considered a naming problem, independent of whether blue is currently the correct color?

**(A) The name describes the current appearance rather than the token's function, so it becomes misleading the moment the actual color changes to anything other than blue**

\(B\) Blue is an invalid color choice for links in any design system

\(C\) Token names are never allowed to contain color words under any circumstance

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Audit a real component library or token set (your own work or a public one like Material Design) for one synonym problem, one ambiguous name, and one implementation-leaking name, and propose a fixed name for each.

**Lecture 290 documentation**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain what a design-system documentation page must contain and why each section exists.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | Good component documentation typically includes: a short description of the component's purpose and when to use it (and explicitly, when not to), its anatomy (labeled diagram of its parts), its full prop/variant list with every option explained, usage guidelines (do's and don'ts, often shown as side-by-side correct/incorrect examples), accessibility notes (keyboard behavior, ARIA roles, contrast requirements), and code snippets for engineers implementing it. Each section serves a different reader and a different moment of need: a designer deciding whether to use this component at all reads the purpose and do's/don'ts; an engineer implementing it reads the prop list and code snippet; someone doing an accessibility pass reads the accessibility notes specifically. Documentation that skips the 'when not to use this' guidance is a common gap, because teams often learn a component's limits the hard way, by someone misusing it in production first. |
| **Worked example**      | The documentation page for a design system's Modal component includes a 'When not to use' callout stating modals shouldn't be used for non-critical, dismissible info (use a toast instead) or for flows requiring more than two steps (use a full page instead), directly preventing the common misuse of stuffing a multi-step wizard into a modal that the team had seen happen twice before writing this guidance.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why does good component documentation explicitly include guidance on when NOT to use a component, not just how to use it?

**(A) It prevents common misuse that teams typically only discover after it has already happened in production, by stating the component's limits up front**

\(B\) Documentation is required by law to list every possible misuse

\(C\) Listing non-uses makes the documentation longer, which is the only reason it's included

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a full documentation outline (purpose, anatomy, props, one do/don't pair, one accessibility note) for a component you've built earlier this month.

**Lecture 291 documentation**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Write complete documentation for a real component, including do/don't examples and accessibility notes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Writing documentation well means making abstract guidance concrete — a 'do' and 'don't' pair should show two near-identical visual examples side by side so the difference is immediately obvious (not just stated in prose), and accessibility notes should specify exact behavior (which key moves focus where, what ARIA role or label is expected) rather than a vague 'make sure it's accessible.' A useful test for documentation quality is whether someone who has never seen the component before could implement it correctly using only the documentation page, with no need to ask the original designer a clarifying question — any question you'd expect them to ask is a sign the documentation has a gap. |
| **Worked example**      | Documentation for a Dropdown component's do/don't pair shows: Do — dropdown with 5 or fewer options, each with a clear label. Don't — a dropdown crammed with 30 unsorted options and no search, with a caption noting that beyond roughly 10 options a searchable combobox component should be used instead. The accessibility section specifies: Tab moves focus to the trigger, Enter or Space opens it, Arrow keys move between options, Escape closes without selecting, and the trigger carries aria-expanded and aria-haspopup attributes.                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** What is a good test for whether a component's documentation page is actually complete?

**(A) Whether someone unfamiliar with the component could implement it correctly using only the documentation, without needing to ask the original designer a clarifying question**

\(B\) Whether the documentation page is longer than every other page in the library

\(C\) Whether the documentation uses the word 'accessible' at least once

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write the complete, final documentation page for one component from this month, including a visual do/don't pair description and specific keyboard/ARIA accessibility behavior, as if a new engineer will implement it using only your page.

**Lecture 292 Month 17 Examination**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Design Systems I · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Demonstrate integrated command of tokens, components, variants, states, naming, and documentation covered this month.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
