| **Teacher explanation** | This exam reviews the month's full design-systems arc: the token concept and its global/semantic/component-specific tiers as the shared source of truth between design and code; components and the atomic-design hierarchy (atoms, molecules, organisms) with the master/instance relationship and prop exposure; variants as mutually-exclusive option sets distinct from independent boolean props, including the combination-explosion risk as variant sets grow; the full interactive-state set (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading/error) with focus treated as a non-negotiable accessibility requirement; naming conventions that keep a library searchable and prevent duplicate creation; and documentation that serves designers, engineers, and accessibility reviewers with concrete do/don't examples. The strongest answers can trace a single component end to end — its tokens, its variant and state set, its naming, its documentation — the way a real design-system contribution actually works. There is no external certification tied to this month; the course's internal passing bar remains 80%, consistent with every other month in the program. |
| **Worked example**      | A worked review scenario: building a new Alert component from scratch using this month's full toolkit — define its tokens by referencing existing semantic color tokens (color-background-danger, color-background-warning, etc.) rather than inventing new globals; classify it as an organism built from an icon atom and text atoms; give it a status variant (success/warning/danger/info) and a dismissible boolean prop; define its full state set including a visible focus ring on its dismiss button; name it and its tokens consistently with the rest of the library; and document it with a do/don't pair and accessibility notes covering screen-reader announcement behavior for newly appeared alerts.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** When building a new component, why should its colors reference existing semantic tokens (like color-background-danger) rather than new raw hex values?

**(A) It keeps the new component consistent with the rest of the library and ensures it automatically inherits future theme or rebrand changes made at the semantic tier**

\(B\) Semantic tokens are only usable by senior designers, not by anyone building a new component

\(C\) New components are always required to introduce their own unique color palette

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Design one new component end to end using every tool from this month: its tokens, its atomic-design classification, its variant and state set, its name, and a complete documentation page.

**Month 18 Design Systems II**

*Allocation: 20 hours \| 20 lectures \| Level: Intermediate*

**Lecture 293 Responsive components**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define a responsive component and explain the difference between fixed and fluid sizing.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | A responsive component adapts its layout, spacing, or visible content as the available screen width changes, rather than being built once at a single fixed width and simply scaled or clipped on other screens. Fixed sizing locks a dimension to an exact value (width: 320px), which looks correct only at the width it was designed for and breaks (overflowing or leaving excess empty space) at other widths; fluid sizing instead uses relative units or rules (percentages, min/max bounds, flexible grid tracks) that let the component resize smoothly within a defined range. Design systems build components fluid by default wherever possible, reserving fixed sizing for cases where a dimension genuinely shouldn't change (an icon's size, a fixed-width sidebar on desktop-only layouts), because a component that only works at its original design width creates constant one-off fixes as it's reused across a growing set of screen sizes. |
| **Worked example**      | A Card component built with a fixed width of 320px looks perfect on the mobile mockup it was designed on, but placed into a three-column desktop grid, each card just sits at an awkward fixed 320px regardless of the available column width, leaving uneven gaps. Rebuilt with fluid sizing (width: 100% of its grid column, with a min-width of 240px and max-width of 400px to prevent it from ever becoming unreadably narrow or absurdly wide), the same card now fills its column correctly at any grid configuration.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a Card component with a fixed 320px width cause problems when reused inside a responsive grid layout?

**(A) It can't adapt to the actual available column width, so it either leaves awkward empty space or doesn't fit the grid's intended proportions at different screen sizes**

\(B\) Fixed-width components are always faster to render than fluid ones

\(C\) A 320px width is too small to ever be used on any screen

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Find a component in a real app that behaves differently across phone and desktop widths, and identify whether it uses fixed or fluid sizing to achieve that adaptation.

**Lecture 294 Responsive components**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain breakpoints and how a component's layout changes across them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | A breakpoint is a defined screen-width threshold where a component or layout deliberately switches to a different arrangement, rather than scaling continuously forever — common breakpoint tiers are roughly mobile (under ~600px), tablet (~600-1024px), and desktop (above ~1024px), though exact values vary by design system and should be based on real content needs, not copied blindly from a framework default. A component can change multiple things at a breakpoint: a navigation bar might collapse into a hamburger menu below a breakpoint and show full horizontal links above it; a card grid might show one column on mobile, two on tablet, and four on desktop. The design decision at each breakpoint isn't just 'make it smaller' — it's often a genuinely different layout strategy, which is why breakpoint behavior needs to be explicitly designed and documented per component rather than assumed to happen automatically. |
| **Worked example**      | A product-listing grid defines three breakpoint behaviors: below 600px, one column with full-width cards and a 'Filter' button that opens a full-screen overlay; 600-1024px, two columns with filters shown as a collapsible side drawer; above 1024px, four columns with filters permanently visible in a persistent left sidebar. Each breakpoint isn't just a column-count change — the filter interaction pattern itself changes to suit the available space.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** Why does switching a navigation bar to a hamburger menu below a certain width breakpoint count as a genuinely different layout strategy, not just a smaller version of the same layout?

**(A) The interaction pattern itself changes (links are hidden behind a toggle instead of always visible), which is a structural change to how users navigate, not merely a size reduction**

\(B\) A hamburger menu always contains exactly the same number of pixels as the full navigation bar

\(C\) Breakpoints only affect font size, never layout structure

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick a component with multi-breakpoint behavior from a real app, and describe the layout strategy (not just the size) at each of its three breakpoints.

**Lecture 295 Responsive components**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Work through a complete responsive-component example across three breakpoints.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | Designing a component across breakpoints well means starting from the content and interaction needs at the most constrained breakpoint (usually mobile) and working outward, rather than starting from desktop and trying to cram everything into a smaller space later — this 'mobile-first' approach tends to produce cleaner, more essential layouts, because you're forced to prioritize what truly matters when space is scarce. At each larger breakpoint, you ask what newly available space should be used for: more columns, more visible metadata, a persistent instead of collapsible panel, rather than just stretching the mobile layout wider. Documenting this as three (or more) explicit, labeled layout states — not a vague 'it adapts' note — is what makes the component actually buildable by an engineer without constant back-and-forth clarification. |
| **Worked example**      | A restaurant app's menu-item component is designed mobile-first: at mobile width, it shows image, name, price, and a compact '+' add button stacked vertically. At tablet width, the same information reflows into a horizontal row (image left, text middle, button right) because there's now room, and a short description line is added since vertical space constraints have relaxed. At desktop width, the row gains a calorie count and an 'ingredients' tooltip trigger, because screen real estate now supports showing more decision-making information without crowding.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Why does mobile-first responsive design typically produce a cleaner final layout than designing for desktop first and shrinking down?

**(A) Starting from the most space-constrained breakpoint forces prioritization of only what's truly essential, which tends to produce a more focused layout that then expands deliberately rather than being crammed down later**

\(B\) Mobile-first design is only a historical convention with no actual design benefit

\(C\) Desktop-first design is always technically impossible to implement

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Design one component mobile-first across three breakpoints, writing what specifically is shown, hidden, or restructured at each one and why.

**Lecture 296 Responsive components**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Run a hands-on critique session identifying common responsive-component mistakes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | A frequent responsive mistake is designing only the two endpoints (smallest and largest screen) and assuming everything in between looks fine, when in practice an awkward 'in-between' width (like a tablet in portrait) often reveals a layout that neither endpoint anticipated, such as text wrapping badly or a button overlapping an image. A second common mistake is hiding content at small breakpoints without a clear strategy for where it goes instead — content that simply vanishes below a certain width, with no alternate access path (a 'More' menu, a different icon), silently removes functionality rather than adapting it. A third mistake is testing responsiveness only by resizing a browser window quickly, which misses real device quirks like actual touch-target sizing, software keyboard overlap, or notch/safe-area insets that only show up on real or emulated devices. |
| **Worked example**      | A critique finds a pricing-comparison table that looks fine at exactly 375px (mobile) and exactly 1440px (desktop) but breaks badly at 800px (a common tablet-portrait width), where three of four plan columns overlap because the breakpoint logic only had two states instead of three. The fix adds a dedicated tablet breakpoint with a two-column, swipeable layout instead of trying to force the desktop four-column layout into the available space.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why is testing a responsive component only at its smallest and largest intended widths considered an incomplete testing approach?

**(A) An in-between width can expose a layout failure that neither endpoint reveals, since the component may not have a defined behavior for that intermediate range**

\(B\) Testing only two widths is the industry-standard best practice and requires no further checking

\(C\) Browsers automatically fix any layout problems that occur between two tested widths

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Resize a real responsive page or component slowly through its full width range (not just jumping between endpoints) and document one in-between width where something breaks.

**Lecture 297 Responsive components**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Synthesize a complete responsive component system tying breakpoints, fluid sizing, and critique together into one documented spec.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | A finished responsive-component spec combines everything from this run: fluid sizing by default with fixed sizing only where deliberately justified, explicitly designed (not assumed) behavior at each breakpoint with labeled layout states, mobile-first prioritization of content, and verification across in-between widths and real devices rather than just the two endpoints. The deliverable that makes this reusable across a team is a single documented spec per component: a short table or diagram showing each breakpoint's layout, what's fluid versus fixed, and any content that's hidden or restructured along with where it reappears, so any engineer can implement the full responsive behavior from one artifact without reverse-engineering it from screenshots. |
| **Worked example**      | The final spec for the restaurant app's menu-item component (from three lectures ago) is written as one page: a labeled three-breakpoint diagram, a note that the image is fixed-aspect but fluid-width while the button is fixed-size, and an explicit statement that the 'ingredients' tooltip (desktop-only) has no mobile equivalent by design because the team decided that information isn't essential below tablet width — a deliberate decision, not a silent omission.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** What distinguishes a complete responsive-component spec from a set of three separate breakpoint screenshots?

**(A) It explicitly documents what's fluid versus fixed and states deliberate decisions about hidden content, rather than leaving an engineer to infer behavior and intent from static images alone**

\(B\) A complete spec must always include exactly five breakpoints, never three

\(C\) Screenshots alone are always sufficient and additional documentation is redundant

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Produce one complete, single-page responsive spec for a component you've designed this run, combining its breakpoint diagram, fluid/fixed sizing notes, and any deliberate content-hiding decisions.

**Lecture 298 accessibility**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain the POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) and WCAG's role in design-system accessibility.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) organizes accessibility requirements around four principles known as POUR: Perceivable (users must be able to perceive the content through at least one sense — text alternatives for images, sufficient color contrast), Operable (all functionality must be usable via keyboard, not just a mouse, with enough time to complete actions), Understandable (content and interface behavior should be predictable and use clear language), and Robust (content must work correctly with assistive technology like screen readers, now and as technology evolves). A design system's job is to bake POUR compliance into its components once, at the source, so every team reusing a compliant Button or Form Field component inherits accessible behavior automatically rather than every individual screen needing a separate accessibility review from scratch. |
| **Worked example**      | A design system's Input component is built POUR-compliant by construction: Perceivable — it has a visible label plus a programmatically associated aria-label; Operable — it's fully reachable and usable via Tab and keyboard input alone, no mouse required; Understandable — error messages use plain language ('Enter a valid email address like name@example.com') rather than a cryptic code; Robust — it uses semantic HTML input elements with correct ARIA attributes rather than a custom div styled to merely look like an input, which screen readers wouldn't recognize as a form field at all.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a design system building accessibility into its base components matter more than accessibility review happening only on finished screens?

**(A) Every team reusing a compliant component automatically inherits accessible behavior, rather than needing a separate manual accessibility audit on every single new screen built from scratch**

\(B\) WCAG only applies to government websites, not to design systems

\(C\) POUR principles are optional recommendations with no bearing on real component construction

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick one component in a real product and evaluate it against all four POUR principles, noting a pass or fail for each with a specific reason.

**Lecture 299 accessibility**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply color contrast and focus-visibility requirements with specific WCAG thresholds.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | WCAG sets numeric contrast ratio minimums: for normal body text, a 4.5:1 contrast ratio between text and background is the standard (AA) requirement; for large text (roughly 18pt+ or bold 14pt+), the minimum drops to 3:1; for non-text elements like icons, borders, and focus indicators, a 3:1 minimum against adjacent colors applies. These aren't aesthetic suggestions — they're measurable with a contrast-checker tool, and a design system should verify every text-on-background and icon-on-background token pairing against these thresholds before it ships, because a token combination that fails contrast will fail it on every single screen that uses it. Focus indicators specifically need their own contrast check against both the component's background and the surrounding page background, since a focus ring that blends into either one defeats its purpose. |
| **Worked example**      | A design system audits its color-text-secondary (a light gray, \#9CA3AF) against color-background-page (white, \#FFFFFF) and finds a contrast ratio of only 2.8:1 — failing the 4.5:1 requirement for body text. The token is darkened to \#6B7280, achieving 4.6:1, and every component using that semantic token (captions, helper text, placeholder text) is fixed library-wide by that single token update, rather than needing dozens of individual component fixes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why does fixing a failing text-contrast semantic token at the token level, rather than per-component, matter for a design system specifically?

**(A) Because every component referencing that semantic token inherits the fix automatically and simultaneously, instead of requiring the same contrast fix to be manually reapplied everywhere that gray was used**

\(B\) Token-level fixes are purely cosmetic and don't actually change the measured contrast ratio

\(C\) WCAG contrast requirements only apply to tokens, never to individually hard-coded colors

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Use a contrast checker on three text/background color pairings from a real product or your own token set, record the actual ratios, and flag any that fail the 4.5:1 (or 3:1 for large text) threshold.

**Lecture 300 accessibility**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Audit a real component for accessibility across color, focus, and screen-reader compatibility.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | A thorough accessibility audit of a single component checks several independent things that can each fail separately: color contrast for every text and icon pairing (measured, not eyeballed), a visible and sufficiently-contrasted focus indicator reachable purely by keyboard Tab, correct semantic HTML or ARIA roles so a screen reader announces the component correctly (a button built from a styled div with no role='button' and no keyboard handler is invisible to a screen reader as an interactive element), and reasonable touch-target size (WCAG recommends at least 24x24px, with 44x44px commonly cited as a comfortable minimum for touch) for anything tappable on a mobile layout. An audit that only checks one of these dimensions and declares the component 'accessible' gives false confidence — a component can pass a contrast check and still be completely unusable by a screen-reader user if it's built from non-semantic markup. |
| **Worked example**      | An audit of a custom dropdown component finds: contrast passes (4.8:1 on its text), but the focus ring disappears when the dropdown is open (focus trap gap), and the component is built from div elements with click handlers but no role='listbox', no aria-expanded, and no keyboard arrow-key support at all — meaning a screen-reader user has no idea options even exist. The audit flags this as failing despite passing contrast, because the ARIA and keyboard gaps make it entirely non-operable for assistive-technology users.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why would an accessibility audit still fail a component that has correct color contrast but no ARIA roles or keyboard support?

**(A) Contrast is only one of several independent accessibility requirements, and a component built from non-semantic markup with no keyboard support is unusable by screen-reader and keyboard-only users regardless of its contrast ratio**

\(B\) Contrast is the only accessibility requirement that actually matters in practice

\(C\) ARIA roles are a deprecated technique that modern screen readers no longer use

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Audit one interactive component in a real app using only your keyboard (Tab, Enter, arrow keys) with no mouse, and separately check its contrast, reporting any gap you find in either dimension.

**Lecture 301 accessibility**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Run a guided exercise fixing a specific set of accessibility defects in an existing component.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | Fixing accessibility defects well means addressing the root cause rather than a surface patch — adding aria-label text to a button that's still unreachable by keyboard fixes screen-reader labeling but not keyboard operability, so both issues need independent fixes, not one assumed to cover the other. A disciplined fix process works defect by defect: identify the specific failing criterion (which POUR principle, which WCAG success criterion), make the minimal correct fix (the right ARIA attribute, the right semantic element, the right contrast value), then re-test with the same method that caught the original defect (keyboard-only navigation, a contrast checker, an actual screen reader) rather than assuming the fix worked by inspection alone. |
| **Worked example**      | Fixing the dropdown from last lecture: role='listbox' and role='option' are added to the correct elements, aria-expanded toggles correctly with open/closed state, arrow-key handlers are added for option navigation, and the focus ring is restored to stay visible while the dropdown is open. Each fix is re-tested independently — keyboard-only navigation confirms arrow keys now move between options, and a screen reader is used to confirm it announces 'listbox, 5 options' and reads each option's name as it's focused.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why should each accessibility fix be re-tested with the same method that originally caught the defect, rather than just visually inspecting the fixed code?

**(A) Visual inspection can't confirm that assistive technology actually behaves correctly; only re-testing with the real method (keyboard-only use, a screen reader, a contrast tool) verifies the fix actually works for the affected users**

\(B\) Re-testing is unnecessary once the correct ARIA attribute has been typed into the code

\(C\) Fixes to accessibility defects are always successful on the first attempt

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take the component you audited two lectures ago, fix one specific defect you found, and re-test it using the same method (keyboard-only, contrast checker, or screen reader) that originally revealed the problem.

**Lecture 302 accessibility**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Synthesize an accessibility checklist for the design system and tie it to a mini sign-off process.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | A design system's accessibility checklist consolidates this run's criteria into one reusable gate every new or updated component passes through before release: contrast ratios measured and passing for every token pairing used, full keyboard operability with a visible focus state at every interactive point, correct semantic markup or ARIA roles verified with an actual screen reader (not just visual inspection), and touch targets meeting minimum size on mobile layouts. Making this a mini sign-off process — a short checklist someone actually initials before a component is marked 'ready' in the library — is what prevents accessibility from being treated as a one-time audit that quietly goes stale as components get modified later; every meaningful update to a component should re-trigger the relevant parts of the checklist, not just its first release. |
| **Worked example**      | A design system adds an 'Accessibility sign-off' section to its component contribution template: four checkboxes (contrast verified, keyboard-only tested, screen-reader tested, touch targets checked) that a reviewer — not the original author — must check off with their name before a component status changes from 'In Review' to 'Released.' When the Button component's padding is later modified for a visual refresh, the touch-target checkbox specifically gets re-verified, since that's the dimension the change could plausibly affect.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the design system require a reviewer other than the original component's author to complete the accessibility sign-off?

**(A) An independent check catches issues the original builder may have missed or assumed were fine, the same reasoning behind any second-reviewer quality gate**

\(B\) Only the original author is legally permitted to test their own component

\(C\) Sign-off has no real function beyond adding delay to the release process

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a four-to-six-item accessibility sign-off checklist for your design system, and apply it to one component you've worked on this month, noting pass/fail for each item.

**Lecture 303 governance**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define design-system governance and explain why an undocumented system tends to decay.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Governance is the set of decisions, roles, and processes that determine who can add, change, or deprecate something in a design system, and how those decisions get made and communicated — without it, a library tends to decay through two failure modes: uncontrolled growth (everyone adds their own one-off component rather than reusing or extending what exists, because there's no process pointing them to it) and silent drift (someone changes a shared component for their own screen's needs, breaking it elsewhere, because no review step caught the blast radius). Governance doesn't mean bureaucracy for its own sake — a lightweight governance model can be a single documented page stating who approves new components and how changes get proposed, but having zero stated process is itself a governance choice, and it's reliably the one that leads to decay. |
| **Worked example**      | A mid-size product team with no governance model finds that three different teams have each built their own slightly different 'Tag' component over eighteen months, none aware the others exist, because there was no documented place to check before building and no one whose job it was to say 'we already have this.' A lightweight governance fix — a single Slack channel and a one-page 'propose a new component' doc requiring a quick check against the existing library first — would have caught this duplication at the first team, not the third.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** What specific failure mode does the three-teams-building-the-same-Tag-component scenario illustrate?

**(A) Uncontrolled growth caused by the absence of any documented process for checking existing components before building new ones**

\(B\) A deliberate and correct governance decision to intentionally duplicate components across teams

\(C\) A contrast-ratio accessibility failure unrelated to governance

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Check whether a design system or component library you have access to (at work, in an open-source project, or a public library) has any documented governance page, and note what it does or doesn't cover.

**Lecture 304 governance**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Compare centralized, federated, and open-contribution governance models and when each fits.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Centralized governance has one dedicated team owning the entire design system, reviewing and building every change — this gives the highest consistency but can become a bottleneck as the number of product teams needing changes grows faster than the central team can review them. Federated governance distributes ownership across product teams for their own components while a smaller core team still owns shared foundations (tokens, core atoms) and sets contribution standards — this scales better but requires clear standards so federated contributions stay consistent with each other. Open-contribution (or 'everyone can propose') governance lets any team submit a component through a defined review process with no fixed owning team, which scales furthest but needs the strongest documented standards and review discipline to avoid quality drift, since there's no single team's reputation riding on every merge. The right model usually tracks organization size: a 10-person startup can get away with one person owning everything informally; a 500-person company usually needs federated or open models with real documented process. |
| **Worked example**      | A 15-person startup design system is centralized by necessity — one designer owns every component, which works because the volume of requests is low enough for one person to handle. As the company grows to 200 people across eight product teams, that same designer becomes a bottleneck with a three-week review queue, prompting a shift to a federated model: a small core team owns tokens and foundational atoms, while each product team can build and own its own domain-specific components as long as they pass a documented contribution checklist reviewed by the core team.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why does centralized governance tend to become a bottleneck as an organization grows, even if it worked well at a smaller size?

**(A) The volume of change requests grows with the organization, but a single central team's review capacity doesn't scale at the same rate, creating a widening queue**

\(B\) Centralized governance always produces lower-quality components than other models

\(C\) Centralized governance is illegal for organizations above a certain headcount

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Identify which governance model (centralized, federated, or open-contribution) best fits an organization you're familiar with, and justify your choice based on its size and the volume of design-system change requests it likely generates.

**Lecture 305 governance**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a real governance scenario: a component change request and its review path.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | A well-governed change request follows a defined path from proposal to release: someone identifies a need (an existing component doesn't support a new use case, or a new component is genuinely needed), checks the existing library first to avoid duplication, submits a proposal through whatever channel governance defines (a ticket, a design review meeting, a PR against a documented template), the proposal gets reviewed against the system's standards (naming, tokens, accessibility, variant/prop design from earlier this month), and only then gets merged into the shared library with updated documentation. Tracing one request through this full path end to end is the best way to understand why each governance step exists — skipping the 'check existing library first' step is what causes duplicate components, and skipping the 'review against standards' step is what causes the inconsistent naming and missing accessibility coverage covered in earlier lectures. |
| **Worked example**      | A product team needs a new 'Stat Card' component to show a metric with a trend arrow. Following governance: they first search the library and find a close cousin, the existing Card component, but confirm it doesn't support the trend-arrow use case. They submit a proposal using the team's documented template (purpose, anatomy, proposed tokens, variant list), a design-system reviewer checks it against naming conventions and confirms it reuses existing semantic tokens rather than inventing new ones, requests one accessibility fix (the trend arrow needs an accessible text equivalent for screen readers, not just a visual arrow icon), and the component is merged with full documentation only after that fix is made.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** In the Stat Card scenario, why does the reviewer require an accessible text equivalent for the trend arrow before approving the component?

**(A) A purely visual arrow icon communicates nothing to screen-reader users, so it fails the accessibility standard the governance review is specifically checking for**

\(B\) Trend arrows are never allowed in any design system under any circumstances

\(C\) The reviewer's only job is to check whether the component's name is spelled correctly

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write out a full change-request scenario for a design system you're familiar with (or hypothetical), tracing it through proposal, existing-library check, standards review, and merge, naming one specific standard the reviewer should check.

**Lecture 306 governance**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Run a critique session identifying common governance failures and mismatches.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | A common governance failure is mismatching the model to the organization's actual size and speed — imposing a heavy centralized-review process on a 10-person startup slows everyone down for no real consistency benefit, while leaving a 300-person company on a fully open, unreviewed contribution model produces exactly the inconsistency and duplication governance was supposed to prevent. A second common failure is governance that exists on paper but isn't actually followed because it was never communicated or enforced — a one-page governance doc that only the person who wrote it has ever read isn't functioning as governance at all. A third failure is having no deprecation process, so the library accumulates components nobody uses but nobody is allowed to delete either, because there's no documented path for retiring something safely. |
| **Worked example**      | A critique of a 250-person company's design system finds their governance doc technically states 'all changes require core-team review,' but in practice, three product teams have been shipping their own one-off components directly for over a year because no one enforces the stated process and the core team doesn't even know it's being bypassed. The critique's recommendation isn't to write a stricter doc — it's to make the existing process genuinely enforced (a required check in the build pipeline, or a contribution template gate) since the policy gap was never the wording, it was the lack of enforcement.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** In the 250-person company scenario, what was the actual root cause of the governance failure?

**(A) The documented process existed but was never enforced in practice, so teams bypassed it with no consequence, rather than the written policy itself being flawed**

\(B\) The company's governance document used the wrong font and formatting

\(C\) The core team was too large and needed more members, not better enforcement

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Find or imagine a governance mismatch (too heavy for the team's size, too light to prevent drift, or unenforced on paper) and propose the one specific change that would fix the actual root cause.

**Lecture 307 governance**

*Year 2 · Month 18 · Design Systems II · 1 guided hour + homework*
