|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply a different generated-content mechanic: designing for content that must be regenerated or iterated on, including variation controls and comparison views.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | A second, deeper mechanic in generated-content UX: because a single generation is rarely the final answer, interfaces need to support iteration efficiently, not just produce one output and stop. Common patterns include generating multiple variations at once so a user can compare options side by side rather than regenerating one at a time and losing the previous attempt, and exposing lightweight controls (more formal/casual, shorter/longer, more realistic/more stylized) that let a user nudge the next generation in a specific direction without having to rewrite their entire original prompt from scratch. This turns content generation from a one-shot gamble into an iterative refinement loop, which better matches how creative and professional work actually happens — nobody expects their first draft of anything to be final, and the UI should reflect that expectation rather than pretend otherwise. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: an AI logo generator that produces only one image per generation and discards the previous one when the user clicks 'regenerate' forces users to screenshot results manually to compare options — frustrating and lossy. A redesign generates four variations per request displayed in a grid, keeps a history panel of all past generations in the session, and adds quick-nudge buttons ('more minimalist,' 'more colorful') that regenerate based on the current best pick plus the nudge, rather than starting over from the original prompt each time.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why is generating four variations at once with a kept history generally better UX than overwriting the single previous result on every regenerate?

\(A\) It uses more computing resources, which is always a sign of better quality.

**(B) It supports iterative comparison and refinement, matching how creative work actually happens, instead of forcing users to manually preserve past attempts.**

\(C\) It is required because AI models cannot generate a single high-quality image reliably.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Design a variation-and-nudge control set (list 3-4 specific nudge buttons) for an AI content-generation feature of your choice, explaining what each nudge changes about the next generation.

**Lecture 337 generated content**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · AI UX Patterns · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a real-world generated-content UX decision: how code-completion tools present AI-suggested code differently from human-written code in an editor.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Worked real-world example: AI coding assistants integrated into code editors face a particularly high-stakes version of the generated-content problem, because suggested code that looks syntactically plausible but is subtly wrong can introduce bugs or security vulnerabilities if accepted without scrutiny. The UX convention that's emerged: AI-suggested code appears as greyed-out 'ghost text' inline, visually distinct from the user's own typed (solid, black) code, and requires an explicit accept keystroke (commonly Tab) rather than being inserted automatically — this preserves a clear visual and interactive boundary between 'what I wrote' and 'what the AI suggested and I chose to accept,' which matters enormously when debugging later and trying to understand where a given line of logic came from. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a developer using an AI coding assistant sees a suggested function completion appear as light grey ghost text while they're mid-sentence in a function. They read it, notice it doesn't handle a null case they care about, and keep typing instead of pressing Tab — the suggestion simply disappears, with zero cost to rejecting it. Contrast this with a hypothetical poor design where AI suggestions insert themselves automatically after a short delay: the developer would need to actively delete unwanted code rather than simply not accepting it, inverting the cost from 'free to reject' to 'costly to reject.'                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why do AI code-completion tools show suggestions as distinct 'ghost text' requiring an explicit accept action, rather than auto-inserting them?

\(A\) Ghost text renders faster than solid text in most code editors.

**(B) It preserves a clear boundary between human-written and AI-suggested code and keeps rejecting an unwanted suggestion free, rather than costly.**

\(C\) Auto-inserting code is technically impossible in modern code editors.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Open any AI coding assistant (or research one) and describe exactly how it visually distinguishes a suggestion from your own code, and what single keystroke or action accepts versus dismisses it.

**Lecture 338 citations**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · AI UX Patterns · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define why generated content needs citations or source attribution, and the specific trust problem citations solve that plain confident-sounding prose does not.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | When an AI system generates a factual claim, the text itself offers no clue about whether that claim came from a reliable source, was inferred loosely, or was outright fabricated — a phenomenon often called hallucination. Citations are the UX mechanism that addresses this: by attaching a visible, checkable source (a document, a webpage, a specific passage) to a generated claim, the product lets the user verify the claim rather than simply trusting the model's confident tone, which carries no correlation to actual accuracy. This is a genuinely different trust problem from traditional content, where a cited academic paper's citation is about giving credit; here, the citation is a verification mechanism, often the only practical way for a user to tell a true generated statement from a fabricated one that happens to read with equal fluency and confidence. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: an AI research assistant answers 'What was the company's revenue growth last quarter?' with a specific number stated in confident, fluent prose and no citation — the user has no way to tell if this number is accurate or hallucinated. The same tool redesigned to append a clickable citation ('\[source: Q3 earnings report, page 4\]') next to the number lets the user click through and verify the actual filing in seconds, turning an unverifiable claim into a checkable one — and when the model cannot find a supporting source, the redesigned version is required to say so explicitly rather than stating a number with no citation at all.                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** What specific trust problem do citations solve in AI-generated content that confident, fluent writing alone cannot solve?

\(A\) Citations make generated text sound more professional and persuasive.

**(B) Citations give the user a checkable source to verify a claim, addressing the fact that fluent, confident-sounding AI text carries no guarantee of accuracy.**

\(C\) Citations are only a legal requirement with no actual UX benefit to the end user.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Find an AI tool that generates factual claims and check whether it provides any source attribution — if it doesn't, describe what a citation UI for it should look like.

**Lecture 339 citations**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · AI UX Patterns · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply citation UX to a hands-on exercise: redesigning an uncited AI answer to include proper source attribution, including handling the case where no good source exists.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Hands-on exercise building directly on the previous lecture's concept: students are given a sample AI-generated answer to a factual question with three distinct claims bundled into one paragraph and no citations at all, and must redesign it with per-claim source attribution rather than one citation awkwardly covering the whole paragraph — because a single end-of-paragraph citation doesn't tell the user which specific sentence it supports. The exercise also requires handling the harder case: what happens when the system genuinely cannot find a supporting source for one of the three claims? The correct answer is not to silently drop the citation requirement for that one claim and hope the user doesn't notice — it's to explicitly flag that specific claim as unverified or lower-confidence, which is more honest and more useful than uniform-looking prose that hides which parts are and aren't backed by a real source. |
| **Worked example**      | Example of the exercise's expected redesign: original uncited paragraph: 'The product launched in 2019, sold 2 million units in its first year, and was discontinued due to supply issues.' Redesigned with per-claim citations: '\[The product launched in 2019\]¹ \[and sold 2 million units in its first year\]². \[It was discontinued due to supply issues\] — this claim could not be verified against available sources.' with footnotes 1 and 2 linking to specific source documents, and the third claim visually flagged as unverified rather than silently presented as equally certain.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** When an AI system can't find a source for one claim in a multi-claim answer, what is the correct citation UX response?

\(A\) Drop the citation requirement silently for that claim so the paragraph still reads smoothly.

**(B) Explicitly flag that specific claim as unverified or lower-confidence, rather than presenting it with the same apparent certainty as the cited claims.**

\(C\) Refuse to answer the entire question if even one claim lacks a source.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Take any AI-generated paragraph with multiple factual claims (real or written by you) and redesign it with per-claim citation markers, including how you'd flag any claim that has no available source.

**Lecture 340 confidence**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · AI UX Patterns · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define how confidence should be communicated to end users in an AI product UI, distinguishing raw numeric scores from calibrated plain-language signals.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Model confidence scores (covered as an ML concept in Month 19) need a UX translation layer before reaching end users, because a raw number like '73% confidence' means very little to most users without context for what counts as high or low in that specific domain, and different users will anchor to wildly different intuitive thresholds for the same number. Effective confidence UX usually avoids showing raw percentages to general consumers and instead uses plain-language tiers ('likely,' 'possible,' 'uncertain') or visual encodings (color, icon, position) calibrated to what actually matters for that decision — the goal is for the user's gut read of the signal to match the model's actual reliability at that level, which is a design and testing problem, not just a matter of picking nice-sounding words. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a medical symptom-checker app initially shows raw confidence percentages next to possible conditions ('Condition A: 61% match, Condition B: 34% match'), and user testing finds people wrongly treat 61% as 'probably this one, don't worry much' when clinically it should prompt seeking care. The redesign replaces percentages with calibrated plain-language tiers reviewed by clinical staff ('Condition A: possible — consider seeing a doctor,' 'Condition B: less likely'), and testing shows users' resulting care-seeking behavior aligns much better with the actual clinical risk level than the raw percentage version did.                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** Why might showing a raw '61% confidence' score to a general consumer be worse UX than a calibrated plain-language tier?

\(A\) Percentages are always technically inaccurate and therefore illegal to display.

**(B) Users anchor to intuitive but inconsistent interpretations of raw percentages, which may not match the actual real-world risk or reliability the number represents.**

\(C\) Plain-language tiers are faster for the system to compute than percentages.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick an AI feature that shows (or could show) a raw confidence percentage, and propose a calibrated plain-language tier system to replace it, defining what range of actual model confidence maps to each tier label.

**Lecture 341 confidence**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · AI UX Patterns · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply confidence-communication design to a guided critique of a flawed interface that uses confidence signals inconsistently across similar features.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Hands-on critique exercise: students review a sample app that shows AI confidence three different ways across three different screens — a raw percentage on one screen, a five-star rating on another, and a simple colored dot (green/yellow/red) with no explanation on a third — with no consistent logic for why each screen chose its format or what the specific thresholds mean. The exercise asks students to identify the core problem (users can't build a reliable mental model of what 'confident' means in this app because the signal keeps changing shape) and to propose a single unified confidence system used consistently across all three screens, with explicitly documented thresholds (e.g., green = above 85%, yellow = 60-85%, red = below 60%) so the mapping is consistent and, ideally, explained once to the user rather than re-learned on every screen. |
| **Worked example**      | Example of the exercise's expected fix: 'Problem: screen A's percentage, screen B's stars, and screen C's unlabeled colored dot cannot be compared to each other, so a user has no consistent way to judge confidence across the app. Fix: adopt one three-tier colored-dot-plus-label system everywhere (green ‘High confidence’, yellow ‘Medium confidence’, red ‘Low confidence — review recommended’) with the same thresholds behind every instance, and add a one-time tooltip the first time a user encounters any confidence indicator, explaining what the colors mean.'                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** What is the core usability problem with an app showing AI confidence as a percentage on one screen, stars on another, and an unlabeled dot on a third?

\(A\) It's not a real problem — more variety in visual design is always better for engagement.

**(B) Users can't build a consistent mental model of what the confidence signal means when its format and thresholds change unpredictably across the same app.**

\(C\) Colored dots are not accessible for colorblind users, which is the only issue present.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Audit an app with more than one AI confidence indicator (or imagine one with several AI features) and check whether it uses a consistent format and threshold logic across all of them — propose a single unified system if it doesn't.

**Lecture 342 correction flows**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · AI UX Patterns · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define what a correction flow is in AI UX and explain why making corrections cheap and specific directly affects both user trust and model improvement.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | A correction flow is the UI path a user takes to tell the system an AI output was wrong and, ideally, supply the right answer instead. This serves two purposes at once: immediately, it lets the user fix their actual task without being stuck with a bad AI output; longer-term, as covered in the Month 19 feedback-loop concept, a well-designed correction becomes a labeled data point that can improve the model later — but only if the correction captures specific, structured information rather than a vague 'thumbs down.' A plain thumbs-down tells engineering that something was wrong but not what was wrong or what the right answer should have been, which is nearly useless for retraining; a correction flow that asks 'what should it have said instead?' or offers a short list of likely correct alternatives to pick from captures far more actionable signal while often being just as fast for the user to use. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a voice-to-text app's correction flow originally only offered a thumbs-down button with no follow-up — engineering receives thousands of thumbs-down events with no idea what was actually mis-transcribed or what the correct transcription should have been. The redesign lets a user tap the specific mis-transcribed word, see the AI's original guess alongside 2-3 likely alternative words generated from acoustic similarity, and either pick one or type the correct word directly — each correction now captures exactly which word was wrong and what it should have been, directly usable as a training example.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a plain thumbs-down button considered weak correction-flow design compared to asking 'what should it have said instead?'

\(A\) Thumbs-down buttons take up too much screen space.

**(B) A thumbs-down signals something was wrong but captures no information about what the correct answer should have been, making it far less useful for both the user and model improvement.**

\(C\) Users dislike seeing a thumbs-down icon for psychological reasons.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Design a correction flow for an AI feature of your choice that goes beyond a simple thumbs-down — specify exactly what information it captures about the correct answer when a user flags an error.

**Lecture 343 correction flows**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · AI UX Patterns · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply correction-flow design to a worked real-world walkthrough, examining how a product routes different types of corrections to different downstream destinations.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | Worked real-world example: a product's correction flow isn't just a UI question but a routing question — different types of AI mistakes should often go to different places. A factual error in a generated answer might route to a 'verify and fix the knowledge source' queue for a content team, while a tone mismatch (correct information, wrong style) might route to a different 'style preference' signal that adjusts personalization settings rather than the underlying facts. We walk through a realistic support-AI example where lumping all corrections into one undifferentiated bucket caused the team to spend weeks manually re-sorting feedback by type before they could act on any of it, versus a redesign that asks a quick one-tap category question at the moment of correction ('Wrong fact / Wrong tone / Didn't understand my question'), so corrections arrive already sorted and immediately actionable by the right downstream team. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a company's AI writing assistant receives 500 corrected drafts per week, all dumped into one unsorted feedback inbox that a single analyst manually triages before any team can act — a multi-week backlog accumulates. After adding a one-tap category chooser to the correction flow itself ('Factually wrong,' 'Wrong tone,' 'Formatting issue'), corrections arrive pre-sorted, and each specialized team (fact-checking, style-model tuning, template design) can pull directly from their own filtered queue the same day instead of waiting on manual triage.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why does adding a one-tap category chooser to a correction flow ('Wrong fact / Wrong tone / Didn't understand') meaningfully speed up how corrections get acted on?

\(A\) It reduces the total number of corrections submitted by users.

**(B) It pre-sorts corrections by type at the moment of capture, letting the right specialized downstream team act directly instead of waiting on manual triage of an undifferentiated feedback pile.**

\(C\) It makes the correction flow load faster on mobile devices.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Design a one-tap category chooser (list 3-4 categories) for the correction flow of an AI feature of your choice, and describe which downstream team or system each category's corrections should route to.

**Lecture 344 Month 20 Examination**

*Year 2 · Month 20 · AI UX Patterns · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Demonstrate integrated understanding of AI UX patterns by reviewing prompt interface design, conversational UI, generated-content treatment, citations, confidence communication, and correction flows across realistic scenarios.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | This examination lecture reviews the full arc of Month 20: Prompt interfaces (329-331) established that free-text input needs scaffolding — example prompts and progressive disclosure — rather than a blank box; conversational UI (332-334) covered multi-turn context retention, streaming/typing-indicator patterns, and the need for legible system-state signals; generated content (335-337) addressed labeling AI output as draft-quality, supporting iteration through variations, and the ghost-text convention for AI-suggested code; citations (338-339) established source attribution as a verification mechanism against hallucination, including per-claim flagging when no source exists; confidence (340-341) covered translating raw model confidence into calibrated, consistent plain-language signals; and correction flows (342-343) covered capturing specific, routable correction data rather than vague thumbs-down signals. No external certification is tied to this month — this is an internal checkpoint only, and the program's internal passing standard remains 80% as with all module exams; review any weak topic before Month 21's AI product discovery work, which will draw directly on this month's human-in-the-loop and uncertainty-communication patterns when scoping new AI use cases. |

**Knowledge check:** What is the internal passing standard for this program's module examinations, consistent across the course?

\(A\) 70%.

**(B) 80%.**

\(C\) 90%.
