**Lecture 359 risk mapping**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · AI Product Discovery · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Synthesize risk mapping into a standard discovery artifact a PM can attach to any AI feature's go/no-go review, including how it should be revisited after launch.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | Synthesis lecture closing out this run: we consolidate the four risk categories, the severity/likelihood prioritization grid, and the mitigation/monitoring split into a single standing artifact format — an 'AI risk map' — that becomes a required input to any AI feature's go/no-go launch review, not a one-time document that's filed away and forgotten. Critically, a risk map isn't static: the real-world case in lecture 357 and the exercise in lecture 358 both show those risks and their actual likelihoods can shift after launch (new data, new user populations, model drift), so the synthesis includes a commitment to revisit the risk map at defined intervals post-launch (not just once at launch) and update severity/likelihood assessments as real production data comes in, treating the risk map as a living document tied to the ongoing monitoring practices from the AI product lifecycle in Month 19. |
| **Worked example**      | Example of the finished standing artifact template a student should produce: 'AI Risk Map — \[feature name\]. Section 1: risks by category (user harm / legal-compliance / reputational / model-performance), each with a one-line description. Section 2: severity/likelihood score and classification (pre-launch mitigation required / post-launch monitoring acceptable) for each risk. Section 3: mitigation or monitoring plan per risk, with an owner assigned. Section 4: review cadence — this risk map will be revisited at launch, 30 days post-launch, and quarterly thereafter, updating likelihood assessments based on real production data.'                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Why should an AI risk map be treated as a living document revisited on a defined cadence, rather than a one-time pre-launch artifact?

\(A\) Because risk maps are only a formality with no real bearing on launch decisions.

**(B) Because real-world severity and likelihood can shift after launch as new data, new user populations, or model drift emerge, so ongoing review keeps the map accurate rather than frozen at a launch-day snapshot.**

\(C\) Because regulations require risk maps to be rewritten entirely every single week regardless of any actual change.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write your own standing 'AI Risk Map' template in your own words (sections and a review cadence), and fill it in for one AI feature idea of your choosing as a worked example.

**Lecture 360 requirements**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · AI Product Discovery · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define what makes AI-specific requirements different from traditional functional requirements, introducing the concept of a model requirements document covering data, performance thresholds, and fallback behavior.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Traditional functional requirements specify what a system must do ('the system shall display the user's order history'). AI-specific requirements need additional categories traditional requirements documents don't cover: data requirements (what training/validation data is needed, including representation across user segments — directly informed by the risk-mapping and use-case work from earlier in this month), performance thresholds (the specific accuracy, precision/recall, or fairness metric the model must meet before launch, tying back to the evaluation stage of the Month 19 lifecycle), and fallback behavior requirements (what the system must do when confidence is low or the model fails outright, tying back to the uncertainty-handling concepts from Month 20). A requirements document for an AI feature that only specifies the happy-path functional behavior and omits these three categories is incomplete by AI product standards, even if it would be a perfectly normal requirements doc for traditional software. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a traditional requirements line for a search feature might read 'the system shall return results matching the user's query.' The AI-specific equivalent requirements document for the same feature adds: 'Data requirement: training data must include representative query examples across all supported languages and at least three device-usage contexts. Performance threshold: top-5 relevance accuracy must exceed 85% on a held-out validation set before launch. Fallback requirement: when model confidence for a query falls below the defined threshold, the system shall display a 'no confident match' state with a manual search-filter fallback, rather than returning low-confidence results with no indication of uncertainty.'                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** What three categories of requirements does an AI-specific requirements document need that a traditional functional requirements document typically does not?

**(A) Data requirements, performance thresholds, and fallback behavior requirements.**

\(B\) Color palette requirements, font requirements, and animation timing requirements.

\(C\) Server hosting requirements, database schema requirements, and API versioning requirements.

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take a traditional functional requirement from any feature you know and write the three AI-specific additions (data, performance threshold, fallback behavior) it would need if that feature were instead AI-powered.

**Lecture 361 requirements**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · AI Product Discovery · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply a second requirements mechanic: writing acceptance criteria that specify a range or threshold rather than a single pass/fail condition, and defining who owns the decision to adjust that threshold post-launch.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | A second, deeper mechanic within AI requirements writing: because AI performance exists on a continuum rather than a binary pass/fail (as established in Month 19), acceptance criteria need to specify where on that continuum the product draws its line, and importantly, who has the authority to move that line later as real-world data comes in. This ownership question is often skipped in requirements docs, leading to confusion post-launch about whether a PM, a data scientist, or a cross-functional committee can authorize lowering an accuracy bar to ship faster, or raising it after a quality complaint — explicitly naming this decision-owner in the requirements document itself, before launch, avoids a scramble or a power vacuum when the question inevitably comes up under launch-deadline pressure. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: an AI requirements document for a content-recommendation feature specifies 'Launch acceptance threshold: engagement-weighted relevance score must exceed 0.72 on validation data, as measured by the data science team. Threshold-change ownership: any proposal to adjust this threshold post-launch (raise or lower) must be approved jointly by the PM and the data science lead, documented with the specific business or technical justification, logged in the feature's decision record.' This single clause prevents a scenario, which the lecture notes is common without it, where an engineer quietly ships a lower-threshold model under deadline pressure with no PM visibility into the change.                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why should an AI requirements document explicitly name who owns the authority to change a launched accuracy threshold, rather than leaving it unstated?

\(A\) Because thresholds, once set at launch, should never be changed under any circumstances.

**(B) Because without a named decision-owner, there's a risk a threshold gets quietly changed under deadline pressure with no proper visibility or justification logged.**

\(C\) Because only engineers are legally permitted to set any accuracy threshold in a product.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write an acceptance-criteria clause for an AI feature of your choice that specifies both a numeric threshold and who explicitly owns the authority to change that threshold after launch, including what justification they must document.

**Lecture 362 requirements**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · AI Product Discovery · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a real-world requirements gap by examining a documented AI product recall or rollback, tracing which requirement category was missing or under-specified.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | Worked real-world example: we examine a well-documented pattern across several reported autonomous-vehicle feature rollbacks and restrictions, where requirements around fallback behavior in edge-case conditions (certain lighting, weather, or road configurations the system was less confident in) were under-specified relative to the core driving-performance requirements, leading to incidents or regulatory action that forced the feature's operating conditions to be restricted after the fact. Tracing this through the requirements categories from lecture 360: data and performance-threshold requirements were clearly present and heavily tested, but fallback-behavior requirements for the specific edge cases where confidence was known to be lower were comparatively under-specified, illustrating that even sophisticated AI products can under-invest in the fallback-behavior requirement category relative to the core performance one. |
| **Worked example**      | Example of the case walkthrough's structure: 'Requirement category present and well-specified: core driving performance thresholds, heavily validated against test-track and real-world mileage data. Requirement category under-specified: fallback behavior for specific known-lower-confidence edge cases (certain lighting/weather conditions) — insufficient pre-launch specification of exactly what the system must do when confidence drops in these conditions led to restrictions being imposed after real-world incidents, rather than being designed and tested for before the feature's operating conditions were finalized.' This reinforces that fallback-behavior requirements deserve the same rigor as performance thresholds, not an afterthought treatment.                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** In the examined case, which requirement category was comparatively under-specified relative to core performance requirements, contributing to post-launch restrictions?

\(A\) Data requirements, since training data volume was insufficient.

**(B) Fallback-behavior requirements for specific known lower-confidence edge cases, which were not as rigorously specified or tested as core performance thresholds.**

\(C\) Branding and marketing requirements for how the feature was named.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Research one other real AI product recall, rollback, or feature restriction (briefly) and identify, using the three requirement categories from lecture 360, which category was most likely under-specified before launch.

**Lecture 363 requirements**

*Year 2 · Month 21 · AI Product Discovery · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Run a guided exercise writing a complete AI-specific requirements document for a new feature, covering functional behavior, data, performance thresholds, fallback behavior, and threshold ownership together.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | Hands-on capstone exercise for this run: students write a complete AI-specific requirements document for a proposed 'AI-powered inventory restock alert' feature (predicting which warehouse items are likely to run out and need reordering), pulling together every piece covered across lectures 360-362 into one deliverable — traditional functional requirements (what the alert does and where it appears), data requirements (what historical inventory and sales data is needed, and representation across seasonal patterns and product categories), performance thresholds (a specific precision/recall target for restock predictions, since both false alarms and missed restocks carry real costs), fallback behavior (what happens for new products with no sales history, an inherent cold-start gap), and threshold ownership (who can adjust the acceptance bar post-launch and what justification they must log). This exercise is the practical synthesis of the entire requirements run, mirroring the real document a PM would produce before an AI feature enters development. |
| **Worked example**      | Example of one section from the expected student output: 'Fallback behavior requirement: for products with fewer than 90 days of sales history, the model's restock prediction confidence is inherently low due to insufficient data (an epistemic uncertainty case, per Month 19); the system shall flag these as 'insufficient history for AI prediction' and fall back to a simple manual reorder-point rule set by the category manager, rather than presenting a low-confidence AI prediction with the same visual weight as a well-supported one.' Students produce equivalent sections for functional behavior, data requirements, performance thresholds, and threshold ownership.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** In the inventory restock alert exercise, what should happen for a new product with fewer than 90 days of sales history?

\(A\) The system should still generate an AI restock prediction with full confidence, since some data exists.

**(B) The system should flag insufficient history for AI prediction and fall back to a simple manual reorder-point rule, rather than presenting a low-confidence prediction with equal visual weight to a well-supported one.**

\(C\) The product should be excluded from the inventory system entirely until 90 days of history accumulate.

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a complete AI-specific requirements document (functional behavior, data, performance threshold, fallback behavior, threshold ownership) for one AI feature idea of your own, following the structure modeled in this exercise.

**Month 22 AI Prototyping**

*Allocation: 16 hours \| 16 lectures \| Level: Intermediate*

**Lecture 365 LLM-assisted prototyping**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · AI Prototyping · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain what LLM-assisted prototyping is and when it beats hand-building a prototype.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | LLM-assisted prototyping means describing a screen, flow, or interaction in natural language and letting a model (Claude, ChatGPT, v0.dev, Galileo AI) generate the markup, component code, or copy as a starting draft rather than a finished artifact. The core principle is specificity in, specificity out: a prompt that names the exact component library, the data shown, and the user's goal produces a usable draft, while a vague prompt produces generic boilerplate that still needs a full rebuild. This differs from traditional static prototyping (Figma click-throughs) because the output is often live code you can actually run, test interaction timing in, and hand to engineering as a starting point. The tradeoff is fidelity risk: generated UI can look polished while hiding accessibility gaps, inconsistent spacing, or components that don't exist in your design system. Treat every LLM-generated screen as a first draft that a designer critiques and repairs, never as a shippable artifact. |
| **Worked example**      | A PM prototyping a 'smart receipts' expense app types into Claude: 'Generate a React component for an expense list screen using Tailwind, with each row showing merchant, amount, and an AI-suggested category badge in blue; include a top bar with a +Add button.' The model returns working JSX in under a minute. The designer then opens it, swaps the generated blue badge color for the product's actual design-token color, and fixes the row height to match the existing list component — keeping the structure but correcting the visual system the model guessed at.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Why is LLM-assisted prototyping considered higher-risk than it looks on the surface?

**(A) Because generated code often runs and looks finished while still containing design-system violations or accessibility gaps that aren't obvious at a glance**

\(B\) Because LLMs cannot generate any visual markup at all and only produce plain text descriptions

\(C\) Because every LLM-generated prototype requires a paid enterprise API key before it can be tested with users

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Generate one LLM-assisted draft of a screen from your current project using a specific, detailed prompt, then list three things in the output you would NOT ship as-is.

**Lecture 366 LLM-assisted prototyping**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · AI Prototyping · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply prompt chaining to scaffold a complex screen in stages instead of one giant prompt.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | The deeper mechanic beyond a single prompt is prompt chaining: splitting a complex screen into sequential sub-prompts — first a layout/structure prompt, then a content/copy prompt, then an interaction/state-logic prompt — so each stage can be reviewed before the next builds on it. This matters because a single mega-prompt tends to produce a model's 'average' guess across everything at once, while chaining lets you lock in structure first and iterate on content and behavior independently without the model re-deciding layout every time. A related technique is constraining the model with a system prompt or pasted design-system snippet ('only use these button and card components, these exact spacing tokens') so output stays on-brand across the chain. Tools like Claude's Artifacts, v0.dev, or a Figma AI plugin support this iteratively: you regenerate just the piece that's wrong rather than the whole screen. The failure mode to watch for is context drift, where by step four the model has quietly abandoned a constraint you set in step one. |
| **Worked example**      | Prototyping an AI meal-planning assistant's results screen: Prompt 1 asks for the layout skeleton (header, filter bar, recipe card grid) with no content. Prompt 2, given that skeleton, asks only for realistic recipe card content (titles, calorie counts, a 'matches your macros' AI tag). Prompt 3 asks for the loading and empty states for that same grid. Because each prompt inherits the locked structure from the previous step, the final screen stays visually consistent instead of each regeneration reshuffling the grid.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main advantage of prompt chaining over one large prompt for a complex screen?

**(A) Each stage can be locked and reviewed before the next builds on it, preventing the model from re-deciding things like layout every regeneration**

\(B\) It removes the need for a human designer to ever review the output

\(C\) It guarantees the model will never hallucinate a component name

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take one screen you'd normally describe in a single prompt and split it into a 3-prompt chain (layout, content, states); run it and compare consistency against a one-shot attempt.

**Lecture 367 LLM-assisted prototyping**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · AI Prototyping · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a full worked example of turning a product requirement into a working AI-prototype screen.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture walks a single scenario start to finish to show the real decisions involved, not just the technique in the abstract: a team needs a clickable prototype of an onboarding flow for an AI-powered meal-planning assistant before a usability test in three days. The PM writes the first prompt naming the exact three onboarding questions (dietary restrictions, cooking skill, weekly budget) and asks for a progress-indicator pattern matching the product's existing stepper component. The designer reviews the draft, rejects the model's invented 'skip for now' link because it conflicts with a compliance requirement to collect allergy data, and re-prompts with that constraint stated explicitly. A third pass asks the model to wire a fake 'generating your plan' loading transition between the last onboarding question and the results screen. The whole arc — prompt, critique, re-prompt, critique — is the realistic rhythm of LLM-assisted work, not a single lucky prompt. |
| **Worked example**      | The final prompt chain output: a three-step stepper (restrictions → skill → budget), each with a back button, no skip link, ending in a 2-second branded loading animation before the first AI-generated meal plan renders. The team ships this exact clickable build to five test participants two days later, skipping a full Figma rebuild entirely.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** In the worked example, why did the designer reject the model's first draft that included a 'skip for now' link?

**(A) It conflicted with a stated compliance requirement to collect allergy data before proceeding**

\(B\) The link was rendered in the wrong font

\(C\) The model generated it in a language other than English

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick a real requirement from your own project with at least one hard constraint (legal, accessibility, or data requirement) and run it through a 3-step prompt-critique-reprompt cycle, documenting what the model got wrong each time.

**Lecture 368 LLM-assisted prototyping**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · AI Prototyping · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique common mistakes teams make when relying on LLM-assisted prototypes, and correct them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | This session is a critique clinic on the mistakes that recur once teams start trusting LLM output too much. The first mistake is accepting hallucinated UI patterns — a model inventing a 'swipe to dismiss' gesture or a component that doesn't exist in the product's actual design system, which then gets tested with users and creates false signal. The second is over-trusting generated copy: models default to confident, marketing-toned microcopy that doesn't match how the real product talks about uncertainty or errors, which is especially dangerous for an AI feature where honest hedging language matters. The third is prompt scope creep, where a PM keeps adding 'also add X' to one long-running chat until the output becomes an unmaintainable one-off that no one can regenerate from scratch. The fix for all three is the same discipline: write down the prompt that produced the current state, review output against the real design system before any user sees it, and restart the chain rather than endlessly patching. |
| **Worked example**      | A team tests a prototype where the model invented a shimmering 'AI is thinking' animation nobody designed, and three of five test participants describe it in the debrief as 'the best part of the app' — flagging that participants reacted to an artifact of the prototyping tool, not a real design decision the team can ship, because engineering has no such animation built.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** What is the risk of testing a prototype that includes a UI pattern the LLM invented but no one designed?

**(A) Participant reactions to that invented pattern create false signal about a decision the team never actually made and may not be able to ship**

\(B\) LLMs are legally prohibited from generating novel UI patterns

\(C\) The prototype will fail to load for any test participant

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Audit your most recent LLM-generated prototype screen for one hallucinated pattern, one mismatched-tone copy line, and one sign of prompt scope creep; fix all three and re-save the clean prompt that produces the corrected version.

**Lecture 369 realistic AI states**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · AI Prototyping · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Identify the distinct states an AI interface must simulate beyond a normal app's loading/success/error set.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | AI products need a richer state model than a typical CRUD screen because the system is often uncertain, slow, and non-deterministic. Beyond ordinary loading/success/error, a realistic AI prototype needs: a 'generating' state (the model is actively producing output, often shown as streaming text or a shimmer), a confidence or uncertainty state (the answer is probabilistic, and the UI should signal when it's a guess versus a sourced fact), a graceful-failure state (the model can't answer and should say so rather than confabulate), and a multi-turn context state (the system is retaining or has lost prior conversation context). Designing these states matters because usability testing an AI prototype that only ever shows the happy-path 'perfect answer' state teaches the team nothing about how real users will react to hedging, delay, or being wrong. Realistic AI state design is where trust is actually won or lost, more than in the happy path. |
| **Worked example**      | A recipe-suggestion assistant's prototype is built with five distinct states mapped out before any screen is drawn: idle, generating (shimmer, 1.5s), confident answer (green checkmark, 'based on your saved preferences'), low-confidence answer (amber dot, 'this is a guess — you haven't rated similar dishes'), and no-answer fallback ('I don't have enough information yet — try rating a few more meals'). Each state is prototyped and tested separately rather than assuming only the confident-answer state will ever be seen.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a confidence/uncertainty state considered essential in an AI prototype, where it wouldn't exist in a typical form-based app?

**(A) Because AI outputs are probabilistic, so the interface needs to signal when an answer is a guess rather than a verified fact**

\(B\) Because confidence states are a legal requirement for all mobile apps

\(C\) Because without it the app cannot display any text at all

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** List the five AI states relevant to a feature in your own project (idle, generating, confident, low-confidence, fallback) and sketch what each one literally looks like on screen.

**Lecture 370 realistic AI states**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · AI Prototyping · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build and compare three different mechanics for simulating AI states in a working prototype.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | There isn't one way to fake an AI state — the mechanic you choose changes what you actually learn from testing it. Streaming text simulation (revealing a response token-by-token, as ChatGPT does) can be built in Figma with staggered Smart Animate frames, in ProtoPie with a timed text-reveal interaction, or with a simple JavaScript interval in a coded prototype; it's worth the extra build time specifically when you need to test whether users start reacting to a partial answer before it finishes. A confidence-score UI (a percentage, a traffic-light badge, or a 'sources' expandable panel) is a static-state mechanic — simpler to build, and the right choice when the research question is about trust in the answer rather than about perceived latency. Multi-turn context state (showing that the system remembers something the user said two messages ago, e.g. 'since you mentioned you're vegetarian...') requires scripting a short fixed conversation rather than a single screen, and is the right mechanic specifically when testing whether users notice and value continuity. |
| **Worked example**      | Testing two mechanics side by side for a support chatbot: Group A sees a streaming-text prototype (words appear progressively over 2 seconds) to measure whether they interrupt or wait; Group B sees a static confidence-badge prototype (instant full answer plus a 'Medium confidence' tag) to measure whether the badge changes how much they trust the answer. The two prototypes answer two different research questions and are deliberately not combined into one build.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** When should a team choose a static confidence-badge mechanic over a streaming-text mechanic for an AI prototype test?

**(A) When the research question is about trust in the answer's accuracy rather than about perceived response latency**

\(B\) When the team has no access to any prototyping tool whatsoever

\(C\) When the product has no AI features to test

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Build the same AI answer screen two ways — once as a streaming reveal, once as an instant answer with a confidence badge — and note which mechanic better matches the specific question you're trying to answer in a future test.

**Lecture 371 realistic AI states**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · AI Prototyping · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a full support-chatbot example that sequences thinking, hedging, and fallback states realistically.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture traces one end-to-end scenario: a customer-support AI chatbot prototype for a telecom billing app, built to be tested with real confused customers rather than just demoed to stakeholders. The flow opens with a 'thinking' shimmer state lasting a deliberately realistic 1.8 seconds (matched to the team's actual backend latency data, not an arbitrary guess) so testers' patience is measured honestly. The response that follows is a low-confidence hedge — 'Based on your last bill, this looks like a data overage, but I'd recommend confirming with a representative' — paired with a visible 'View my bill details' source link, because hedged AI answers are more trustworthy when they show their work. When a tester types a question outside the bot's scope (a password reset request), the prototype branches to a graceful handoff state: 'That's outside what I can help with — connecting you to a human agent now,' rather than forcing the model to bluff an answer it doesn't have. |
| **Worked example**      | In the actual usability session, two of six participants tried to argue with the hedge response ('but I'm sure it's not an overage'), revealing a real design gap: the prototype had no state for the AI acknowledging pushback and re-checking, which the team added to their backlog as a new required state before the real build started.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why was the chatbot's 'thinking' delay set to match real backend latency data instead of being shortened for a snappier demo?

**(A) Because testing with inflated speed would teach the team nothing about how real users react to actual wait times they'll experience in production**

\(B\) Because long delays are a legal requirement for AI chat products

\(C\) Because the prototyping tool used cannot render any delay shorter than two seconds

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pull your own feature's actual or estimated backend latency and rebuild one 'thinking' state's timing to match it exactly, rather than an arbitrary round number.

**Lecture 372 realistic AI states**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · AI Prototyping · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique common mistakes in how teams fake AI states, and correct the ones most likely to mislead a usability test.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | The most common mistake in simulating AI states is making the 'thinking' delay too fast or too uniform — a prototype that always resolves in exactly one second regardless of question complexity trains test participants to expect a speed the real system can't deliver, which then shows up as disappointment in production rather than in testing, where it's cheap to catch. A second mistake is scripting only confident, correct mock answers, which inflates measured trust and task-success scores because real models are wrong or hedge far more often than a cherry-picked prototype answer suggests. A third, subtler mistake is never testing the error or fallback state at all — teams build five happy-path screens and zero 'I don't know' screens, then discover in production that users have no idea what to do when the AI actually fails. The fix is to deliberately script a distribution of outcomes into the test plan — some confident, some hedged, some outright failures — so the states tested match the states users will actually encounter. |
| **Worked example**      | A reviewer audits a prototype test plan for an AI tutor feature and finds all eight scripted questions have confident, correct, pre-written answers; she flags it and the team adds two questions designed to trigger a hedge and one designed to trigger a full 'I can't help with that' fallback, changing the measured 'trust score' from an inflated 92% down to a more honest 71% that better reflects real-world performance.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** What problem does testing only confident, correct AI answers create for a team's usability metrics?

**(A) It artificially inflates trust and success scores because real AI systems hedge or fail far more often than a cherry-picked happy path suggests**

\(B\) It makes the prototype file too large to open in most design tools

\(C\) It is the only state that can legally be shown to test participants

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Review your current AI prototype's test script and count what fraction of scripted responses are confident/correct versus hedged or failed; if it's not close to your real system's actual accuracy rate, rewrite the script to match it.

**Lecture 373 tool flows**

*Year 2 · Month 22 · AI Prototyping · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
