|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique common mistakes in AI roadmapping: vendor-dependency overcommitment and hidden uncertainty.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | The most common AI roadmapping mistake is overcommitting to a date that depends on a third-party model vendor's own roadmap — promising a Q3 launch of a feature that requires a longer context window or lower API pricing the team doesn't control and has only been told is 'coming soon,' which puts the team's credibility at the mercy of a vendor's own slipped timeline. A second mistake is presenting roadmap items with uniform visual confidence regardless of actual certainty — a committed, nearly-shipped item and a speculative bet sitting in the same font weight and column styling trains stakeholders to treat both as equally reliable, which erodes trust the first time the speculative one slips. The fix for the first mistake is simple and should be standard practice: any roadmap item dependent on an external vendor capability gets an explicit dependency note and sits no earlier than 'next,' never 'now.' The fix for the second is visually encoding confidence directly into the roadmap format — solid fill for committed, outlined or striped for exploratory — so the format itself communicates the uncertainty without requiring a caveat conversation every time someone reads it. |
| **Worked example**      | A roadmap reviewer flags an item reading 'Q2: Real-time multilingual voice assistant, pending \[Vendor\]'s announced but unreleased low-latency speech model' sitting in the 'Now' column with the same solid styling as a fully-committed internal feature; the fix moves it to 'Later,' adds an explicit note ('blocked on vendor release; no committed date until vendor ships'), and changes its visual style to an outlined, lower-confidence box so a stakeholder scanning the roadmap doesn't mistake it for a sure thing.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** What is the fix for a roadmap item that depends on a third-party AI vendor's unreleased capability?

**(A) Give it an explicit dependency note and place it no earlier than 'next' or 'later,' never treated as a committed 'now' item**

\(B\) Remove the item from the roadmap entirely with no explanation

\(C\) List it as committed to pressure the vendor into shipping faster

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Audit your current AI product roadmap for any item dependent on a third-party vendor capability; if its column or visual styling doesn't reflect that dependency honestly, move and restyle it.

**Lecture 401 metrics**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Lay out the three-layer metrics taxonomy for AI products: model, product, and business metrics.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | AI products need metrics tracked at three distinct layers, and conflating them is a common and costly mistake. Model metrics measure the AI system's raw technical performance in isolation — precision, recall, latency, perplexity — and answer 'is the model doing its narrow job well,' independent of whether anyone is using the feature built on top of it. Product metrics measure how real users actually engage with the feature — adoption rate, retention, task completion, time-to-value — and can move independently of model metrics entirely: a highly accurate model wrapped in a confusing interface can still show poor product metrics, and a mediocre model with excellent UX framing (clear hedging, easy correction) can outperform expectations on product metrics despite average model metrics. Business metrics measure the actual commercial or organizational outcome — revenue, cost savings, churn reduction — and are the ultimate justification for the whole effort, but they're also the slowest and noisiest signal, meaning a team that waits for business metrics alone to evaluate an AI feature will learn far too late if something's wrong at the model or product layer. |
| **Worked example**      | An AI customer-support deflection feature is reviewed across all three layers simultaneously: model metrics show the underlying classifier has 88% intent-recognition accuracy (a model-layer number data science cares about), product metrics show only 40% of eligible customers actually try the AI-suggested answer before escalating to a human (a product-layer number revealing a UX or trust problem independent of model accuracy), and business metrics show support cost per ticket is down only 3% despite the model's strong accuracy — the three layers together reveal the bottleneck is adoption and trust, not model quality, which a business-metrics-only view would have misdiagnosed as 'the AI isn't good enough.'                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why is it a mistake to evaluate an AI feature using only business metrics like revenue or cost savings?

**(A) Business metrics are slow and noisy, so a team relying on them alone learns about model- or product-layer problems far too late**

\(B\) Business metrics are never actually affected by AI features

\(C\) Model metrics and product metrics always move in exact lockstep with business metrics

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Define at least one metric at each of the three layers (model, product, business) for an AI feature in your own project, and identify what each layer would reveal that the others would miss.

**Lecture 402 metrics**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define north star and guardrail metrics specific to an AI feature, and explain why both are required together.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | A north star metric is the single measure that best represents the core value the AI feature is meant to deliver — for a support-deflection AI, that might be 'tickets resolved without human escalation.' A guardrail metric is a separate, independently tracked measure that must not degrade while the team optimizes the north star, specifically chosen to catch a way the north star could be gamed or a real cost could rise unnoticed — for the same feature, a guardrail might be hallucination rate or customer-reported dissatisfaction, because a team narrowly chasing deflection rate alone could technically improve it by making the AI falsely confident and wrong less often escalated, which would be a genuine regression in quality hidden behind an improving headline number. Choosing a north star without a guardrail is how a team optimizes itself into a worse product while every dashboard says things are improving; the guardrail's entire purpose is to be the metric that catches that exact failure mode before it reaches customers at scale. |
| **Worked example**      | A document-summarization AI feature sets 'percentage of summaries accepted without edits' as its north star and 'factual error rate per summary, audited on a weekly random sample' as its guardrail. Three months in, the acceptance-without-edits rate climbs steadily — until the guardrail audit catches that the model has started omitting a caveat sentence that made summaries look cleaner (and thus more likely to be accepted unedited) while quietly dropping a material fact, revealing the north star's improvement was partly an artifact the guardrail was specifically designed to catch.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** What is the specific purpose of a guardrail metric alongside a north star metric?

**(A) To catch a way the north star could be gamed or a real quality cost could rise while the headline number still looks like it's improving**

\(B\) To replace the north star metric entirely once it is defined

\(C\) To guarantee the AI model never makes an error

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Define a north star metric and at least one guardrail metric for an AI feature in your own project, specifically naming the failure mode the guardrail is designed to catch.

**Lecture 403 metrics**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through building a complete metrics dashboard for an AI customer-support deflection feature.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture builds one full metrics dashboard end to end for a real scenario: an AI feature meant to resolve customer support tickets without human escalation. The dashboard's north star tile is 'deflection rate' (tickets resolved by AI without escalation, as a percentage of eligible tickets), defined precisely enough to be unambiguous — eligible tickets exclude categories the AI isn't scoped to handle, so the denominator can't be quietly inflated by excluding hard cases after the fact. Guardrail tiles include hallucination rate (sampled and human-audited weekly, not self-reported by the model) and a customer-satisfaction score specific to AI-resolved tickets, tracked separately from overall CSAT so a dip can't hide inside a larger, noisier aggregate number. A model-layer tile tracks raw intent-classification accuracy so data science can diagnose whether a dashboard dip originates in the model or downstream in the product experience. Each tile on the dashboard carries a stated target threshold agreed before launch, not added retroactively once real numbers came in and someone wanted to declare success. |
| **Worked example**      | The finished dashboard specification states target thresholds explicitly next to each tile: 'Deflection rate target: 35% of eligible tickets by end of quarter. Hallucination guardrail: must stay below 2% of sampled resolved tickets, audited weekly — if it exceeds 2% two weeks running, deflection is automatically paused pending review.' That automatic-pause rule, written into the dashboard spec itself rather than left as an informal intention, is what actually makes the guardrail enforceable rather than aspirational.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the dashboard specify an automatic pause rule tied to the guardrail metric rather than just displaying the guardrail number for review?

**(A) Writing an enforceable action into the spec, not just displaying a number, is what makes the guardrail actually protective rather than purely informational**

\(B\) Automatic pause rules are a legal requirement for any AI dashboard

\(C\) Guardrail metrics have no practical use once displayed on a dashboard

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Build a complete metrics dashboard specification for an AI feature in your project with a precisely-defined north star, at least one guardrail with an explicit enforcement action, and a model-layer diagnostic tile.

**Lecture 404 metrics**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique common AI metrics mistakes: vanity metrics and Goodhart's law risk.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | A recurring metrics mistake in AI products is tracking a vanity metric that sounds impressive but doesn't reflect real value — 'number of AI responses generated' rises simply because the feature is used more, regardless of whether those responses actually helped anyone, which makes it a poor substitute for a value metric like 'tickets resolved without escalation' that ties directly to the outcome that matters. A second, related risk is Goodhart's law: once a metric becomes the explicit target that a team (or worse, the model itself through reinforcement or fine-tuning) is optimized against, the metric can be gamed in ways that technically satisfy it while betraying its original intent — a model fine-tuned hard against 'user accepts the response without editing it' can learn to produce shorter, vaguer, less-committal answers that are trivially easy to accept precisely because they say less, which improves the metric while making the product worse. The defense against both mistakes is the same discipline from the previous two lectures: pair every target metric with a guardrail that specifically checks whether the headline number's improvement is real value or a gamed artifact. |
| **Worked example**      | A team celebrates a 40% rise in 'AI suggestions accepted' for a coding-assistant feature until a guardrail audit reveals the model has started suggesting shorter, more generic code completions that are easier to accept at a glance but require more manual follow-up editing later — the acceptance metric improved while actual developer time saved, measured separately, got worse, exposing the acceptance number as a partly-gamed vanity metric rather than real value delivered.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** What is the core risk described by Goodhart's law in the context of AI product metrics?

**(A) Once a metric becomes the explicit optimization target, it can be satisfied in ways that technically improve the number while betraying the original intent behind it**

\(B\) Goodhart's law states that AI metrics always improve at a constant, predictable rate

\(C\) Goodhart's law only applies to metrics measured in currency

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Identify one metric currently used for an AI feature in your project that could plausibly be gamed, and design a specific guardrail metric that would catch that exact gaming behavior.

**Lecture 405 experimentation**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define the core AI experimentation toolkit: A/B testing, holdout groups, and offline versus online evaluation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Experimentation for AI features borrows from standard A/B testing but adds layers specific to probabilistic systems. A/B testing an AI feature usually means comparing two prompts, two model versions, or two response styles against each other with users randomly split between them, measuring a predefined success metric rather than relying on anecdotal impressions. A holdout group — a segment of users who never see the AI feature at all, for the length of the experiment — matters specifically for AI features because it's the only way to measure the feature's true incremental value against doing nothing, rather than just comparing one AI variant against another and assuming both are better than no AI. Offline evaluation tests a model's performance against a static, held-out labeled dataset before it ever reaches a real user, which is fast and cheap but can miss real-world input distribution shifts; online evaluation tests the model against real live traffic and user behavior, which is slower and riskier but catches the gaps offline evaluation can't see. The right experimentation plan usually sequences offline evaluation first as a gate, then online A/B testing with a holdout once the model clears that gate. |
| **Worked example**      | A document-summarization feature's experimentation plan runs offline evaluation first against a held-out set of 500 human-graded summaries, requiring a minimum quality score before any real user ever sees the model; once it clears that bar, the team runs an online A/B test splitting real users into variant-A summary style, variant-B summary style, and a holdout group who get no AI summary at all, specifically to measure whether either style actually beats the no-AI baseline, not just which of the two beats the other.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why does an AI experimentation plan need a holdout group that receives no AI feature at all, rather than only comparing two AI variants against each other?

**(A) Comparing only two AI variants cannot reveal whether either one actually outperforms doing nothing, which only a true holdout group can measure**

\(B\) Holdout groups are a formality with no measurable purpose

\(C\) Online evaluation always produces identical results to offline evaluation

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Design an experimentation plan for an AI feature in your project that includes an offline evaluation gate, an online A/B comparison of at least two variants, and a true holdout group.

**Lecture 406 experimentation**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Compare shadow testing, canary rollout, and multi-armed bandit testing as three distinct AI rollout experimentation strategies.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Beyond a standard A/B test, three more specialized experimentation strategies fit different AI rollout risk profiles. Shadow testing runs a new model version silently alongside the current production model on real traffic, logging what the new model would have returned without ever showing it to users — this is the right strategy specifically when you need to validate a risky new model version's real-world behavior before any user is exposed to it at all, at the cost of not learning anything about actual user reaction. Canary rollout exposes the new model version to a small, real percentage of live traffic (often 1-5%) with active monitoring and an immediate rollback trigger, which is the right strategy once shadow testing has de-risked the model's basic behavior and the remaining question is how real users respond, not whether the model's outputs are reasonable at all. Multi-armed bandit testing dynamically shifts traffic allocation toward whichever of several variants is currently performing best, rather than holding a fixed 50/50 split for the test's full duration, which is the right strategy when the cost of continuing to serve an underperforming variant is high and you want the experiment to self-correct traffic allocation as evidence accumulates, at the cost of statistical cleanliness compared to a fixed-split A/B test. |
| **Worked example**      | A recommendation-engine team sequences all three before a major model upgrade: shadow testing for two weeks confirms the new model's recommendations are directionally sensible on real traffic without anyone seeing them, a 3% canary rollout for one week catches a latency regression under real load that shadow testing's offline-style comparison never would have revealed, and only after both pass does a multi-armed bandit test run across four prompt-style variants in full production, automatically shifting traffic toward the best performer as data accumulates.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Why is shadow testing typically run before a canary rollout rather than the other way around?

**(A) Shadow testing validates a model's basic real-world behavior with zero user exposure risk, which should happen before any real users are exposed via canary rollout**

\(B\) Canary rollouts are always safer than shadow testing for any new model version

\(C\) Shadow testing requires more real user traffic than a canary rollout does

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For an upcoming model or prompt change in your own project, sequence which of the three strategies (shadow, canary, bandit) you'd run first, second, and third, and justify the order by risk.

**Lecture 407 experimentation**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a complete A/B test plan for comparing two summarization prompt strategies on a document-AI product.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture builds one full experiment plan end to end: comparing two summarization prompt strategies — a bullet-point extraction style versus a narrative-paragraph style — for a document-AI product. The plan states the primary metric (summary acceptance without manual edit) and the guardrail metric (a weekly-audited factual-accuracy score, so a style that's easier to skim but drops facts doesn't win by default) before the test launches, exactly following the earlier lectures' discipline. The sample-size calculation is done explicitly rather than guessed — given the baseline acceptance rate and the minimum detectable difference the team cares about, the plan states the number of documents needed per variant to reach statistical significance, and a minimum test duration to avoid a false-positive novelty effect from users simply reacting to something new rather than genuinely preferring it. A true holdout group, following lecture 405's pattern, receives no AI summary at all, to confirm either style actually beats a human reading the full document unaided on the team's chosen metric. |
| **Worked example**      | The finalized test plan specifies: '2,400 documents per variant needed to detect a 5-percentage-point difference in acceptance rate at 95% confidence; minimum four-week run to rule out novelty effect; guardrail — factual accuracy score (weekly audit of 50 random summaries per variant) must not drop below 90% for either style to be declared a winner, regardless of acceptance rate.' Writing the guardrail's veto power over the primary metric explicitly into the plan prevents an uncomfortable post-hoc argument later about whether a style with great acceptance but degraded accuracy should actually be allowed to win.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the A/B test plan specify a minimum four-week run duration rather than ending the test as soon as a difference first appears?

**(A) A longer minimum duration helps rule out a novelty effect, where users react to something merely being new rather than genuinely preferring it**

\(B\) Four weeks is a universal legal minimum for any AI experiment

\(C\) Test duration has no effect on whether a result reflects a real or temporary preference

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a complete A/B test plan for an AI feature comparison in your own project, including a calculated or estimated sample size, a minimum duration justified against novelty effect, and a guardrail metric with explicit veto power over the primary metric.

**Lecture 408 experimentation**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique common AI experimentation mistakes: early peeking, novelty-effect confusion, and narrow test input diversity.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | The most common AI experimentation mistake is peeking at results early and stopping the test as soon as a favorable-looking difference appears, which inflates the false-positive rate dramatically compared to waiting for the pre-registered sample size or duration — a discipline that's especially tempting with AI experiments because early results can look dramatic and teams are often under pressure to ship a win quickly. A second mistake is confusing a novelty effect with a genuine improvement: users engaging more with a new AI feature variant simply because it's new and different, a bump that frequently fades within weeks, which is exactly why lecture 407's minimum-duration discipline exists and why a one-week test declaring victory is especially suspect for anything involving a visibly new AI behavior. A third mistake is testing with too narrow a range of real input diversity — validating a summarization model only against well-formatted, English-language business documents and then being surprised when it performs badly on messy scanned PDFs or non-English documents in production, because the test population never represented the real-world input distribution the model would actually face. |
| **Worked example**      | A team declares victory on a new AI chat response style after three days, seeing a 15-point engagement lift; a more experienced reviewer points out the test hasn't run the pre-registered two weeks and the lift closely matches the classic shape of a novelty-effect curve from past experiments — the team extends the test, and by week two the lift has decayed to a statistically insignificant 2 points, confirming the early result would have shipped a change with no real benefit had it not been caught.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why is an AI experiment showing a dramatic early result especially suspect, rather than simply good news to act on quickly?

**(A) Early, dramatic-looking results are more likely to reflect noise or a fading novelty effect than a genuine, durable improvement**

\(B\) Dramatic early results are always a sign of a broken experiment with no valid data at all

\(C\) AI experiments cannot produce early results of any kind before their full duration completes

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Review a past or current AI experiment in your project for all three mistakes (early stopping, unaccounted novelty effect, narrow input diversity) and identify which, if any, might have affected a decision already made.

**Lecture 409 launch planning**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Lay out the essential components of a launch plan for an AI feature: phased rollout and a readiness checklist.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | Launching an AI feature responsibly means treating launch as a sequence of deliberately widening exposure, not a single flip-the-switch event. A phased rollout typically moves through internal alpha (the team and close internal stakeholders use the real feature on real or realistic data, catching obvious problems cheaply), a limited beta (a defined, consenting group of real external users, often with extra monitoring and a direct feedback channel), and a staged general availability rollout (gradually widening the percentage of all users exposed, following the canary-rollout discipline from lecture 406, rather than 100% at once). A readiness checklist gates the transition between each phase and should explicitly include: QA test coverage of the feature's failure and fallback states (not just its happy path), legal and compliance sign-off specific to the feature's risk profile, and support-team training so the humans who'll field confused or frustrated users after launch actually understand how the AI behaves and fails, not just how to use the feature's basic happy path. |
| **Worked example**      | An AI meeting-notes feature's readiness checklist explicitly requires, before beta can start, that the support team has completed a training session covering five specific AI failure scenarios (missed action item, misattributed quote, hallucinated decision, failed transcription due to accent, and total service outage) and knows the exact script for each — a requirement the team added after an earlier AI feature's beta launch overwhelmed support with tickets nobody knew how to triage because training had only covered the happy path.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the readiness checklist specifically require support-team training on failure scenarios, not just normal feature usage?

**(A) Because support staff need to be able to triage and respond to the AI's actual failure modes, not just explain how the feature works when it's working correctly**

\(B\) Because support training is a formality with no bearing on launch quality

\(C\) Because AI features never have any failure scenarios once they reach general availability

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a readiness checklist for an AI feature's phase transition (e.g., alpha to beta) in your own project, naming at least one specific failure-state item that must be verified before the gate opens.

**Lecture 410 launch planning**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Address go-to-market messaging specific to AI features, focused on avoiding overpromising and choosing an assistive-versus-autonomous framing.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | Launching an AI feature's go-to-market messaging carries a risk that a traditional feature launch doesn't: overpromising what the AI can reliably do, sometimes called AI-washing, sets customer expectations the real system can't consistently meet and produces a credibility cost that's expensive to repair once trust is damaged. A core messaging decision is framing the feature as assistive (the AI helps the human do the task faster or better, and the human remains clearly in control and responsible for the final outcome) versus autonomous (the AI performs the task independently with the human only reviewing or overseeing), and this framing decision should be made deliberately based on the feature's actual confidence and risk profile covered in Month 23's requirements and responsible-AI lectures — not chosen for whichever framing sounds more impressive in a press release. Marketing copy for an assistive feature should explicitly invite correction ('review and edit before sending') while autonomous-framed copy carries a much higher bar of required reliability and transparency before it's honest to use that language at all. |
| **Worked example**      | A legal-document review AI tool's marketing copy is revised before launch after a legal review: the original draft read 'Our AI reviews your contracts for risk' (implying autonomous, completed review), and was changed to 'Our AI flags potential risk areas in your contracts for your review' (assistive framing, explicitly inviting human judgment) — a wording change driven directly by the fact that the underlying model's precision wasn't yet high enough to responsibly claim a completed, autonomous review.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why should the choice between 'assistive' and 'autonomous' marketing framing for an AI feature be driven by its actual confidence and risk profile?

**(A) Because overclaiming autonomous reliability the system can't consistently deliver creates customer expectations that damage trust when the system falls short**

\(B\) Because autonomous framing is always illegal to use in AI product marketing

\(C\) Because assistive framing guarantees higher revenue regardless of the feature's actual performance

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Review the current marketing or in-product copy for an AI feature in your project and determine whether its assistive-versus-autonomous framing honestly matches the feature's actual confidence and risk profile; rewrite any line that overclaims.

**Lecture 411 launch planning**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a full phased launch plan for an AI meeting-notes feature, including a rollback kill-switch.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture builds one complete launch plan end to end for an AI feature that automatically generates meeting notes and action items. The internal alpha phase runs for two weeks with the product and engineering teams using it on their own real meetings, specifically chosen to surface obvious failure patterns (missed action items, misattributed quotes) cheaply before any customer sees them. The beta phase expands to 50 named customer accounts who've explicitly opted in and been told they're testing an early feature, with a dedicated feedback channel and daily monitoring of the guardrail metrics defined back in lecture 403's dashboard pattern. The staged general-availability rollout widens from 5% to 25% to 100% of eligible accounts over three weeks rather than all at once, following the canary discipline from lecture 406, with a feature-flag kill-switch that lets the team instantly roll any percentage back to 0% if a guardrail metric breaches its threshold at any stage — a mechanism tested in a dry run before the real launch, not assumed to work when it's actually needed. |
| **Worked example**      | The launch runbook includes a literal line the on-call engineer can execute without judgment calls under pressure: 'If hallucination-guardrail audit shows \>2% error rate at any rollout stage, immediately flip feature flag to 0% for all cohorts and notify the PM and support lead within 15 minutes.' Having this pre-written and pre-tested, rather than improvised in the moment, is what makes the kill-switch a real safety mechanism rather than an aspiration.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** Why was the feature-flag kill-switch tested in a dry run before the real launch, rather than trusted to work when first needed?

**(A) A mechanism assumed to work without being tested under realistic conditions may fail exactly when it's actually needed during a real incident**

\(B\) Dry runs are a regulatory requirement for any AI feature regardless of risk level

\(C\) Kill-switches cannot technically be built for AI features

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a complete phased launch plan (alpha, beta, staged GA percentages) for an AI feature in your own project, including a specific, pre-written kill-switch trigger condition and the exact action it initiates.

**Lecture 412 launch planning**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*
