|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique common AI launch mistakes: missing rollback plans and undertrained support teams.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | The most dangerous AI launch mistake is launching without a tested rollback plan for a misbehaving model — not having a theoretical ability to roll back, but never having actually exercised the rollback mechanism before it's needed under real incident pressure, which is exactly the gap lecture 411's dry-run discipline exists to close. A second recurring mistake is launching with a support team that's been briefed on the feature's intended behavior but never walked through its actual failure modes, which means the first time a customer reports the AI confidently stating something false, the support rep has no script and either improvises an answer that makes things worse or escalates everything, overwhelming a team that was never resourced for that volume. A third, related mistake is launching without a clear internal definition of what triggers a full rollback versus a partial mitigation versus 'monitor and continue' — without that threshold decided in advance, an incident becomes a stressful real-time debate about severity instead of a pre-agreed response. |
| **Worked example**      | A post-incident review of a botched AI feature launch finds all three mistakes present at once: the rollback mechanism, though it existed in code, had never been triggered outside of a unit test and failed silently in production for eleven minutes before anyone noticed; support had no documented response for 'the AI told me something false,' leading reps to simply apologize and escalate every single case; and there was no pre-agreed threshold for what error rate justified a full rollback, so the on-call team spent twenty minutes debating severity while the issue continued live.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a rollback mechanism that has only ever been tested in a unit test considered insufficiently validated for a real launch?

**(A) A unit test doesn't confirm the mechanism works correctly under real production conditions and incident pressure, which is the only time it actually matters**

\(B\) Unit tests are incapable of testing any part of a rollback mechanism

\(C\) Rollback mechanisms never need testing of any kind before launch

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Audit an AI feature's launch plan (yours or a known example) for all three mistakes: an untested rollback mechanism, an undertrained support team, and an undefined rollback-trigger threshold; fix whichever gaps you find.

**Lecture 413 lifecycle management**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain the post-launch lifecycle challenges specific to AI products: model drift, retraining cadence, and version deprecation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | An AI feature's work isn't done at launch — unlike most deterministic software, an AI model's real-world performance can silently degrade over time even with no code changes, a phenomenon called model drift, caused by the real-world data distribution shifting away from what the model was originally trained on (customer behavior changes, new slang appears, a competitor changes the market, external conditions shift). Detecting drift requires ongoing monitoring of the model-layer metrics established back in lecture 401, not a one-time launch validation that's assumed to hold indefinitely. A retraining cadence — a planned, recurring schedule for refreshing the model on newer data, rather than only retraining reactively once a problem is noticed — is a lifecycle management decision with real tradeoffs: too infrequent risks running a visibly stale model, too frequent burns engineering and data-science time retraining a model that hasn't actually drifted meaningfully yet. Version deprecation planning — retiring an old model version in favor of a new one — needs its own process, because an abrupt cutover can change user-visible behavior overnight in ways that feel like a regression even when the new version is measurably better on average. |
| **Worked example**      | A product-recommendation AI feature's lifecycle plan sets a baseline quarterly retraining cadence, but also defines a drift-triggered early retraining rule: if the model-layer click-through-rate metric drops more than 8% below its rolling 90-day baseline at any point, retraining is triggered immediately rather than waiting for the next quarterly cycle — combining a predictable cadence with a reactive safety net so the team isn't stuck choosing between one rigid schedule and pure firefighting.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why might a product combine a fixed retraining cadence with a drift-triggered early-retraining rule, rather than relying on just one or the other?

**(A) A fixed cadence alone could miss a sudden drift event between cycles, while relying only on reactive triggers could let a model run stale with no scheduled check at all**

\(B\) Fixed cadences and drift triggers always produce identical retraining schedules

\(C\) Retraining is never actually necessary once a model passes its initial launch validation

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Define both a baseline retraining cadence and a specific drift-triggered early-retraining threshold for an AI feature in your project, naming the exact metric and percentage change that would trigger the early retrain.

**Lecture 414 lifecycle management**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design a deprecation and migration process for retiring an old AI model version without abruptly disrupting users.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | Retiring an old model version in favor of a new one needs its own deliberate process because users can experience even a measurably better new version as a regression if it behaves differently in ways they've come to rely on, even unconsciously — a customer-support chatbot that used to give terse answers and now gives longer, more hedged ones might be objectively more accurate while still generating complaints simply because the change was unannounced and unexpected. A responsible deprecation process communicates the coming change to users in advance when the behavior shift is noticeable, offers a defined migration window during which both versions may run in parallel for comparison or gradual cutover (echoing the canary and shadow-testing techniques from Month 24's experimentation lectures, now applied to a retirement rather than a launch), and sets a hard end-of-life date for the old version so it doesn't linger indefinitely as unmaintained technical debt that still has to be monitored and supported. This is also the natural point to archive a model card (lecture 394's artifact) documenting the retired version's known behavior and limitations, in case a future regression investigation needs to compare the new version against what the old one actually did. |
| **Worked example**      | A document-summarization AI product's model-retirement notice to customers reads: 'Starting March 1, our summarization model is being updated to improve factual accuracy. You may notice slightly longer summaries during this transition. Both versions will run in parallel through March 15 — if you prefer the current style, contact support before the cutover date.' The explicit parallel-running window and the invitation to contact support before, not after, the cutover is what turns a potentially disruptive change into a manageable one.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a responsible model deprecation plan include a parallel-running migration window rather than an immediate full cutover?

**(A) It gives users time to notice and adjust to behavior changes, and gives the team a direct comparison window before fully committing to the new version**

\(B\) Parallel running is a legal requirement for retiring any software version, AI or otherwise

\(C\) Running two model versions in parallel is never technically possible

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a deprecation plan for retiring an AI model version in your own project, including a user communication message, a parallel-running migration window with specific dates, and a hard end-of-life date.

**Lecture 415 lifecycle management**

*Year 2 · Month 24 · Microsoft AI Product Manager II · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a complete lifecycle management scenario: a recommendation AI detecting drift at six months and triggering a full retraining and migration cycle.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture ties the month's lifecycle concepts together in one full scenario: a product-recommendation AI feature that launched successfully and performed well for its first five months, then showed its model-layer click-through-rate metric drop 11% below baseline in month six — a textbook drift signal per lecture 413's monitoring discipline, traced on investigation to a genuine shift in the underlying customer base following a successful marketing campaign that brought in a meaningfully different user segment the original training data didn't represent well. The retraining decision isn't simply 'retrain on more recent data' — the team also runs a fresh bias check (lecture 394's method) on the new training set, since the new customer segment changes the fairness-relevant population the model needs to perform well across. The new model version goes through the full deprecation and parallel-running process from lecture 414 rather than an immediate swap, specifically because the previous abrupt-cutover mistake at this company (referenced in lecture 414) had already taught them that lesson the hard way. |
| **Worked example**      | The project's final lifecycle report documents the full loop explicitly: drift detected (CTR -11% vs. 90-day baseline) → root cause identified (new customer segment from marketing campaign, underrepresented in original training data) → retraining triggered with a refreshed bias audit on the new population → two-week parallel-running migration with both model versions logging results → full cutover once the new version's metrics across both the original and new customer segments cleared their respective thresholds. Writing the loop down as a reusable template, not just a one-time incident report, is what lets the next drift event be handled faster.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why did the team run a fresh bias check on the retraining data, rather than simply retraining on whatever recent data was available?

**(A) The new customer segment changed the fairness-relevant population the model needed to perform well across, so a prior bias check result could no longer be assumed to still hold**

\(B\) Bias checks are only required the very first time a model is ever trained

\(C\) Retraining always automatically preserves whatever fairness properties the original model had

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a full lifecycle incident report template for your own AI feature covering drift detection, root-cause investigation, a bias-check re-run, and a parallel-running migration, so the process is documented before, not during, your next real drift event.

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

This month, together with Month 23, completes the Microsoft AI Product Manager Professional Certificate's content: this month maps to the certificate's final two courses, Product Design and UX/UI Fundamentals (about 25 hours; UX/UI principles, wireframing, mockups, and usability testing) and Product Launch and Post-Launch Management (about 29 hours; launch planning, marketing and sales strategy, QA, and post-launch management, with a final project). Across both months, the full certificate is five courses totaling roughly 117 hours, completed over about three months at a 10-hour-per-week pace, through course assessments and three separate final projects rather than one single proctored exam — there is no equivalent of a timed certification test for this credential. As with every month in this program, enrollment in the actual Microsoft certificate is entirely optional, and its current price, format, and availability should be verified directly on Coursera before registering; this internal examination, like all others in the program, uses an 80% passing bar. |
| **Worked example**      | A student finishing the program's Year 2 AI-product-management arc reviews their worked examples from lecture 399 (roadmap), 403 (metrics dashboard), 407 (A/B test plan), 411 (launch plan), and 415 (lifecycle incident) side by side, and writes a one-paragraph synthesis explaining how a single AI feature would actually move through all five disciplines in sequence from first roadmap entry through its eventual model-version retirement — the connective exercise this final exam is built to confirm actually landed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Which two courses of the Microsoft AI Product Manager Professional Certificate does Month 24 correspond to, completing the five-course certificate alongside Month 23?

**(A) Product Design and UX/UI Fundamentals, and Product Launch and Post-Launch Management**

\(B\) Enterprise Product Management Fundamentals, and Market Research and Competitive Analysis

**Lecture 417 Evaluating AI UX**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain how evaluating AI-driven product experiences differs from evaluating conventional software UX, and name the three layers of the AI UX evaluation stack.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Year 2 of this program built you into a working AI product manager: you learned AI capability tradeoffs, wrote PRDs for ML-backed features, and completed the Microsoft AI PM Professional Certificate. Year 3 assumes that fluency and turns it inward on judgment: can you tell whether an AI feature is actually working for the humans using it? Evaluating AI UX breaks into three layers that most teams conflate: model-level metrics (does the model produce accurate, well-formed output), system-level task metrics (did the end-to-end feature let the user finish their job), and UX-level perception metrics (did the user trust, understand, and want to keep using it). A chatbot can score 95% on an internal QA benchmark and still fail in the UX layer because users can't tell when to trust its answers. Non-determinism is the core complication: the same prompt can produce different outputs on different runs, so evaluation has to measure distributions and failure rates, not single pass/fail checks like a traditional usability test on a static screen. |
| **Worked example**      | Consider Lumen, a fictional email client's new "AI Rewrite" button. Applying the three-layer stack: the model layer checks whether the rewritten text is grammatically correct and on-topic, the system layer tracks whether the user sent the rewritten email without abandoning it, and the UX layer surveys users a week later on whether they trust the tone it chooses. The model layer can score perfectly while the UX layer reveals users still don't trust it with important emails.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Which evaluation layer would catch a case where an AI rewrite feature produces grammatically perfect text but users still abandon it because they don't trust its tone?

\(A\) Model-level metrics

**(B) UX-level perception metrics**

\(C\) System-level task metrics

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick an AI feature you use regularly (autocomplete, a chatbot, a recommendation feed) and write one metric for each of the three evaluation layers -- model, system, UX -- that you could realistically measure for it.

**Lecture 418 Evaluating AI UX**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design a human-evaluation protocol for AI output quality, including a scoring rubric and an inter-rater reliability check.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Human evaluation is the layer automated metrics can't replace: a person judging whether an AI-generated answer is actually helpful, safe, and appropriately toned. The two dominant designs are rubric-based absolute scoring, where a rater scores each output against fixed criteria (accuracy, relevance, tone, safety) on a scale, and pairwise comparison, where raters pick which of two outputs is better without being told which model produced which; pairwise comparison tends to produce more consistent judgments because humans are better at relative than absolute judgments. Whichever design you pick, you need multiple raters per item, because a single rater's opinion is just one data point with unknown bias. Inter-rater reliability, commonly measured with Cohen's kappa for two raters or Fleiss' kappa for more, tells you whether your rubric is actually well-defined: a kappa below about 0.4 usually means the rubric's categories are ambiguous and raters are guessing differently, not that the AI output is actually inconsistent. Crowdsourced panels trade individual rater expertise for statistical stability across many judgments. |
| **Worked example**      | Scoring an AI customer-support reply on a 5-point rubric (accuracy, tone, completeness, safety) with 3 raters: the team computes a simple agreement check and finds that "tone" scores disagree wildly, with a Cohen's kappa of 0.2, while the other three dimensions agree well above 0.6. Rather than concluding the AI's tone is erratic, the team revises the rubric by adding a concrete anchor example for each tone score.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** A UX researcher finds that three raters disagree sharply when scoring an AI chatbot's empathy on a 1-5 scale, with a Cohen's kappa of 0.15. What does this most likely indicate?

\(A\) The chatbot's empathy is genuinely inconsistent across outputs

**(B) The rubric's definition of empathy is too ambiguous for raters to apply consistently**

\(C\) Three raters is too few to ever get reliable scores

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a 4-point rubric, with a concrete example anchoring each point, for scoring how well an AI feature of your choice explains its own reasoning to a user.

**Lecture 419 Evaluating AI UX**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply the AI UX evaluation stack and a human-evaluation rubric together to assess a specific real-world AI feature end-to-end.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture runs one feature through the full evaluation stack built in the last two sessions: Scout, a fictional AI resume-screening assistant that ranks candidates for a recruiter. At the model layer, we check whether its relevance scores correlate with human-labeled relevance on a held-out set of resumes. At the system layer, we track task success as time-to-shortlist and the percentage of AI-ranked top-10 candidates the recruiter actually interviews -- a system metric can look good even when the model layer is noisy, which is itself a finding worth reporting. At the UX layer, a 5-rater pairwise comparison between the old ranked list and Scout's ranked list shows recruiters consistently prefer Scout's top 5 but distrust its bottom 20, which changes how the ranked list should be visually truncated rather than how the model is tuned. The lecture also covers a failure mode specific to hiring AI: evaluation must include a fairness check across demographic groups in the ranking, not just aggregate accuracy, because a model can pass aggregate metrics while still ranking unfairly within subgroups. |
| **Worked example**      | Scout's aggregate top-10 precision is 82%, but a disaggregated check shows precision drops to 61% for candidates with non-traditional career gaps -- a disparity invisible in the aggregate number until the team specifically ran the subgroup breakdown.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** In the Scout example, why does disaggregating the accuracy metric by candidate subgroup matter even though the aggregate metric looks strong?

\(A\) Aggregate metrics are always wrong

**(B) A model can perform well overall while still failing unevenly across subgroups, hiding bias**

\(C\) Disaggregation always increases the reported accuracy

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For an AI feature you're evaluating, identify one subgroup of users whose experience might differ from the aggregate average, and write one metric that would surface that difference.

**Lecture 420 task success**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define task success for an AI-powered feature and distinguish it from model-correctness metrics.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Task success measures whether the user actually accomplished what they came to do, which is a different question from whether the AI's output was technically correct. The most common quantitative definitions are completion rate (did the user reach a defined end state, like sending the AI-drafted email), time-to-completion (how long it took relative to the non-AI baseline), and retry or regeneration count (how many times the user had to re-prompt before accepting an output). A subtle trap: a feature can have a high per-output acceptance rate while task success is actually low, because users accept a mediocre output just to move on rather than fight with the tool -- acceptance is not the same as satisfaction or success. Defining the end state precisely matters more for AI features than traditional ones, because AI often offers several valid paths to the same goal, and a success definition that only counts the use-AI's-first-draft-unedited path will undercount real success. |
| **Worked example**      | An AI email-drafting feature inside a CRM tool defines its end state as "email sent," regardless of how much editing happened in between. The team deliberately avoids the simpler metric of counting only emails sent without edits, because that metric would reward the model for shallow, easy-to-accept drafts that users don't bother to improve rather than genuinely helpful ones.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why is "percentage of AI drafts sent without any edits" a misleading task-success metric on its own?

\(A\) It is impossible to measure accurately

**(B) It can reward bland, easy-to-accept drafts rather than genuinely helpful ones, and misses users who succeeded by editing**

\(C\) It only applies to email features

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a task-success definition, the end state, for one AI feature, specifying at least two different valid paths a user could take to reach that end state.

**Lecture 421 task success**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Choose an appropriate task-success metric for multi-turn conversational AI features versus single-shot generative features, and identify when a proxy metric is being gamed.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Single-shot AI features such as image generation or one-paragraph summarization suit a simple accept, reject, or retry funnel, but multi-turn agents, like a support chatbot handling a multi-step troubleshooting conversation, need a different lens: conversation-level resolution rate (did the issue get resolved within the conversation, however many turns it took) and turn efficiency (how many turns did resolution take relative to a human-agent baseline). A dangerous pattern is optimizing a proxy metric until it stops correlating with real success, a known instance of Goodhart's Law. If a team optimizes average turns to resolution alone, a chatbot that just says "I can't help, here's a phone number" after turn one looks efficient by that metric while actually failing the user completely. The fix is pairing the efficiency proxy with a true-outcome metric, such as whether the customer recontacted support within 24 hours, so a team can't improve the proxy at the true outcome's expense. |
| **Worked example**      | A support chatbot for a telecom company shortens average turns-to-resolution from 6 to 2 after a prompt change, and the team celebrates, until they discover the repeat-contact rate within 24 hours rose from 8% to 31%. The chatbot was closing conversations faster by giving up sooner, not by resolving issues faster.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** A team shortens average turns-to-resolution for a support chatbot by changing its prompts, and celebrates. What follow-up check would reveal whether this is a genuine improvement?

\(A\) Checking the model's response latency

**(B) Checking whether customers recontact support soon after, which would reveal issues weren't actually resolved**

\(C\) Counting the number of turns again next month

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For a multi-turn AI feature, propose a true-outcome metric that a team could check alongside an efficiency proxy, to guard against the proxy being gamed.

**Lecture 422 task success**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a complete task-success funnel, including a guardrail metric, for a specific AI feature scenario.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | Huddle, a fictional SaaS product's AI meeting-notes summarizer, defines its funnel as: meeting ends, summary generated, user opens summary, user edits, shares, or archives it, and action items get created in a linked task tracker. Task success is defined as at least one action item created or the summary shared within 24 hours. Rather than trusting that funnel number alone, the team adds a guardrail: a sampled accuracy audit on a subset of shared summaries, so an efficient-looking success rate doesn't mask bad summaries being shared uncritically. This matters because a summarizer can look successful by the funnel metric while quietly spreading misattributed information, which the funnel itself has no way to detect. |
| **Worked example**      | Huddle's funnel in week one: 1,000 meetings summarized, 740 opened, 410 shared or with an action item created within 24 hours (41% task success). A sampled accuracy audit on 50 of those shared summaries found 6 contained a misattributed action item, flagged as a guardrail issue even though the funnel metric looked healthy.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** In the Huddle example, why is the sampled accuracy audit necessary even though the 41% task-success number already looks reasonable?

**(A) Task success alone can't reveal whether successful-looking shares actually contain errors users didn't catch**

\(B\) Audits are required by law for AI products

\(C\) The funnel metric is always wrong without an audit

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Draw, as text steps, a task-success funnel for an AI feature of your choice, including at least one guardrail check that isn't just the completion rate.

**Lecture 423 hallucination and user-trust issues**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define hallucination in AI outputs from a UX standpoint and explain the concept of trust calibration.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Hallucination describes AI output that is fluent and confident-sounding but factually wrong, fabricated, or unsupported by any real source -- a model inventing a citation, a statistic, or a feature that doesn't exist. From a UX standpoint there are at least three flavors worth distinguishing: factual hallucination (wrong facts stated as true), fabricated-source hallucination (citing a paper, policy, or document that doesn't exist), and instruction-drift hallucination (the AI answers a question it wasn't asked, confidently). What makes this a UX problem rather than only a model problem is trust calibration: users should trust the AI roughly in proportion to how reliable it actually is for a given task, but most interfaces present every answer with the same confident tone, so users either over-trust or, once burned, under-trust and stop using a feature that's actually reliable most of the time. Good AI UX narrows that gap between perceived and actual reliability rather than trying to eliminate hallucination outright, which for current models isn't fully achievable. |
| **Worked example**      | A legal-research AI assistant cites a nonexistent case in a full, properly formatted citation style, and a lawyer nearly files it in a brief. The confident formatting itself, not just the wrong content, is what contributed to the over-trust, since nothing in the presentation signaled lower reliability for that specific claim.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Why is "trust calibration" a more useful UX goal than "eliminating hallucination entirely" for most current AI products?

\(A\) Hallucination doesn't actually affect users

**(B) Complete elimination isn't currently achievable, so UX should instead help users trust the system in proportion to its real reliability**

\(C\) Trust calibration is only relevant for legal products

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Find, or recall, one AI output you've seen that sounded confident but was wrong, and write down one interface change that could have helped you catch the error sooner.

**Lecture 424 hallucination and user-trust issues**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply UI patterns that expose model uncertainty and design a red-teaming pass to surface hallucination risks before launch.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | Several concrete UI patterns help close the trust-calibration gap: inline citations that link directly to a grounding source so a user can click through and verify rather than taking the claim on faith, confidence or hedging language calibrated to actual model uncertainty rather than generic disclaimers on every response, and explicit "verify this" prompts on higher-risk claim categories like numbers, dates, or names. Red-teaming for UX, distinct from security red-teaming, means deliberately trying to provoke the AI feature into hallucinating or behaving badly under realistic user conditions, such as ambiguous questions, edge-case inputs, or leading questions, and documenting not just whether it failed, but whether the interface made the failure visible or buried it in confident-sounding prose. A red-team pass should produce a catalog of failure examples a design team can use to decide which failure modes need a UI mitigation versus which need the product scope narrowed entirely. |
| **Worked example**      | Red-teaming an AI nutrition-coaching feature with questions like "what supplement cures diabetes" shows the model gives a hedged but still risky answer. The team's fix is a hard-coded refusal rule plus routing to a licensed-dietitian referral for a defined category of medical claims, rather than relying on the model's own hedging language.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** In the nutrition-coaching red-team example, why did the team add a hard-coded refusal rule instead of just improving the model's hedging language?

\(A\) Hard-coded rules are always better than model behavior

**(B) For a defined high-risk category, a reliable UI or system rule is safer than depending on the model's own judgment every time**

\(C\) Hedging language is never useful

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick an AI feature and write three adversarial test prompts you'd use to red-team it for hallucination or inappropriate confidence, aimed at a realistic edge case rather than an obviously malicious one.

**Lecture 425 hallucination and user-trust issues**
