*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a full hallucination incident for an AI feature and design the UX mitigations and test protocol that follow from it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Aura, a fictional telehealth app's AI symptom-checker, tells a user that a common antihistamine is safe to combine with their prescribed MAOI, a dangerous drug interaction the model got wrong. The post-incident review has three parts. First, root-causing where the error happened: it wasn't the model inventing a fact entirely, it retrieved an outdated drug-interaction document, which matters because the fix differs for bad source data versus a fabricated fact. Second, designing the mitigation: because drug interactions are a defined high-risk claim category, the team adds a mandatory grounding citation with a document date for any medication-interaction answer, plus a hard floor that routes monitored high-risk drug classes to a pharmacist-reviewed answer instead of a live model response. Third, writing the test protocol that would have caught this before launch: a standing regression set of known drug-interaction questions checked against a known-correct reference, re-run after every model or data update, not just at initial launch. |
| **Worked example**      | The team builds a standing regression set of 40 known drug-interaction question-and-answer pairs, checked automatically after every data refresh, with any mismatch blocking release rather than only testing this set once before the original launch.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the team specifically re-run the drug-interaction regression test after every underlying data update, not just before the initial launch?

\(A\) Regression tests are only useful once

**(B) Because the error came from outdated retrieved data, a future data refresh could reintroduce the same kind of error**

\(C\) Regression tests improve model creativity

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For a high-stakes AI feature, write one standing regression test, a small fixed set of known-answer questions, that should be re-checked every time the underlying model or data changes.

**Lecture 426 qualitative testing**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Run a think-aloud usability session adapted for an AI feature's non-deterministic outputs, with probes targeting user trust and mental models.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Standard think-aloud protocol asks a participant to narrate their thoughts while using a static interface, but AI features complicate this because the same task can produce a different output for the next participant, so you can't simply compare whether everyone got the same screen. The adaptation: run multiple participants through the same prompt or task, but treat variation in the AI output itself as data worth probing rather than noise to control out, asking "is this what you expected the AI to say?" after each response. Mental-model probes are especially important for AI features because users bring inconsistent assumptions about how aware the system is: some assume it remembers prior sessions when it doesn't, others assume it fact-checks itself when it doesn't. A good moderator surfaces these assumptions directly, asking something like "what do you think happens if you ask it the same thing again tomorrow?" rather than only observing silently. |
| **Worked example**      | In a moderated session for an AI shopping assistant, a participant assumes the assistant remembers their size preference from last week, which it doesn't, causing confusion. A moderator probe reveals the mental-model mismatch, pointing to a UI fix, a visible "remembered preferences" panel, rather than a model fix.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a moderator running think-aloud on an AI feature need to actively probe participants' mental models, rather than only observing silently as in standard usability testing?

\(A\) AI features don't need observation

**(B) Users often hold incorrect assumptions about what the AI remembers or verifies, and silent observation alone won't surface that mismatch**

\(C\) Probing is only needed for voice interfaces

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write two mental-model probe questions you'd ask during a think-aloud session for an AI feature, aimed at uncovering what the user assumes the AI remembers or checks.

**Lecture 427 qualitative testing**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design a Wizard-of-Oz study to qualitatively test an AI feature concept before any model is built.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | Wizard-of-Oz testing has a human secretly stand in for the AI, responding to live participant input in real time, so a team can qualitatively test the experience of an AI feature before investing in model development. The researcher sits behind the scenes, often relaying typed responses from another room, and must resist being a better AI than the one actually being built: if the human secretly checks facts the real model wouldn't check, results will be falsely optimistic. A good Wizard-of-Oz protocol fixes a response-time delay matching the real system's expected latency, and limits the wizard to only the capabilities the real model will actually have, so the qualitative reactions reflect the planned feature rather than an idealized one. |
| **Worked example**      | Testing a proposed AI trip-planning concierge chat feature before any model integration, a researcher manually types draft itineraries behind a curtain, deliberately introducing the same kind of generic suggestions the real model is expected to produce, and observes that participants get frustrated with vague day-by-day plans, feedback that reshapes the prompt design before a single API call is built.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** In a Wizard-of-Oz test, why must the human wizard be restricted to only the capabilities the real AI will actually have?

\(A\) It saves money

**(B) Otherwise the test will show artificially positive results that won't hold once the real, more limited AI is built**

\(C\) Restriction is required for ethical reasons only

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick an AI feature idea you haven't built yet and write a short Wizard-of-Oz test script: what a hidden human would need to do and not do to fairly simulate it.

**Lecture 428 qualitative testing**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique a qualitative AI-feature test plan for common mistakes and revise it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | Here is a qualitative test plan a fictional junior researcher wrote for an AI resume-tailoring feature, and the mistakes worth catching before running it. It tests only one AI-generated resume variant per participant, so there's no way to tell whether a bad reaction was about that specific output or the feature generally; the fix is giving each participant at least two independently generated outputs for the same input. It asks "don't you think the AI's suggestions were helpful?" which primes agreement; the fix is a neutral prompt like "walk me through what you thought as you read this." It has no mental-model probe at all, despite resume AI being a feature where users commonly assume the AI read the whole job posting when it only processed a pasted snippet; the fix adds a probe like "what information do you think it used to write this?" And it plans to have the lead researcher secretly rewrite any noticeably bad AI output live during the session to keep the session on track, a Wizard-of-Oz violation that will make the unedited feature look better in testing than it will in production. |
| **Worked example**      | The rewritten version changes "Don't you think the AI version reads more professionally?" to "How does this version compare to what you'd have written yourself?" -- the second phrasing elicits an honest comparison instead of priming agreement with a built-in positive framing.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** What is wrong with asking a participant "Don't you think the AI's suggestions were helpful?" during a qualitative AI feature test?

\(A\) It's too long

**(B) It's a leading question that primes the participant toward a positive answer rather than revealing their honest reaction**

\(C\) It doesn't mention the AI directly

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Take a qualitative test script you've written, or one from an earlier lecture, and rewrite any leading questions into neutral, open-ended versions.

**Lecture 429 quantitative testing**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Select an appropriate automated quality metric for a given type of AI-generated output.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | Automated metrics give you cheap, repeatable signal at scale, but each only fits certain output types. For text generation compared against a reference answer, BLEU and ROUGE measure word and phrase overlap, useful for summarization or translation where there's a correct-ish reference, but a poor fit for open-ended chat where many different phrasings are equally valid. Embedding similarity, the cosine similarity between vector representations of generated versus reference text, catches semantic closeness even when wording differs, fixing BLEU and ROUGE's biggest blind spot, but it can also mask a confidently-wrong paraphrase as similar. Perplexity measures how surprised a language model is by its own output and is mainly useful for comparing model versions during development, not for judging end-user helpfulness. For classification-style AI features such as spam detection or content moderation, precision, recall, and F1 score matter more than raw accuracy whenever classes are imbalanced, because a spam filter that labels everything not-spam on a dataset that's 95% legitimate mail scores 95% accuracy while being useless. |
| **Worked example**      | Choosing F1 over raw accuracy for an AI email-triage classifier where only 4% of incoming mail is actually urgent: a model that marks nothing urgent gets 96% accuracy but zero recall on the thing that matters.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Why is raw accuracy a misleading metric for an AI classifier when the categories are imbalanced, like 4% urgent versus 96% non-urgent email?

\(A\) Accuracy can't be computed for imbalanced data

**(B) A model can score very high accuracy by simply predicting the majority class and ignoring the rare but important class**

\(C\) Accuracy only applies to text generation

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For an AI feature with an imbalanced classification task, you can invent one, explain why you'd report precision and recall instead of, or alongside, accuracy.

**Lecture 430 quantitative testing**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design an online A/B test for an AI feature that balances statistical power against the cost of serving the AI model.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | A/B testing AI features online adds a wrinkle traditional feature A/B tests don't have: every request to the treatment arm costs real inference money, so sample size and test duration trade off directly against budget. This pushes teams toward smaller, targeted traffic allocations, like sending 5% of traffic to the AI variant, combined with guardrail metrics, secondary metrics watched to catch harm even while the primary metric looks fine, such as support ticket rate or session abandonment rate alongside the primary task-completion metric, since AI features can lift a primary metric while quietly damaging trust in ways that show up elsewhere. Statistical significance is harder to reach with the smaller sample sizes AI cost constraints often force, so teams need to decide in advance whether they'll accept a longer test window or a larger minimum detectable effect, rather than peeking at results daily and stopping early once they look good, which inflates false positives. |
| **Worked example**      | An e-commerce AI product-description generator A/B test runs at 10% traffic allocation for cost reasons; the primary metric, conversion rate, shows a small, not-yet-significant lift after one week, but the guardrail metric, return rate, ticks up, flagging that the AI descriptions may be overselling features, worth investigating before scaling traffic even though the primary metric alone wouldn't have blocked the rollout.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** In the product-description A/B test, why does a rising return rate matter even though the primary conversion metric shows a positive, if not yet significant, lift?

\(A\) Return rate is always the most important metric

**(B) A guardrail metric can reveal the AI is causing harm, such as overselling, that the primary metric alone wouldn't catch**

\(C\) Return rate and conversion rate always move together

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For an AI feature A/B test, name one guardrail metric you'd track alongside the primary success metric, and explain what kind of harm it would catch that the primary metric might miss.

**Lecture 431 quantitative testing**

*Year 3 · Month 25 · AI Research + Evaluation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Combine automated metrics and an online A/B test design into one quantitative evaluation plan for a specific AI feature.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Reviewly, a fictional AI-powered code-review-comment suggester inside a dev tool, gets a two-stage quantitative evaluation plan tying together the last two lectures. Offline, the team measures an automated metric: precision of suggested comments against a labeled set of real past review comments. Online, they run a 5% traffic A/B test with a primary metric of pull-request merge time and a guardrail metric of the rate at which reviewers dismiss suggestions as not useful. Combining an offline automated check with a cost-aware online test lets the team get signal at two different stages before committing full traffic, rather than relying on either method alone. |
| **Worked example**      | Offline, Reviewly's suggestions matched held-out real reviewer comments with 68% precision. Online at 5% traffic, pull-request merge time dropped 9%, not yet significant at one week, while the not-useful dismiss rate held steady at 12%, giving the team enough signal to extend the test rather than ship or kill it immediately.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the Reviewly team choose to extend the test rather than immediately ship or kill the feature after one week?

\(A\) One week is never long enough for any test

**(B) The primary metric showed a promising but not-yet-significant result and the guardrail metric showed no red flag, which argues for more data rather than a premature decision**

\(C\) Extending tests is always the safest choice regardless of data

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a short quantitative evaluation plan, one offline metric plus one online A/B primary metric plus one guardrail metric, for an AI feature of your choice.

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

| **Learning outcome**    | Demonstrate mastery of Month 25's AI evaluation methods -- evaluating AI UX, task success, hallucination and trust, and qualitative and quantitative testing -- by reviewing and self-assessing against the program's 80% internal passing bar.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | This exam reviews the full arc of Month 25: the three-layer AI UX evaluation stack and human-evaluation rubrics from Evaluating AI UX, defining and avoiding Goodhart's-Law traps in task success metrics, distinguishing hallucination types and designing trust-calibration UI alongside red-teaming from the hallucination and user-trust unit, adapting think-aloud and Wizard-of-Oz methods for qualitative testing of non-deterministic AI output, and choosing automated metrics alongside cost-aware A/B testing for quantitative testing. As with every month in this program, the internal passing standard is 80%: treat any topic you can't confidently explain out loud, without looking at your notes, as a signal to revisit that lecture's worked example before moving into Month 26's advanced research methods, which assume you can already design an evaluation plan, not just define these terms. |

If not, revisit lecture 431 before the exam.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** Which of Month 25's topics specifically addressed the risk of a metric looking good while the underlying feature actually gets worse?

\(A\) Evaluating AI UX's three-layer stack

**(B) Task success and its discussion of proxy metrics and Goodhart's Law**

\(C\) Qualitative testing's think-aloud adaptation

**Month 26 Advanced UX Research**

*Allocation: 16 hours \| 16 lectures \| Level: Advanced*

**Lecture 433 Moderated testing**

*Year 3 · Month 26 · Advanced UX Research · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Distinguish concurrent from retrospective think-aloud in moderated testing and apply techniques to reduce moderator bias.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | Moderated testing comes in two think-aloud flavors: concurrent, where the participant narrates thoughts while performing the task, and retrospective, where the participant performs the task silently and then reviews a recording afterward to narrate what they were thinking. Concurrent think-aloud captures reactions in the moment but can slow participants down and alter their natural behavior; retrospective avoids that distortion but relies on memory, which fades fast and can be reconstructed rather than recalled. Moderator bias creeps in through small things: a moderator who acknowledges a correct action warmly but stays silent after a mistake unintentionally signals which answers are right, and leading phrasing like "was that confusing?" presumes an answer. Mitigations include a written moderator script with neutral acknowledgments used identically regardless of outcome, and having a second observer code the same session independently to catch bias the moderator themselves can't see. |
| **Worked example**      | A moderator testing a budgeting app's new AI insight card catches themselves saying an enthusiastic "nice" every time a participant clicks the card and staying silent when they scroll past it. A second observer flags this pattern from a recording, and the script gets revised to a single neutral phrase used for every participant action.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** Why is retrospective think-aloud sometimes preferred over concurrent think-aloud, despite relying on memory?

\(A\) It's always more accurate

**(B) It avoids forcing the participant to verbalize while performing the task, which can otherwise slow them down and change their natural behavior**

\(C\) It requires no moderator at all

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a neutral moderator script line you'd use consistently regardless of whether a participant succeeds or struggles at a task step.

**Lecture 434 Moderated testing**

*Year 3 · Month 26 · Advanced UX Research · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design a moderated check-in protocol to add depth to an ongoing diary study.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | A diary study alone, participants self-logging entries about their experience over days or weeks, gives you breadth over time but shallow depth per entry, since people write quick notes, not analysis. Pairing it with moderated check-ins, a short call every few days reviewing recent entries together, recovers depth without asking participants to write essays: the moderator picks one or two entries and asks follow-up questions like "you wrote this felt frustrating on Tuesday, walk me through what happened right before that." This hybrid also catches entries too terse to be useful on their own and lets the researcher probe inconsistencies between what someone logged and what they later recall, which is itself informative when the two don't match. The scheduling tradeoff is real: check-ins add moderator time and participant burden on top of the diary itself, so most studies schedule them at natural milestones, like midpoint and end, rather than after every entry. |
| **Worked example**      | A 3-week diary study of a new habit-tracking app schedules a 15-minute moderated call at the end of week 1 and week 3. The week-1 call surfaces that a participant's brief diary note "forgot to log again" actually meant the app's reminder notification wasn't firing, a bug invisible from the diary text alone.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why does pairing a diary study with periodic moderated check-ins help, beyond what the diary entries alone provide?

\(A\) Check-ins replace the need for diary entries entirely

**(B) Check-ins let the researcher probe behind terse or ambiguous entries to uncover detail diary text alone wouldn't reveal**

\(C\) Check-ins are required for all research regardless of method

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For a diary study you might run, write two follow-up questions you'd ask a participant about a specific entry during a midpoint check-in call.

**Lecture 435 Moderated testing**

*Year 3 · Month 26 · Advanced UX Research · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a full moderated test session script, including probes, for a specific AI feature.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | This session walks through a full moderated script for Penny, a fintech app's AI feature that flags unusual spending. The warm-up avoids priming toward the AI feature directly, asking instead how the participant usually checks their spending, so baseline behavior is visible before they encounter Penny's insight card. The task uses concurrent think-aloud with a neutral prompt at each step, and the script flags two specific moments to probe regardless of what the participant does: the instant they first notice the insight card, to catch first impressions before they fade, and the moment right after they dismiss or act on it, to catch the decision rationale while fresh. The session ends with a short retrospective segment reviewing just that one card interaction, asking what the participant thought Penny was basing this on, a mental-model probe adapted from Month 25's qualitative-testing unit, now folded into a fully moderated session design. |
| **Worked example**      | A sample verbatim script line: "I'm going to let you use the app like you normally would, just talk through what you're noticing as you go. There's no wrong way to do this." The probe at first notice of the card: "What's your first reaction to seeing this?"                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the script specifically flag the instant the participant first notices the insight card as a moment to probe, rather than waiting until the end of the session?

\(A\) First impressions are irrelevant to usability testing

**(B) First reactions fade quickly from memory, so capturing them in the moment preserves detail a later retrospective recall would lose**

\(C\) The moderator has nothing else to ask about

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a moderated test script outline, warm-up, task, two specific probe moments, retrospective close, for an AI feature of your choice.

**Lecture 436 unmoderated testing**

*Year 3 · Month 26 · Advanced UX Research · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Choose between moderated and unmoderated testing methods for a given research question, and run an unmoderated tree test or first-click test.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Unmoderated testing removes the moderator and lets participants complete tasks on their own time via a platform, trading the depth and follow-up-question flexibility of moderated sessions for scale and lower cost per participant. Two classic unmoderated techniques: tree testing, where participants see just a site's navigation structure, no visual design, and are asked to find where they'd click to complete a task, isolating whether the information architecture itself makes sense; and first-click testing, where participants see a real screen and the only thing measured is where they click first, which correlates strongly with eventual task success, since a wrong first click dramatically lowers the odds of completing the task at all. The tradeoff that matters most for AI features specifically: unmoderated tests can't adapt their questions to a surprising AI output the way a moderator can, so they fit testing a fixed AI-feature interface shell much better than testing variable AI-generated content itself. |
| **Worked example**      | Running an unmoderated tree test on a redesigned settings menu that now includes a new AI-preferences section, before any visual design is built, to check whether users can find where to turn off AI features without the test being influenced by actual AI output quality.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the lecture argue that unmoderated testing fits testing the AI-feature interface shell better than testing variable AI-generated content itself?

\(A\) Unmoderated tests can't be run online

**(B) A moderator's ability to follow up on a surprising AI output doesn't exist in unmoderated formats, so they work best where the thing being tested doesn't vary per participant**

\(C\) Unmoderated tests are always less reliable than moderated ones

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Identify one part of an AI feature's interface, not its AI-generated content, that would be well suited to an unmoderated tree test or first-click test, and explain why.

**Lecture 437 unmoderated testing**

*Year 3 · Month 26 · Advanced UX Research · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design an unmoderated diary study to capture experience-over-time, including entry prompts, frequency, and incentive structure.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | A diary study asks participants to self-report their experience over an extended period, days to weeks, making it the main tool for studying how an experience changes with repeated use, something a single-session test can't capture at all. Design choices that make or break a diary study: whether entries are periodic, once a day regardless of activity, or event-triggered, logged right after the behavior of interest happens; event-triggered entries capture fresher, more specific detail but require a reliable trigger mechanism, such as a push notification tied to feature use. Entry length should be deliberately short, 2-3 guided questions rather than open essays, because long prompts cause diary fatigue and dropout by day 3. Incentive structure usually combines a per-entry micro-incentive with a completion bonus, because paying only for full completion rewards participants who stop bothering once they realize they've missed too many days to qualify. |
| **Worked example**      | A 3-week diary study of a fitness app's AI workout-adjustment feature uses event-triggered entries, a prompt fires right after each AI-adjusted workout, with three fixed questions: what did it change, did that feel right, would you have wanted something different, plus a \$2 per-entry incentive and a \$20 completion bonus designed to keep late-study participants from giving up once they've missed a few entries.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why does an event-triggered diary entry, logged right after the AI feature is used, typically capture more useful detail than a once-daily periodic entry?

\(A\) Event-triggered entries are always shorter

**(B) Logging right after the behavior happens captures fresher, more specific detail before memory fades, compared to recalling it once at the end of the day**

\(C\) Periodic entries are illegal in most research contexts

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Design the entry prompts, 2-3 short questions, and incentive structure for a 2-week diary study of an AI feature you choose.

**Lecture 438 unmoderated testing**

*Year 3 · Month 26 · Advanced UX Research · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Produce a complete unmoderated diary study plan for a specific AI feature, from recruitment through analysis handoff.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | A meditation app's AI-personalized session recommender gets a 3-week diary study plan. Recruitment requires participants to be in their first month of app use, not power users who already have fixed habits, because the study is studying how trust in the recommender forms over time. Entry prompts are event-triggered, firing right after each AI-recommended session, with three short questions. A mid-study check avoids requiring a full moderated call: an automated reminder fires if 2 days pass with no entry. The handoff format for the synthesis team bundles raw entries with timestamps and a running completion-rate tally per participant. |
| **Worked example**      | Entry prompts: what did it recommend, did it match what you needed right then, what would you have picked instead, if anything. Recruitment requires participants in their first month of app use, and the incentive is \$3 per entry plus a \$15 bonus for completing at least 12 of 15 possible event-triggered entries over 3 weeks.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the meditation-app diary study specifically recruit participants in their first month of use rather than long-time power users?

\(A\) New users are easier to recruit

**(B) The study is studying how trust in the AI recommender forms over time, which requires participants who haven't already settled into fixed habits**

\(C\) Power users refuse to participate in diary studies

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a one-paragraph recruitment screener question set for a diary study, designed to exclude participants whose existing habits would make the study's specific question, such as trust formation, hard to observe.

**Lecture 439 synthesis**

*Year 3 · Month 26 · Advanced UX Research · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply affinity mapping and thematic coding to move from raw qualitative data to organized insight.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | Affinity mapping is the act of clustering raw data points, individual quotes, observations, diary entries, into groups based on similarity, done bottom-up so the categories emerge from the data rather than being decided in advance; the researcher writes each discrete observation on its own note and moves notes next to similar ones until clusters stabilize, then names each cluster.
