|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Evaluate a design decision using the cost-of-change curve and articulate why late-stage usability fixes are categorically more expensive than early ones.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | A second advanced-practice mechanic: the cost-of-change curve, the well-documented pattern that the cost of fixing a usability or design flaw rises sharply the later it's caught — a flaw found in a paper wireframe costs a redraw; the same flaw found in a shipped product costs an engineering sprint, a support burden, and reputational cost. This lecture trains students to use this curve as an argument for when and how much usability investment is justified at each stage, and to recognize the organizational trap of skipping early, cheap validation ('we don't have time to test wireframes') that predictably creates expensive late-stage rework ('now we don't have time to fix this before launch, so we ship it anyway'). |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a team skips testing a checkout flow's wireframes to save a week, ships it, and discovers in post-launch analytics that 18% of users abandon at the shipping-address step because of an ambiguous field. The fix now requires a code change, QA regression testing, and a re-deploy — roughly 15x the effort a wireframe-stage fix would have taken, which is the cost-of-change curve made concrete with real numbers from one team's own project.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** According to the cost-of-change curve, why is a usability flaw caught in a wireframe review dramatically cheaper to fix than the same flaw caught after launch?

\(A\) Wireframe tools are free while production deployments cost money

**(B) At the wireframe stage nothing has been built yet, so the fix is a redraw; after launch the fix requires code changes, QA, redeployment, and addressing already-affected users**

\(C\) Usability flaws found after launch are legally required to go through a longer review process

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Estimate the cost-of-change multiplier for one real flaw you've encountered in a product (wireframe-stage fix vs. post-launch fix) and write two sentences justifying your estimate.

**Lecture 483 advanced UX practice**

*Year 3 · Month 28 · Advanced UX + NN/g Preparation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Synthesize usability principles, interaction patterns, and heuristics into a single advanced UX audit of one real product screen.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | This synthesis lecture closes Month 28's main arc by requiring students to combine all three frameworks taught this month into one integrated audit: usability principles (effectiveness/efficiency/satisfaction) to frame what's being measured, interaction patterns to name what mechanism is at play, and the 10 heuristics to structure the specific findings. The point is that a professional-grade UX audit doesn't pick one lens — it moves fluidly between them, using whichever gives the sharpest diagnosis for a given issue, and presents findings in a prioritized, severity-rated format that a product team can act on in a sprint planning meeting.   |
| **Worked example**      | Example: auditing a project-management app's task-assignment screen, the synthesis audit notes an effectiveness failure (assigning a task to an inactive teammate silently fails with no feedback — also a 'visibility of system status' heuristic violation, severity 3), an interaction-pattern mismatch (a confirm dialog appears for the low-stakes, reversible action of reassigning a task, when an undo toast would reduce friction), and an efficiency complaint (reassigning 10 tasks requires repeating the same 4-click flow 10 times, with no bulk-action pattern available) — three distinct findings, each diagnosed with the lens that best explains it. |

**Knowledge check:** In a synthesis UX audit combining usability principles, interaction patterns, and heuristics, what determines which framework is used to diagnose a given finding?

\(A\) All three frameworks must be applied to every single finding for the audit to be valid

**(B) Whichever framework most precisely explains the specific issue — effectiveness/efficiency for outcomes, interaction patterns for mechanism mismatches, heuristics for structured findings**

\(C\) The frameworks are interchangeable and any one can be used for any finding

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick one real screen and write a 3-finding mini-audit, using a different one of this month's three frameworks (principles, interaction patterns, heuristics) to diagnose each finding.

**Lecture 484 Month 28 Examination**

*Year 3 · Month 28 · Advanced UX + NN/g Preparation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Demonstrate mastery of Month 28's advanced UX material and understand the real scope, format, and cost of NN/g UX Certification preparation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | This exam lecture reviews Month 28 end to end: usability principles (Nielsen's five components and the ISO 9241-11 effectiveness/efficiency/satisfaction triad), interaction patterns (direct manipulation, optimistic UI, undo-over-confirm, and matching pattern to frequency/stakes), and Nielsen's 10 usability heuristics with severity-rated heuristic evaluation. The course's internal passing bar for this exam, as throughout the program, is 80%. Because this month is explicitly framed as NN/g UX Certification preparation, it also covers the real structure of that credential accurately: NN/g's UX Certification is not a single proctored exam like many tech certifications — it requires passing 5 separate courses plus each course's own individual timed exam (each exam due within 35 days of attending its course), totaling 30+ hours of live, real-time instructor-led training, at an approximate cost of USD 6,500, which changes periodically and should be verified directly with NN/g before registering. Enrollment in NN/g is entirely optional and external to this program. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a review question bank item asks a student to diagnose a real interaction (an e-commerce 'Add to Cart' button with no visible state change after being clicked) using the month's three frameworks together — it's an effectiveness/visibility-of-system-status failure by heuristic evaluation, and a missed opportunity for optimistic UI feedback by interaction-pattern analysis — exactly the kind of multi-framework synthesis question this exam uses to confirm readiness, alongside a short section confirming the student can correctly state NN/g's 5-course-plus-5-exam structure and approximate cost rather than assuming it works like a single-sitting exam.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Which statement correctly describes the NN/g UX Certification's actual requirements, as covered this month?

\(A\) It is a single 3-hour proctored exam similar to other industry certifications

**(B) It requires passing 5 separate courses plus each course's own individual timed exam, roughly 30+ hours of training, at an approximate cost of USD 6,500**

\(C\) It is a free, self-paced course-completion badge with no exam component

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a one-paragraph self-assessment against Month 28's 80% internal passing bar, citing one specific concept each from usability principles, interaction patterns, and heuristics that you feel confident explaining to someone else, plus the NN/g certification's real 5-course-plus-exam structure and approximate cost.

**Month 29 Accessibility + Inclusive AI**

*Allocation: 16 hours \| 16 lectures \| Level: Advanced*

**Lecture 485 WCAG concepts**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain the four WCAG POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) and correctly classify a given accessibility issue under one of them.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, currently at version 2.2 with level AA as the common legal/industry target) organizes all accessibility requirements under four principles, nicknamed POUR: Perceivable (users must be able to perceive the content through at least one sense — so an image needs alt text for users who can't see it), Operable (users must be able to operate the interface — so every mouse-only interaction needs a keyboard equivalent), Understandable (content and operation must be predictable and comprehensible — plain language, consistent navigation), and Robust (content must work with current and future assistive technology, which is why semantic HTML matters more than div-soup with CSS that only looks right). Every specific WCAG success criterion falls under exactly one of these four, which gives a fast way to triage: if an issue can't be perceived at all, it's a Perceivable problem; if it can be perceived but not acted on, it's Operable. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a modal dialog that traps keyboard focus so a screen-reader or keyboard-only user can tab in but never tab back out is a POUR 'Operable' violation (the interface can be perceived and understood but not successfully operated), distinct from a modal with no alt text on its close icon, which is a 'Perceivable' violation. Diagnosing which POUR category an issue falls under points directly at the right kind of fix — focus-trap bugs need keyboard-event code fixes, missing alt text needs content fixes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** A video player has captions and a visible transcript, but the play/pause button only responds to mouse clicks, not keyboard input. Which POUR principle does this violate?

\(A\) Perceivable

**(B) Operable**

\(C\) Understandable

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick one app or website and find one real accessibility issue, then classify it under the correct POUR principle (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, or Robust) with one sentence of justification.

**Lecture 486 WCAG concepts**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply the conformance levels A, AA, and AAA and the specific success-criterion structure of WCAG to evaluate whether a feature meets a stated accessibility target.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | This second WCAG lecture goes deeper into the standard's mechanics: WCAG success criteria are organized into three conformance levels — A (minimum, must-have baseline), AA (the level required by most legal standards including the ADA's practical benchmark and the EU's EN 301 549), and AAA (the highest, often impractical to apply site-wide, reserved for specific high-value content). Each success criterion has a number (e.g., 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) is AA) and precise, testable language — '4.5:1 contrast ratio for normal text' is not a suggestion, it's a measurable pass/fail. This lecture trains students to look up and cite the actual criterion number and level when making an accessibility claim, rather than saying something vague like 'the contrast feels low.' |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a design system's body text is light gray (#999999) on a white background, which measures at a 2.85:1 contrast ratio using a contrast-checking tool — this fails WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), an AA-level criterion requiring 4.5:1 for normal-size text. The fix isn't aesthetic preference; it's a specific, numbered, testable failure against a specific conformance level, and the team can state exactly which darker gray value (e.g., \#595959, which measures 7:1) would pass.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Why does citing the specific WCAG success criterion number and conformance level (e.g., '1.4.3 AA') matter more than saying 'this fails WCAG'?

\(A\) Because WCAG criteria numbers are required by law in every jurisdiction

**(B) Because it makes the finding specific, testable, and tied to an exact measurable standard rather than a vague impression**

\(C\) Because AAA is always the correct target to cite regardless of context

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Use a contrast-checking tool on three text/background color pairs from a real app and report which WCAG conformance level (A, AA, AAA) each pair passes or fails, citing criterion 1.4.3.

**Lecture 487 WCAG concepts**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Audit a real screen against a representative set of WCAG success criteria and produce a pass/fail list with criterion numbers and fix recommendations.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | This is the hands-on application of WCAG concepts: a guided audit of one real screen against a curated set of 8-10 common success criteria spanning all three conformance levels and multiple POUR categories — contrast (1.4.3), text resizing (1.4.4), keyboard access (2.1.1), focus visibility (2.4.7), consistent navigation (3.2.3), and name/role/value for assistive tech (4.1.2), among others. Students work through each criterion as a checklist item against a live interface, which mirrors how a professional accessibility audit is actually produced for a client or internal stakeholder — not a subjective design critique, but a criterion-by-criterion pass/fail report with citations. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: auditing a restaurant-reservation site, the checklist finds: 1.4.3 (contrast) passes on body text but fails on the 'Reserve' button's disabled state (gray-on-gray at 2.1:1); 2.1.1 (keyboard) fails because the date picker calendar widget cannot be navigated with arrow keys; 4.1.2 (name/role/value) fails because a custom dropdown built from styled divs has no ARIA role, so a screen reader announces it as plain unlabeled text instead of as a selectable control. Each line item in the audit names the exact criterion, the exact element, and a specific recommended fix (add role="combobox" and ARIA attributes, for the dropdown example).                                        |

**Knowledge check:** In a formal WCAG audit, why is it important to cite the specific success criterion number next to each finding rather than just describing the problem in plain language?

**(A) It allows the finding to be verified against the standard's exact testable requirement and tracked for compliance**

\(B\) Plain-language descriptions are not allowed in professional audits

\(C\) Criterion numbers are only needed for AAA-level findings

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Conduct a mini WCAG audit of one real screen against 5 success criteria of your choice (citing criterion numbers), producing a pass/fail table with one fix recommendation per failure.

**Lecture 488 keyboard flows**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain and test the three core keyboard-accessibility requirements: full operability without a mouse, visible focus indicators, and logical tab order.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | Keyboard accessibility is foundational because many assistive technologies (screen readers, switch devices, voice control) rely on the same underlying keyboard-navigable structure as a sighted keyboard-only user — if an interface isn't keyboard operable, it's very likely not accessible to several different disability groups at once. This lecture covers the three testable requirements: every interactive element must be reachable and operable via Tab/Shift+Tab/Enter/Space/arrow keys with no mouse at all (2.1.1 Keyboard); every focused element must show a visible focus indicator so the keyboard user can see where they are (2.4.7 Focus Visible); and the tab order must follow a logical, predictable sequence matching the visual/reading order, not the order elements happen to appear in the DOM. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a product page has a visually prominent 'Buy Now' button positioned above a 'Reviews' section in the layout, but because of how the CSS was written, the Reviews section's elements come first in the DOM and therefore first in tab order — a keyboard user tabbing through the page hits review-related links before reaching Buy Now, breaking the logical flow a sighted mouse user experiences naturally. The fix is reordering the DOM (or using tabindex carefully) to match the visual reading order.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** A keyboard-only user reports that pressing Tab repeatedly jumps around the page in an order that doesn't match what they see on screen. Which keyboard-accessibility requirement is being violated?

\(A\) Visible focus indicator (2.4.7)

**(B) Logical tab order matching visual/reading order**

\(C\) Full operability without a mouse (2.1.1)

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Unplug your mouse (or set it aside) and try to complete one common task on a website using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, and arrow keys. Note any point where you got stuck or lost track of focus.

**Lecture 489 keyboard flows**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Diagnose and fix a keyboard focus trap, and explain why custom interactive components (modals, dropdowns, date pickers) are the most common source of keyboard flow bugs.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | A second, deeper mechanic in keyboard flows: focus traps, where keyboard focus gets stuck inside (or locked out of) a component and the user cannot Tab their way out — the single most common and most severe keyboard-accessibility bug, because it can make a whole page unusable rather than just inconvenient. Focus traps overwhelmingly originate in custom-built interactive components (a modal, a custom dropdown, a date picker, a carousel) built from generic divs and spans with JavaScript-managed behavior, rather than native HTML elements (button, select, dialog) that come with correct keyboard behavior built into the browser for free. This lecture teaches the diagnostic habit: when you find a focus trap, check first whether a native HTML element could have been used instead of a custom-built one. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a custom-built modal for a newsletter signup opens on page load and, due to a missing focus-trap release, never lets Tab reach outside the modal even after the user clicks the visible 'X' close button with a mouse — the modal visually disappears but keyboard focus is still logically trapped inside the now-invisible element, so a keyboard user is stuck indefinitely. The fix (beyond better focus management) is often to use the native HTML dialog element, which handles correct focus trapping and release automatically.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why are custom-built components (like a div-based modal or dropdown) the most common source of keyboard focus traps?

\(A\) Custom components are always visually styled, which confuses screen readers

**(B) Native HTML elements come with correct keyboard behavior built into the browser automatically, while custom components require the developer to manually and correctly reimplement that behavior in JavaScript**

\(C\) Focus traps only occur in components built with CSS Grid

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Find one custom interactive component (a modal, dropdown, or carousel) on a website, test its keyboard behavior, and note whether focus can be trapped or lost — then identify whether a native HTML element could replace it.

**Lecture 490 keyboard flows**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Run a guided keyboard-flow walkthrough of a real multi-step process (e.g., checkout or signup) and document every point of friction or failure.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | This hands-on lecture applies keyboard-flow principles across an entire multi-step real-world task rather than one isolated component, since keyboard accessibility failures often compound across a flow — a minor tab-order issue on step 1 combined with a focus trap on step 3 can make an entire checkout process impossible to complete by keyboard alone, even though each individual bug seems minor in isolation. Students complete a full flow using only the keyboard, documenting every point of friction with a timestamp-style log (which step, which element, what went wrong), which mirrors the deliverable format used in professional accessibility QA sign-off before a feature ships. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: walking a multi-step signup flow by keyboard only, the log reads: 'Step 1 (email/password): fine, logical tab order. Step 2 (plan selection): radio buttons not reachable by Tab, had to use mouse. Step 3 (payment): focus visible but lands on a hidden element after submitting, no indication the page moved.' This single document, built from a real end-to-end attempt, is far more useful to engineering than a general statement like 'the signup flow needs accessibility work,' because every row names the exact step and exact failure.                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why is testing an entire multi-step flow by keyboard more valuable than testing each screen in isolation?

\(A\) Multi-step testing takes less time overall

**(B) Accessibility failures can compound across steps, and a flow that looks fine screen-by-screen can still be fully blocked for a keyboard user by one bug partway through**

\(C\) Isolated screen testing is not a valid WCAG method

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Complete one multi-step real flow (signup, checkout, or a settings change) using only your keyboard, and produce a step-by-step log noting every friction point or failure.

**Lecture 491 screen-reader considerations**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain how screen readers interpret semantic HTML and ARIA, and identify why a visually correct interface can still be announced incorrectly or not at all.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | Screen readers (VoiceOver, NVDA, JAWS, TalkBack) don't see pixels — they read the accessibility tree, a structure the browser builds from HTML semantics and ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes, announcing each element's role (button, link, heading), name (the label text), and state (checked, expanded, disabled). This means a div styled to look exactly like a button is, to a screen reader, just an unlabeled block of text with no role at all — nothing is announced as interactive, so a screen-reader user may never discover it's clickable. This lecture establishes the core mental model: visual correctness and accessibility-tree correctness are two separate systems, and a design can be pixel-perfect while being functionally invisible to a screen reader. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a 'favorite' icon-only button (a heart icon with no visible text label) is built as a clickable span with a background-image. Visually it works perfectly. To a screen reader it announces as nothing — not even 'clickable' — because it has no role and no accessible name. Adding role="button", tabindex="0", and aria-label="Add to favorites" makes the exact same visual element announce correctly as 'Add to favorites, button,' with zero visual change.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why might a custom icon button that looks and functions correctly for a sighted mouse user be completely invisible to a screen-reader user?

\(A\) Screen readers cannot process any icon-based buttons under any circumstances

**(B) Screen readers read the accessibility tree built from HTML/ARIA semantics, not the visual appearance — an element with no role or accessible name isn't announced as interactive even if it looks like a button**

\(C\) Icon buttons are deprecated under current WCAG guidelines

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Turn on a screen reader (VoiceOver on Mac, Narrator on Windows, or TalkBack on Android) and navigate one screen of an app with your eyes closed or the display off. Note one element that was announced confusingly or not announced at all.

**Lecture 492 screen-reader considerations**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply ARIA live regions and correct heading structure to fix two of the most common screen-reader-specific failures: silent dynamic updates and unnavigable page structure.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | A second, deeper mechanic in screen-reader design: two specific, very common failure patterns beyond basic labeling. First, dynamic content updates (a form validation error appearing, a cart total changing, a toast notification) are completely silent to screen-reader users unless marked with an ARIA live region (aria-live="polite" or "assertive"), because screen readers only announce what's currently focused — they don't notice content that changes elsewhere on the page unless told to. Second, screen-reader users navigate long pages primarily by jumping between headings (h1-h6) using a dedicated shortcut, which only works if headings are used for actual structure (not just styled to look big) and nest in a logical order — skipping from an h1 straight to an h4, or using headings purely for visual size, breaks this core navigation method entirely. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: an e-commerce page shows '3 items added to cart' as a toast notification with no aria-live attribute — a sighted user sees it appear and fade, but a screen-reader user, who was focused on the 'Add to Cart' button the whole time, hears nothing and has no idea the action succeeded. Adding aria-live="polite" to the toast's container makes the screen reader automatically announce the new text the moment it appears, with no change to visual design.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** A toast notification confirming 'Item added to cart' appears and disappears, but a screen-reader user never hears it announced. What is the most direct fix?

\(A\) Make the toast stay on screen longer

**(B) Add an ARIA live region (e.g., aria-live="polite") to the toast's container so screen readers announce the new content automatically**

\(C\) Increase the toast's font size

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Inspect the heading structure (h1-h6) of one real webpage using browser dev tools or a heading-outline extension, and note whether headings are used for structure, skip levels, or are missing where a section clearly needs one.

**Lecture 493 screen-reader considerations**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Conduct a real screen-reader walkthrough of a form or multi-step task and document specific announcement failures using correct ARIA/semantic terminology.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | This hands-on lecture has students perform an actual screen-reader task completion (using VoiceOver, NVDA, or TalkBack) on a real form or checkout-like flow, documenting exactly what was announced at each step versus what should have been announced, using the terminology from the previous two lectures (role, name, state, live region, heading structure). This mirrors professional accessibility QA practice, where a tester's notes need to distinguish precisely between 'this field has no accessible name' (an ARIA/labeling bug) versus 'this error appeared but wasn't announced' (a missing live-region bug) versus 'I couldn't find the submit button by heading navigation' (a structure bug) — three different bug classes with three different fixes. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: testing a password-reset form with VoiceOver, the walkthrough log reads: 'Email field: announced as "edit text," no label — accessible-name bug, needs aria-label or a \<label\> element. Submit button: announced correctly as "Reset Password, button." Error state after invalid email: no announcement at all when the red error text appeared — missing live-region bug.' Each row isolates one specific, fixable bug class rather than a vague note like 'the form is hard to use with a screen reader.'                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** A screen-reader tester notes 'the submit button announces correctly, but an error message that appears after a failed submission is never announced.' What specific class of bug is this, and what's the fix?

\(A\) An accessible-name bug on the button, fixed by adding aria-label

**(B) A missing live-region bug on the error message, fixed by adding aria-live to its container**

\(C\) A heading-structure bug, fixed by converting the error text to an h2

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Complete one real form using a screen reader with your eyes closed (or display off), and log at least 3 specific findings using the categories: accessible-name bug, live-region bug, or heading-structure bug.

**Lecture 494 bias**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define algorithmic bias and distinguish its three common sources: biased training data, biased labeling/measurement, and biased deployment context.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | Bias in AI-driven products doesn't come from one cause — this lecture breaks it into three distinct sources that require different fixes. Biased training data happens when the data used to train a model under- or over-represents some group relative to reality (a resume-screening model trained mostly on past hires at a historically homogeneous company learns to favor applicants who resemble that history). Biased labeling/measurement happens when the thing being measured or labeled is itself a biased proxy (using 'arrests' as a proxy for 'crime' bakes in whatever bias already exists in policing patterns, not actual crime rates). Biased deployment context happens when a model performs fine on average but is deployed in a context where its blind spots disproportionately harm one group (a voice-assistant trained mostly on American English accents deployed globally without acknowledging a known accuracy gap for other accents). Diagnosing which source is at play changes the fix — more diverse data, a better proxy label, or different deployment safeguards. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a well-documented real case, the COMPAS criminal-risk-assessment tool, was found by independent researchers (ProPublica, 2016) to flag Black defendants as high-risk at a higher rate than white defendants with similar actual recidivism outcomes — traced back to using 'rearrest' as the training label, a measurement proxy already skewed by disparities in policing and arrest patterns, which is a labeling/measurement bias, not simply 'the algorithm is prejudiced' as a vague claim.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** A hiring-screening AI was trained only on resumes of employees hired in the past 10 years at a company with a historically narrow hiring pattern. What source of bias does this most directly illustrate?

\(A\) Biased deployment context

**(B) Biased training data**

\(C\) Biased labeling/measurement

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Find one real documented case of algorithmic bias (a news article or research paper is fine) and identify which of the three sources — training data, labeling/measurement, or deployment context — it primarily illustrates, with one sentence of justification.

**Lecture 495 bias**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply bias-auditing techniques — disaggregated evaluation and proxy-variable review — to assess whether an AI feature performs equitably across user subgroups.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | A second, deeper mechanic for addressing bias: disaggregated evaluation, meaning a model's accuracy or error rate must be measured and reported separately for relevant subgroups (not just as one overall average), because an aggregate metric can look fine while hiding a large gap for one group — a facial-recognition system with 99% average accuracy can still have 65% accuracy for one demographic subgroup, a gap the aggregate number completely conceals. Alongside this, proxy-variable review means scanning input features for variables that correlate strongly with a protected characteristic (zip code often proxies for race and income; name can proxy for gender and ethnicity) even when that characteristic isn't used directly, since removing the explicit variable doesn't remove the bias if a strong proxy remains in the model. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a credit-scoring model audit disaggregates approval rates by self-reported demographic group and finds a 15-point gap in approval rate between groups with otherwise similar income and repayment history — a gap invisible in the model's single overall accuracy metric. Further proxy-variable review finds that 'zip code' is one of the model's top five weighted features, which the audit flags as a likely proxy for race and income even though race was never an input field.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** A model's overall accuracy is reported as 97%. Why might this number alone be insufficient to confirm the model is unbiased?

\(A\) 97% is below the industry standard threshold for AI deployment

**(B) An aggregate accuracy figure can conceal a much lower accuracy for a specific subgroup; disaggregated evaluation is needed to reveal subgroup-level gaps**

\(C\) Accuracy percentages are only meaningful above 99%

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick one AI-driven feature (a recommendation engine, a screening tool, a chatbot) and list two input variables it likely uses that could serve as proxies for a protected characteristic, even if that characteristic isn't an explicit input.

**Lecture 496 bias**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique a real or hypothetical AI product bias-mitigation plan, identifying at least one gap between a stated fix and the bias source it's supposed to address.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | This critique session targets a common failure in industry bias-mitigation efforts: proposing a fix that sounds responsible but doesn't actually match the diagnosed source of bias from lecture 494. A frequent example is a company responding to a training-data bias finding by adding a generic 'fairness disclaimer' to the product UI instead of actually diversifying the training data or reweighting the model — a UX/legal fix layered on top of an unaddressed technical problem. Students practice reading a mitigation plan skeptically and asking: does this fix the data, the label, the deployment context, or does it just add a warning label while leaving the underlying bias mechanism untouched? |
| **Worked example**      | Example: after a disaggregated-accuracy audit reveals a facial-analysis feature performs significantly worse for darker skin tones, a product team's proposed fix is to add a small disclaimer reading 'results may vary by lighting and skin tone.' The critique identifies this as not a mitigation at all — it's a liability disclaimer that leaves the actual accuracy gap in place; a real mitigation would involve retraining on a more representative dataset or disabling the feature for the affected subgroup until it's fixed.                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** A bias audit finds a feature performs worse for one demographic subgroup. The team's response is to add a disclaimer noting 'results may vary.' What is the strongest critique of this response?

\(A\) The disclaimer is a legally sufficient and complete fix for any bias finding

**(B) The disclaimer addresses legal exposure but does not fix the underlying accuracy gap for the affected subgroup, which is the actual problem identified by the audit**

\(C\) Disclaimers are never appropriate in AI products

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Find one real company statement or policy about AI fairness/bias mitigation and assess whether it describes an actual technical fix (data, labels, model) or primarily a disclaimer/communication response.

**Lecture 497 inclusive AI design**

*Year 3 · Month 29 · Accessibility + Inclusive AI · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply inclusive design principles specifically to AI-driven features, covering transparency about AI involvement, user control over AI decisions, and graceful degradation for users AI serves poorly.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | Inclusive AI design extends general inclusive-design principles to the specific risks AI introduces. Transparency means users should know when they're interacting with or being evaluated by an AI system, especially where the stakes are meaningful (a resume being auto-screened, a chat being handled by a bot rather than a human) — hiding this erodes trust and removes the user's ability to calibrate how much to rely on the output. User control means providing an override or appeal path when an AI decision affects someone materially (a human-review option when an automated content moderation decision is made), rather than treating the model's output as final and unquestionable. Graceful degradation means designing for the users the model serves worst — if accent-recognition accuracy is known to be uneven, a voice interface needs an easy, undegraded fallback to text or a human, not a frustrating loop of repeated 'I didn't understand that.' |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a customer-support chat widget clearly labels AI-handled messages with a small 'AI Assistant' tag and offers a persistent, one-tap 'Talk to a human' option visible at every step, rather than letting the bot pretend to be a human agent or burying the escalation option three menus deep — this directly implements transparency (users know it's AI) and user control (an easy override exists) as inclusive-AI-design requirements, not just nice-to-haves.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why does inclusive AI design call for a visible, easy-to-find 'talk to a human' option in an AI chat interface, rather than relying on the AI to eventually recognize it should escalate?

\(A\) Because AI chat interfaces are legally required to offer human escalation in all cases

**(B) Because the AI may serve some users poorly in ways it cannot reliably detect itself, so a user-initiated override preserves control for exactly the users the AI handles worst**

\(C\) Because human agents are always faster than AI at resolving issues

***Correct answer: B***
