|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain statistical significance, p-values, and sample-size calculation well enough to judge whether a test result is trustworthy.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | Statistical significance addresses one specific question: if there were truly no difference between control and variant, how likely would it be to see a result at least this extreme by chance alone — a p-value below the conventional 0.05 threshold means that chance explanation is unlikely, not that the effect is large or important. A result can be statistically significant but practically meaningless (a 0.1% lift that doesn't justify the engineering cost), and a result can be a genuinely large, important effect that fails to reach significance simply because the sample was too small. This is why sample-size calculation has to happen before running the test: given a baseline conversion rate, a minimum effect size worth detecting, and a desired confidence level, a sample-size calculator tells you how many users per group the test needs — running a test with too few users and declaring 'no significant difference' is often just an underpowered test, not real evidence of no effect. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: an e-commerce site's checkout-button test shows control converting at 4.0% and variant at 4.3% after one week, with a p-value of 0.22 — not significant. Rather than concluding the new button doesn't work, the team checks their pre-test sample-size calculation and finds they'd planned for three weeks of traffic to reliably detect a 0.3-point lift at their baseline rate; stopping at one week means the test was simply underpowered, not that the effect is absent.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** In the checkout-button example, why is it a mistake to conclude the new button 'doesn't work' after one week with a non-significant result?

**(A) The test was planned to need three weeks of traffic to reliably detect the effect size in question, so stopping early means the test was underpowered, not that there's no real effect**

\(B\) A p-value of 0.22 actually indicates a highly significant positive result

\(C\) One week is always sufficient for any A/B test regardless of traffic volume or effect size

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For a test you specified in the previous exercise, estimate (even roughly) what minimum lift would actually be worth detecting, and think through why a tiny sample would make that lift hard to detect reliably.

**Lecture 547 A/B testing concepts**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Product Analytics + Experimentation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a complete A/B test from hypothesis to decision, including the full statistical readout.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture runs one test end to end the way a product team actually would: state a specific hypothesis tied to a mechanism (not just 'let's try a different color'), define the primary metric and guardrail metrics (secondary metrics that shouldn't get worse even if the primary one improves), run the test for the pre-calculated duration, and read the result against both significance and practical significance before deciding to ship, iterate, or abandon. Guardrail metrics matter because a change can win on the primary metric while quietly damaging something else — a more aggressive upsell prompt might lift short-term revenue per session while increasing cancellations, which only shows up if cancellation rate was being watched as a guardrail from the start. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a subscription app hypothesizes that showing social proof ('12,000 people joined this week') on the pricing page will increase signups, because it addresses a specific trust barrier identified in earlier user interviews. Primary metric: signup conversion rate. Guardrail metrics: 7-day refund rate (to catch signups made from inflated expectations) and page load time (the social-proof widget adds a network call). After the planned two-week run: signup conversion rises from 6.1% to 6.8% (p = 0.01, significant and practically meaningful), refund rate is flat, and load time increases by 80ms — acceptable. The team ships the change, specifically because all three metrics were checked together, not just the one that looked good.                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the subscription-app team check guardrail metrics (refund rate, load time) in addition to the primary signup metric before deciding to ship?

**(A) A change can improve the primary metric while quietly harming something else, and guardrails catch that only if they're monitored from the start of the test**

\(B\) Guardrail metrics are only required for tests run on pricing pages specifically

\(C\) Checking multiple metrics always increases the statistical significance of the primary result

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For a hypothetical test, name one guardrail metric that could get worse even if your primary metric improves, and explain the mechanism by which that could happen.

**Lecture 548 A/B testing concepts**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Product Analytics + Experimentation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Identify and avoid the most common A/B testing pitfalls: peeking, multiple comparisons, and novelty effects.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | Peeking — checking results repeatedly before the planned sample size is reached and stopping as soon as the result looks significant — inflates the false-positive rate well above the nominal 5%, because each additional look is another chance to catch a random fluctuation that crosses the threshold; the fix is committing to a stopping rule in advance (fixed duration/sample size, or a formal sequential-testing method designed for early stopping). The multiple-comparisons problem arises when testing many variants or many metrics simultaneously: if you check 20 metrics at a 5% significance threshold, you'd expect roughly one to look significant by chance alone even with zero real effect, so results from tests with many simultaneous comparisons need a stricter threshold or a pre-registered primary metric. Novelty effects inflate short-term results for any change that's simply different or attention-grabbing (a new badge, an animation) — the lift measured in week one can fade by week four as users habituate, so tests on visually novel changes benefit from a longer run or a follow-up check weeks after launch. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a team tests five different homepage banner designs simultaneously against a single control, checking results daily. By day three, Variant C shows p = 0.04 and the team ships it immediately. Two problems stacked: checking daily (peeking) increased the chance of catching a random early fluctuation, and testing five variants at once (multiple comparisons) meant roughly a 1-in-4 chance that at least one variant would appear significant purely by chance even with zero real effect. A follow-up check a month later shows Variant C's lift has disappeared.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** In the five-variant banner example, why does testing five variants simultaneously increase the risk of a false positive beyond what a single control-vs-variant test would have?

**(A) Running more simultaneous comparisons increases the chance that at least one shows a significant result purely by chance, even with no real underlying effect**

\(B\) Testing more variants always makes the test take less time to reach significance

\(C\) Multiple variants only increase risk if they are visually similar to each other

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick one pitfall from this lecture (peeking, multiple comparisons, or novelty effect) and describe a specific rule you'd put in place before running a test to avoid it.

**Lecture 549 evidence-based product decisions**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Product Analytics + Experimentation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain why triangulating qualitative and quantitative evidence produces more reliable product decisions than either alone.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | Quantitative data (funnels, A/B results, usage metrics) tells you what is happening and at what scale, but rarely tells you why; qualitative data (interviews, usability tests, support tickets) tells you why but from a small, non-representative sample that can't tell you how common the pattern is. Triangulation means deliberately pairing the two before acting on either: a quantitative signal (a funnel drop-off, an A/B result) generates a hypothesis that qualitative research then explains, or a qualitative finding (a recurring complaint from five interviews) gets checked against usage data to see if it's a widespread pattern or an edge case before being prioritized. Acting on quantitative data alone risks solving the wrong problem efficiently; acting on qualitative data alone risks solving a real but rare problem at the expense of a bigger one you haven't measured. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a budgeting app's quantitative data shows a 30% drop-off at the 'link your bank account' step — a clear, measurable problem, but the number alone gives no fix. Five follow-up interviews with drop-off users reveal most didn't trust the app enough yet to share banking credentials, not that the flow was technically confusing. The fix the data alone would never suggest — adding security-reassurance content and well-known partner-bank logos before the connection step — comes only from combining the two evidence types.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** In the budgeting-app example, what would the team have missed by looking only at the quantitative drop-off number?

**(A) The actual reason for the drop-off (lack of trust, not technical confusion), which only the qualitative interviews revealed**

\(B\) The exact step where users were dropping off, which only qualitative data can identify

\(C\) Quantitative data would have shown the same reassurance-content fix directly without any interviews

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For a drop-off or negative metric you've encountered (real or from an earlier exercise in this module), describe what qualitative method you'd pair with it to find the 'why' behind the 'what'.

**Lecture 550 evidence-based product decisions**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Product Analytics + Experimentation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Use a lightweight decision record to document product decisions with their evidence and confidence level.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | Borrowing from the engineering practice of Architecture Decision Records, a product decision record captures, at the moment a decision is made: the decision itself, the evidence that informed it (naming specific data sources, not just 'research showed'), the confidence level in that evidence (strong — large sample, repeated finding; moderate; weak — single small study or anecdote), and what would change the team's mind. This matters because product teams frequently revisit old decisions without any memory of why they were made or how solid the evidence was, leading to either re-litigating settled questions or, worse, treating a weak-evidence decision as if it were strongly validated just because it's been in place a long time. Recording confidence level explicitly also protects against the common failure where an initial hunch, stated confidently in a meeting, calcifies into treated-as-fact over several months. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a team decides to remove a 'save for later' feature based on usage data showing only 2% of users ever click it. The decision record states the evidence (2% usage over 90 days, from product analytics), confidence (moderate — single data source, no qualitative follow-up on why usage is low), and what would change their mind (a user complaint pattern suggesting the low usage is due to poor discoverability rather than lack of demand). Eight months later, when a new PM proposes re-adding the feature, the record immediately surfaces the original reasoning and its stated confidence level, instead of the team re-debating from scratch or assuming the original removal was more rigorously validated than it was.                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why does explicitly recording the confidence level of a decision's evidence (strong/moderate/weak) matter, beyond just recording the decision itself?

**(A) It prevents a weak-evidence decision from being mistakenly treated as strongly validated later just because it's been in place for a while**

\(B\) Confidence levels are only useful for compliance and legal documentation

\(C\) Recording confidence level is equivalent to recording the decision's financial cost

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a short decision record (decision, evidence, confidence level, what would change your mind) for one real or recent product decision you're aware of.

**Lecture 551 evidence-based product decisions**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Product Analytics + Experimentation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Work through a real scenario where quantitative and qualitative evidence pointed in different directions, and how the conflict was resolved.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture is a worked case study in the harder, more realistic version of triangulation: not evidence that neatly combines, but evidence that actively conflicts, and how a team should think through that rather than just picking whichever source they prefer. The resolution process isn't 'trust the bigger dataset' by default — it's examining whether the two sources are actually measuring the same thing, checking for sampling bias in whichever source seems off, and when genuinely unresolved, running a small targeted test to adjudicate rather than deciding from existing evidence alone.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Worked example**      | Example: an A/B test shows a new, more detailed product-comparison table on a shopping site increases add-to-cart rate by 5% (clear quantitative win). But five usability interviews conducted the same week show participants describing the table as 'overwhelming' and reporting they felt pressured rather than informed. Rather than dismissing either signal, the team checks whether the add-to-cart lift translates to actual completed purchases (it does, at a smaller but still positive 2%) and whether the 'overwhelmed' feedback correlates with abandoned carts in session recordings (it doesn't strongly). The resolution: ship the table, but soften its visual density based on the qualitative feedback, since the quantitative outcome held up under scrutiny but the qualitative discomfort was still worth addressing without reversing the decision. |

**Knowledge check:** In the product-comparison-table example, why didn't the team simply dismiss the qualitative 'overwhelming' feedback once the A/B test showed a quantitative win?

**(A) The qualitative discomfort could still indicate a real, worth-addressing problem even if it didn't outweigh the measured purchase lift, so the team softened the design rather than ignoring the signal entirely**

\(B\) Qualitative feedback should always override quantitative results when the two disagree

\(C\) The A/B test result was statistically insignificant, so the qualitative feedback was the only valid evidence

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Describe a scenario (real, recalled, or plausible) where quantitative and qualitative evidence about the same feature pointed in different directions, and propose one way you'd check which signal to trust more before deciding.

**Lecture 552 Month 32 Examination**

*Year 3 · Month 32 · Product Analytics + Experimentation · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Demonstrate integrated command of this month's product analytics and experimentation concepts.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | This exam reviews the full analytical toolkit from Month 32: funnel analysis (choosing meaningful steps, cohort segmentation to reveal hidden differences, root-cause investigation, and avoiding measurement mistakes like session-vs-user counting), usability metrics (SUS, SEQ, task success rate, and NPS each answering a different question, plus avoiding overgeneralization from small samples), A/B testing (valid single-variable tests, statistical significance and sample-size planning, guardrail metrics, and pitfalls like peeking, multiple comparisons, and novelty effects), and evidence-based decision-making (triangulating quantitative and qualitative evidence and documenting decisions with their confidence level). The common thread is intellectual honesty about what a given number can and can't tell you — a funnel number without investigation, a SUS score without task data, a p-value without power analysis, or a single data source without triangulation, all invite the same mistake of overclaiming certainty. This program's internal passing bar is 80%, so revisit any topic where you can't yet explain why a specific number alone would be misleading. |
| **Worked example**      | Example review scenario: a team sees a new feature's usage funnel improve after a redesign (quantitative), investigates with cohort segmentation to confirm it's not just one channel skewing the number, runs a proper A/B test with a pre-calculated sample size and guardrail metrics to confirm the change actually caused the improvement rather than coincidence, supplements with usability testing (SUS and SEQ) to understand the experience behind the numbers, and documents the final ship decision with its evidence and confidence level — demonstrating every concept from the month working together in one real decision rather than in isolation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** What mistake do overclaiming a funnel drop-off number, a SUS score, an underpowered p-value, and a single data source all share, as covered this month?

**(A) Each presents a number as more certain or complete than the evidence actually supports, without the follow-up investigation or triangulation needed to justify that certainty**

\(B\) They are all examples of metrics that cannot be calculated without specialized statistical software

\(C\) They all specifically relate to checkout and payment flows rather than general product decisions

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Before the next module, pick one metric you have access to (work, a personal project, or a product you use) and apply at least two concepts from this month to it: segment it, question its sample size, or pair it with a qualitative check.

**Month 33 AI Product Strategy**

*Allocation: 20 hours \| 20 lectures \| Level: Professional / Job-ready*

**Lecture 553 Market/problem framing**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI Product Strategy · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define a job-to-be-done and explain why framing an AI product around the job, not the model, avoids the most common AI product failure.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | The single most common AI product failure is starting from a capability ('we have access to a great language model, what should we build?') instead of a job-to-be-done ('what specific, recurring task is someone struggling with, and is AI actually the best way to solve it?'). A job-to-be-done is defined independently of any technology: the underlying need a customer is trying to satisfy, stated in terms of the outcome they want, not the feature they'd ask for. Framing the problem this way first forces a separate, honest second question — is a probabilistic, sometimes-wrong system actually suited to this job, or does the job need deterministic reliability — which a capability-first approach skips entirely, leading to AI being bolted onto jobs where it adds novelty but not value. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a legal-tech company has access to a strong document-analysis model and considers building 'an AI that answers any legal question.' Framing from the job-to-be-done instead, interviews with paralegals reveal the actual recurring pain is 'quickly finding which of 200 pages of a contract mentions termination clauses' — a narrower, well-defined job where AI-assisted search and extraction is a strong fit, versus the vague 'answer any legal question' framing, which would need near-perfect reliability on a job (general legal advice) where being wrong carries real consequences.                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why does starting from 'what should we build with this model' tend to produce weaker AI products than starting from a job-to-be-done?

**(A) Capability-first framing skips the honest question of whether AI is actually the best fit for the job, risking AI added for novelty rather than value**

\(B\) Models are technically incapable of being applied to more than one job-to-be-done

\(C\) Job-to-be-done framing always points to building a chatbot specifically

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick an AI feature or product idea you've seen pitched, and try to state the underlying job-to-be-done in outcome terms, independent of any mention of AI or the specific feature.

**Lecture 554 Market/problem framing**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI Product Strategy · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply a build-vs-buy-vs-fine-tune decision framework to the AI capability underlying a product idea.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Once a job-to-be-done is defined, the next framing decision is how to source the underlying AI capability: use a general-purpose foundation model via API as-is (fastest, lowest control, works when the job matches the model's existing strengths), fine-tune or add retrieval on top of a foundation model (moderate effort, needed when the job requires domain-specific knowledge or consistent formatting the base model doesn't reliably produce), or build/train a custom model (slowest and most expensive, justified only when the job has requirements — proprietary data advantage, strict latency, on-device/offline operation, or regulatory constraints on data handling — that no API-based option can meet). The common mistake is defaulting to the most expensive option (custom training) out of a belief that 'real' AI products train their own models, when most successful AI products are thin, well-designed layers over a general-purpose model plus retrieval. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a customer-support software company evaluates building an AI reply-drafting feature. A plain foundation-model API handles general tone and grammar well but doesn't know the company's specific product details or policy exceptions. Rather than training a custom model, the team adds retrieval over their own help-center articles and past resolved tickets (grounding the model's answers in company-specific content) — solving the actual gap at a fraction of the cost and time a custom-trained model would require, since the job didn't actually need a different model, just better-grounded context.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** In the customer-support example, why did adding retrieval over company content solve the problem instead of requiring a custom-trained model?

**(A) The gap was a lack of company-specific grounding, not a limitation of the base model's general language ability, so retrieval addressed the actual need at far lower cost**

\(B\) Custom-trained models are technically incapable of handling customer support use cases

\(C\) Retrieval and fine-tuning are the same technique with different names

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For an AI feature idea, walk through the build-vs-buy-vs-fine-tune framework and identify which tier fits, explicitly naming which specific requirement (data advantage, latency, cost, compliance) drives that choice.

**Lecture 555 Market/problem framing**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI Product Strategy · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply market and problem framing together to a realistic AI product scenario from pain point to feasibility check.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture works a full framing example end to end: starting from an observed market pain point, defining the job-to-be-done precisely enough to be falsifiable, then running it through a feasibility screen that checks three things together — is the job well-matched to what AI does reliably, is there a sourcing option (API, fine-tune, or custom) that fits the team's actual constraints, and is the market problem big and painful enough that solving it with AI (rather than a simpler non-AI tool) is worth the added complexity and risk AI introduces.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a logistics company notices dispatchers spend hours manually matching delivery routes to driver availability and vehicle capacity, a job with clear, measurable pain (time spent, frequent suboptimal matches). Framing the job precisely as 'given today's deliveries and available drivers, produce a feasible route assignment in under two minutes,' the team checks feasibility: this is fundamentally an optimization problem with hard constraints, which classical constraint-solving algorithms handle more reliably than a language model would — AI-powered natural-language explanation of the solution is a reasonable add-on, but the core matching logic is deliberately framed as not an AI problem, avoiding the common mistake of forcing a probabilistic model onto a job that needs a deterministic, verifiable answer. |

**Knowledge check:** In the logistics example, why does the team conclude the core route-matching logic should not be solved primarily with a language model?

**(A) The job has hard constraints and needs a deterministic, verifiable answer, which a classical optimization approach handles more reliably than a probabilistic model**

\(B\) Language models cannot be used in any logistics or operations software

\(C\) The job wasn't painful enough to justify any kind of automated solution

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take a real operational pain point you know of (at work or from a product you use) and run it through the three-part feasibility screen: AI fit, sourcing option, and whether the pain justifies AI's added complexity.

**Lecture 556 Market/problem framing**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI Product Strategy · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Critique a poorly framed AI product pitch and identify the specific framing mistakes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | This hands-on critique session works through the recurring tells of a solution-first AI pitch: the pitch describes the technology before the user problem ('we'll use a multi-agent system to...' before any mention of who needs what), the target user is described in generic terms that could apply to almost anyone, the described job could already be done adequately with existing non-AI tools (making AI an expensive solution to an already-solved problem), and success is defined in terms of model capability metrics rather than user or business outcomes. Spotting these patterns quickly is a practical skill for both pitching and evaluating AI product ideas — most weak pitches share two or three of these tells simultaneously. |
| **Worked example**      | Example critique: a pitch for an 'AI-powered home inventory assistant' describes using computer vision and a knowledge graph to catalog household items, but never names who specifically struggles with this or why (generic 'homeowners'), and the described job — listing what's in your house — is already solved adequately by a basic spreadsheet or a photo album for most people's actual need (insurance documentation, moving). The critique identifies this as AI-looking-for-a-problem: an impressive technical capability applied to a job that wasn't painful enough, for a user who wasn't specifically identified, to justify the complexity.                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** What is the core framing problem with the 'AI-powered home inventory assistant' pitch in the example?

**(A) It applies an impressive technical capability to a job that isn't clearly painful enough, for a vaguely defined user, rather than starting from a specific validated need**

\(B\) Computer vision is technically incapable of cataloging household items

\(C\) The pitch didn't mention a specific AI model provider by name

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Find or recall an AI product pitch (real or from media coverage) and check it against the four tells from this lecture: solution-first framing, generic user, already-solved job, and capability-metric success criteria.

**Lecture 557 Market/problem framing**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI Product Strategy · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Synthesize job-to-be-done, build-vs-buy, and feasibility screening into a one-page AI product problem brief.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | This synthesis lecture is the mini-project that closes the run: compressing everything from the prior four lectures into a single-page brief format a team could actually use to greenlight or reject an AI feature idea before investing in design or engineering. The brief forces explicit answers to the questions the run has built toward in sequence: the specific job-to-be-done (not the feature), the target user (specific, not generic), the feasibility screen result (is AI actually suited to this job), the sourcing decision (API/fine-tune/custom, with the deciding constraint named), and a falsifiable success metric tied to the user or business outcome rather than a model-capability number.                                                                                      |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a one-page brief for an AI meeting-notes feature states the job ('capture accurate action items from a call without anyone taking manual notes'), the user (team leads running 5+ recurring meetings a week), the feasibility note (speech-to-text plus summarization is a well-matched AI use case; verification by participants is still needed since full autonomy on action-item accuracy isn't reliable yet), the sourcing decision (foundation model API plus a lightweight fine-tune on the company's own meeting-note style, chosen because off-the-shelf summarization missed company-specific terminology), and the success metric (percentage of meetings where a human doesn't need to correct more than one action item, tracked over the first month) — not a model benchmark score. |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the brief in the example define success as 'percentage of meetings needing fewer than one human correction' rather than a model benchmark score?

**(A) Success should be tied to the actual user outcome the job-to-be-done was framed around, not an abstract model-capability metric disconnected from real use**

\(B\) Benchmark scores are technically impossible to measure for summarization models

\(C\) Correction counts are easier to compute than any other metric regardless of relevance

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a one-page problem brief (job-to-be-done, specific user, feasibility note, sourcing decision, outcome-based success metric) for one AI feature idea of your own.

**Lecture 558 product differentiation**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI Product Strategy · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Identify the core differentiation levers available to an AI product and explain why most are temporary.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | AI products can differentiate on four main levers: proprietary data (training or grounding data a competitor can't easily replicate), model or fine-tuning quality (a meaningfully better result on the specific task, not just access to a capable base model), UX and workflow integration (fitting into how the user already works rather than requiring a new habit), and distribution (existing audience, channel, or platform access that gets the product in front of users cheaper than a competitor can). The critical insight for this lever set is durability: raw model-quality advantages erode quickly as foundation models improve and competitors catch up within months, while data advantages and deep workflow integration erode much more slowly, because they depend on accumulated usage and switching costs rather than a point-in-time capability gap. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: an AI writing tool initially differentiates by using a particularly capable model before competitors adopt it — a quality edge that lasts roughly two months before every competitor has access to an equally capable model. The team that survives the inevitable quality-gap closure is the one that spent that window building a genuine data advantage (a growing library of the specific user's writing style and brand voice, accumulated over months of use) and deep integration (plugins inside the tools the user already writes in), neither of which a competitor can replicate just by adopting the same underlying model.                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a model-quality advantage considered one of the least durable differentiation levers for an AI product?

**(A) Foundation models improve quickly and competitors can adopt equally capable models within months, closing a point-in-time quality gap**

\(B\) Model quality has no actual effect on user preference for an AI product

\(C\) Data advantages and model quality erode at exactly the same rate in practice

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For an AI product you're familiar with, identify which of the four levers (data, model quality, UX/integration, distribution) it's actually relying on, and estimate how durable that advantage is likely to be.

**Lecture 559 product differentiation**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI Product Strategy · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply model-selection trade-offs (cost, latency, quality, context window) as an active differentiation and product decision.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | Choosing which underlying model (or mix of models) powers a feature is itself a product decision with real trade-offs, not just an engineering detail: a larger, higher-quality model typically costs more per request and responds more slowly, while a smaller, faster, cheaper model may be sufficient for simpler sub-tasks within the same product. Context window (how much text the model can consider at once) matters directly for jobs involving long documents or long conversation history — too small a window forces awkward truncation or summarization that can drop important details. Mature AI products often route different parts of the same user flow to different models: a cheap, fast model for simple classification or formatting, reserved for the harder generative step, which meaningfully affects both cost structure and perceived responsiveness. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: a customer-support platform routes an incoming ticket first through a small, fast, inexpensive model that just classifies urgency and topic (a job that doesn't need a large model's reasoning ability), then only escalates complex tickets needing a drafted response to a larger, slower, more expensive model. This two-tier routing cuts average per-ticket model cost substantially while keeping response latency low for the high-volume simple cases, a product decision that directly shapes the unit economics of the whole feature.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the customer-support platform use a small model for classification and a larger model only for complex drafted responses, rather than one large model for everything?

**(A) Using a large model for every request, including simple classification that doesn't need its reasoning ability, would increase cost and latency without a corresponding quality benefit for that step**

\(B\) Small models are technically incapable of being combined with large models in the same product

\(C\) Context window size has no relationship to which model is chosen for a task

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** For an AI feature with multiple distinct sub-tasks, propose which steps could use a cheaper/faster model and which genuinely need a more capable model, and justify the split.

**Lecture 560 product differentiation**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · AI Product Strategy · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Compare two competing AI products on differentiation axes to identify where real advantage lies versus surface-level feature parity.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | This worked example compares two AI products that look similar in a feature list — both offer chat-based drafting, both cite sources, both have mobile apps — and digs beneath the surface to the four levers from earlier in this run to find where the actual advantage lies. Feature lists converge quickly in AI products because most teams have access to similar underlying model capabilities; the comparison that matters is which product has accumulated a harder-to-copy advantage in data, integration depth, or distribution, since that's what determines which one wins as the feature-list gap closes. |
| **Worked example**      | Example: two AI writing assistants both offer 'brand voice matching.' Product A implements this by letting users paste a style guide into the prompt each session (no memory, no accumulation — a competitor can replicate this by copying the UI exactly). Product B implements it by building a persistent style profile from every piece of content the user has ever approved, improving automatically over months of use — a genuine data-accumulation advantage that a competitor can't replicate by copying the feature, only by waiting for an equal amount of usage history to build up themselves.            |
