\(C\) It lists every software tool and certification the designer has ever used

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write your homepage's hook sentence (one sentence, specific value, not a job title) and draft captions for 3 proof tiles using outcome language.

**Lecture 591 Portfolio structure**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Assemble a complete portfolio site skeleton — sitemap, homepage wireframe, and case-study page template — as a synthesis deliverable ready to populate with real content.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the run synthesizes the structural decisions from the prior two lectures into one concrete, buildable skeleton: a finalized sitemap with case studies in priority order, a homepage wireframe following hook-proof-path, and a reusable case-study page template with placeholder sections (problem statement, decision highlights, visuals, outcome) that every case study will follow for visual consistency across the site. Establishing this template now — before Month 35's later lectures on case-study writing and documentation — means content gets dropped into a structure that's already been through structural critique, rather than structure being retrofitted around finished writing. |
| **Worked example**      | A student produces three artifacts: (1) a final sitemap — Home, Case Study: AI Scheduler, Case Study: Healthcare Intake, Case Study: Design System, About, Contact; (2) a homepage wireframe with labeled hook/proof/path zones and placeholder text; (3) a case-study template with five labeled sections (Problem, My Role & Decisions, Process Visuals, Outcome, Reflection) that will be reused identically across all three case studies so a reader's navigation pattern stays consistent project to project.                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture establish a reusable case-study page template before any individual case study is written in later lectures?

\(A\) Because templates are a strict legal requirement for publishing a portfolio site

**(B) Because a consistent template lets content be dropped into pre-validated structure, and gives readers a predictable navigation pattern across projects**

\(C\) Because writing content first and retrofitting structure afterward is technically impossible in modern web tools

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Produce your three-part skeleton: final sitemap, homepage wireframe, and a labeled case-study template with placeholder sections you'll reuse for every project.

**Lecture 592 case-study writing**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Draft a complete case-study narrative for one portfolio project using the problem-decision-impact structure established earlier in the program, written as final publishable prose.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | Case-study writing is a distinct skill from case-study refinement (Month 34): refinement improves existing drafts, while writing here means producing a full first draft of final prose for a project that may not have been written up at all yet. The approach is to draft section by section in a fixed order that mirrors how a reader's attention actually works: a 2-3 sentence problem statement with a concrete number or concrete user pain if one exists, a 'my role' clarifier (critical for team projects, naming exactly what the writer decided versus what the team decided), 3-4 decision-log paragraphs, and a results section that states outcome honestly — including modest or inconclusive results, framed as a learning, rather than inflating a weak result into a false claim. |
| **Worked example**      | A student drafts a case study for a volunteer-coordination app redesign: problem statement names a 40% volunteer no-show rate at scheduled shifts; 'my role' clarifies 'I led the research and interaction design; a teammate handled visual design and branding'; three decision-log paragraphs cover the choice of SMS reminders over push notifications (based on the user base's device habits), a confirm-and-recall-day pattern, and a waitlist feature; results honestly state 'In a 3-week pilot with 20 volunteers, no-shows dropped to 28% — a meaningful but partial improvement, and I've flagged shift-time mismatch as a likely remaining cause for further research.'                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the case-study writing method require an explicit 'my role' clarifier for team projects?

\(A\) Because portfolio hosting platforms legally require a credits section on every page

**(B) Because it tells the reader exactly which decisions belonged to the writer versus the rest of the team, which hiring managers specifically look for**

\(C\) Because without it, the case study cannot include any visuals created by teammates

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Draft a full first-pass case-study narrative for one of your projects, including problem statement, 'my role' clarifier, at least 3 decision-log paragraphs, and an honest results section.

**Lecture 593 case-study writing**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply visual storytelling techniques — annotated screens, before/after comparisons, and flow diagrams — to make a case study's key decisions legible without requiring the reader to read every paragraph.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Most hiring managers skim visuals before reading prose, so a case study's images carry real argumentative weight, not just decoration. This lecture covers three specific visual techniques: annotated screens (a screenshot with 2-4 short callout labels pointing at the specific elements a decision affected, not a generic 'final screen' image), before/after comparisons (placed side by side, with the change that matters highlighted, not just two unlabeled screenshots), and simplified flow diagrams (showing only the decision points that matter to the story, stripped of every screen in the actual flow, since a literal screen-by-screen walkthrough buries the one decision worth seeing). The test for any visual: could a reader understand the key decision from the image alone, without reading the surrounding paragraph? |
| **Worked example**      | For the volunteer-app case study, the student creates: an annotated screenshot of the reminder screen with two callouts ('SMS chosen over push — user base skews low-smartphone-literacy' and 'Confirm-or-cancel reply reduces no-shows without an app open'); a before/after pair showing the old generic reminder text next to the new specific shift-detail reminder, with the added shift time and location highlighted in a different color; and a 4-node simplified flow diagram (Sign up -\> Get matched -\> Receive reminder -\> Confirm/cancel) that omits a dozen minor screens irrelevant to the no-show story.                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** What is the test this lecture proposes for whether a portfolio visual is doing its job?

\(A\) Whether the image uses the designer's personal brand colors consistently

**(B) Whether a reader could understand the key decision from the image alone, without reading the surrounding paragraph**

\(C\) Whether the image file size is small enough to load quickly on mobile

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Create one annotated screen, one before/after comparison, or one simplified flow diagram for your case study, and test it on a peer without letting them read the surrounding text first.

**Lecture 594 case-study writing**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Produce a fully finished, publication-ready case study by combining the narrative draft and visual storytelling techniques from this run into one complete, polished artifact.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the run is the synthesis project: take the narrative draft from the first lecture and the visuals from the second, and merge them into one finished case-study page — not a rough draft, a page that could be published today. The integration work that matters here is pacing: visuals and decision-log paragraphs should alternate so a reader's attention is refreshed roughly every 150-200 words, rather than a wall of text followed by a gallery of images at the end, which is the single most common structural flaw in first-draft case studies written by designers new to this format. |
| **Worked example**      | A student finalizes the volunteer-app case study: problem statement and 'my role' open the page; the SMS-vs-push decision paragraph is immediately followed by its annotated screenshot; the reminder-copy decision paragraph is immediately followed by the before/after comparison; the overall flow decision paragraph is followed by the simplified diagram; the honest results section closes the page. No more than 200 words pass before the next visual appears, keeping the page scannable end to end.                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** What is identified as the most common structural flaw in first-draft case studies by designers new to this format?

\(A\) Including too many quantified outcomes in the results section

**(B) A wall of text followed by a gallery of images at the end, instead of alternating text and visuals throughout**

\(C\) Writing the problem statement before the 'my role' clarifier

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Finalize one case study by interleaving your decision-log paragraphs with their corresponding visuals, keeping no more than ~200 words between visual breaks.

**Lecture 595 design rationale**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Articulate the underlying reasoning framework behind a design decision — not just what was chosen, but the evaluation criteria that made it the right choice given specific constraints.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Design rationale is the explicit record of why a decision was made, and it differs from a decision log (Month 34) in scope: a decision log entry documents one choice within a case study's narrative flow, while design rationale is the deeper discipline of making the evaluation criteria themselves visible — what trade-offs were weighed, what constraints bounded the options, and why those constraints outranked others. A well-formed rationale names at least three things: the options genuinely considered (not a strawman), the criteria used to judge them (performance, learnability, technical feasibility, brand fit, accessibility, etc.), and which criterion won and why, given the specific context — because the same decision can be correct in one context and wrong in another. |
| **Worked example**      | A designer choosing between a carousel and a grid for a product-browsing screen writes a rationale, not just a decision: 'Options: carousel (space-efficient, hides items), grid (shows more at once, requires more vertical scroll). Criteria weighed: discoverability (grid wins — users browse more items per scroll), but also loading performance on low-end devices (carousel wins — fewer images rendered at once). Given this app's target market skews toward budget Android devices with slow connections, I weighted performance higher than raw discoverability and chose carousel with a clear 'see all' escape hatch to recover the discoverability cost.'                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** How does design rationale differ from a case-study decision log as described in this lecture?

\(A\) They are identical techniques with different names used interchangeably

**(B) A decision log documents one choice within a narrative, while design rationale makes the deeper evaluation criteria and context-dependent trade-offs explicit**

\(C\) Design rationale applies only to visual design, while decision logs apply only to research methods

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick one design decision from your portfolio project and write a full rationale: the real options considered, the criteria you weighed, and which criterion won given your specific context.

**Lecture 596 design rationale**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Defend a design rationale under adversarial questioning in a mock stakeholder-pushback exercise, strengthening the rationale's weakest link under real-time scrutiny.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | A rationale that only survives on paper isn't finished — in a real job, design decisions get challenged by stakeholders with competing priorities (engineering wants less complexity, sales wants a louder CTA, legal wants a disclaimer), and the designer's job is to defend or revise the rationale under that pressure without getting defensive or caving reflexively. This lecture runs a mock pushback exercise: a partner plays a skeptical stakeholder and fires specific challenges ('why not just do X, it's simpler to build') at a rationale, and the designer must either strengthen the argument with the criteria already established, or honestly concede the point and revise — both are valid outcomes, but capitulating without reasoning or defending without listening are both failure modes. |
| **Worked example**      | A student defends their carousel-over-grid rationale against a partner playing an engineering stakeholder who pushes 'grid is a simpler component to build, why add carousel complexity?' The student doesn't cave immediately, but also doesn't dismiss the concern: 'That's fair — grid is simpler to build. But our performance data showed carousel reduces load time by 40% on the low-end devices that make up 60% of our user base, which I'm weighting above build simplicity for this specific screen.' If the stakeholder countered with new information the student hadn't considered, a genuine concession would be the correct response instead.                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** In the mock stakeholder-pushback exercise, what are the two failure modes identified for defending a design rationale?

\(A\) Speaking too quietly and speaking too confidently

**(B) Capitulating to pushback without reasoning, and defending the decision without genuinely listening to the challenge**

\(C\) Using too many technical terms and using too few technical terms

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Run the pushback exercise with a partner: have them challenge your rationale from lecture 595 with at least two specific objections, and write down how you responded to each.

**Lecture 597 design rationale**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Compile a portfolio-ready 'rationale appendix' for one case study that documents the full reasoning behind its 2-3 most contested or non-obvious decisions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the run produces a specific, reusable artifact: a rationale appendix attached to (or linked from) a case study, covering the decisions most likely to draw stakeholder or interviewer questions — not every decision, since an appendix covering everything becomes noise, but the 2-3 decisions that were genuinely contested, non-obvious, or where a different answer was clearly tempting. This selectivity is itself part of the skill: a designer who can identify which decisions actually need defending (versus which were uncontroversial) demonstrates the judgment interviewers are specifically probing for when they ask 'walk me through a decision you're proud of.' |
| **Worked example**      | For the volunteer-app case study, the student writes a rationale appendix covering exactly two decisions: SMS-vs-push (survived mock pushback from a 'just use push, it's free' stakeholder) and the confirm-or-cancel reply pattern (survived pushback from an 'just send one reminder, don't overcomplicate it' stakeholder). A third decision — button color — is deliberately excluded from the appendix because, despite being discussed, it was never genuinely contested and including it would dilute the two decisions that matter.                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture emphasize including only 2-3 decisions in a rationale appendix rather than documenting every decision made?

\(A\) Portfolio hosting platforms impose a strict word-count limit on appendix sections

**(B) Covering every decision turns the appendix into noise, while selecting only the genuinely contested or non-obvious ones demonstrates the judgment interviewers probe for**

\(C\) Design rationale is only legally required for decisions involving user data

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a rationale appendix of 2-3 entries for your case study, selecting only decisions that were genuinely contested or non-obvious, and explain in one sentence why you excluded any others.

**Lecture 598 prototypes**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Select and build the appropriate prototype fidelity (low, mid, or high) for a specific portfolio case study's story, matching fidelity to what that story needs to prove.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | Portfolio prototypes serve a different purpose than process prototypes made during a project: a process prototype tests a hypothesis with users, while a portfolio prototype's job is to let a reviewer quickly experience the key interaction the case study is about. This means fidelity should match the story, not maximize polish: a case study about information architecture decisions might only need a clickable low-fidelity prototype showing navigation logic, while a case study about a novel micro-interaction (an AI-suggestion accept/reject gesture, say) demands a high-fidelity, animated prototype because the interaction's feel is the entire point and can't be conveyed in static screens or vague description. |
| **Worked example**      | For the volunteer-app case study (about reminder timing and reply logic, not visual polish), the student builds only a mid-fidelity clickable prototype of the SMS reply flow — enough to click through confirm/cancel/reschedule paths — rather than investing in high-fidelity animation, since the decision being showcased is informational flow, not motion. For a different case study about a drag-to-reorder task list with spring-physics feedback, the same student builds a high-fidelity, fully animated prototype, because the physics feel is the actual decision being showcased and can't be conveyed any other way.                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** How should fidelity level be chosen for a portfolio prototype, according to this lecture?

\(A\) Always build the highest fidelity possible, since more polish is always better for a portfolio

**(B) Match fidelity to what the specific case study's story needs to prove — low/mid fidelity for IA or flow logic, high fidelity when the interaction's feel is the point**

\(C\) Fidelity should match whatever tool the designer is most comfortable using, regardless of the story

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For your case study, decide and justify in one sentence what fidelity level (low/mid/high) your portfolio prototype needs, based on what decision it's meant to showcase.

**Lecture 599 prototypes**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Record and edit a short prototype walkthrough video or GIF that lets a reviewer experience a key interaction without needing to click through the prototype themselves.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | Many portfolio reviewers never actually click into an embedded prototype — they skim past it, especially on mobile or when reviewing many portfolios quickly — so a short captured walkthrough (a 10-20 second looping GIF or a 30-45 second narrated screen recording) often communicates the interaction more reliably than the live prototype link alone. The editing discipline that matters: trim dead time (no 3-second pause before the first tap), keep the capture focused on the one interaction the case study is about rather than a full click-through of every screen, and for narrated video, write a tight script beforehand rather than ad-libbing, since unscripted narration reliably runs long and buries the point. |
| **Worked example**      | For the drag-to-reorder prototype, the student records a 12-second looping GIF showing exactly one reorder gesture with the spring-back animation, trimmed so it starts the instant the drag begins (no idle screen beforehand) and loops seamlessly. For the SMS-reply flow, instead of a silent GIF, they record a 35-second narrated video with a pre-written script: 'Here's what happens when a volunteer gets a reminder and replies CANCEL instead of CONFIRM' — scripted in advance so the narration stays exactly on that one path.                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture recommend writing a script in advance for a narrated prototype walkthrough video, rather than narrating live?

\(A\) Live narration is technically impossible to record with standard screen-capture tools

**(B) Unscripted narration reliably runs long and buries the specific point the clip is meant to make**

\(C\) Scripts are required by most video hosting platforms before upload is permitted

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Record a short GIF or narrated video walkthrough (under 45 seconds) of one key interaction from your prototype, trimmed to remove dead time at the start.

**Lecture 600 research evidence**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Select and present the strongest piece of research evidence for a case study, choosing the format (quote, chart, annotated transcript excerpt) that makes the finding most credible and legible.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | A case study's credibility rests heavily on whether its claimed insights are backed by visible evidence rather than asserted from nowhere — 'users found the form confusing' convinces no one, while a specific piece of evidence does. This lecture is about selection and presentation: from a pool of research artifacts (interview notes, survey results, usability-test recordings), pick the single piece that most directly supports the case study's central claim, and present it in the format that preserves its credibility — a direct, short quote with attribution context ('P4, a first-time user: ...'), a simple chart for quantitative findings (avoid over-designed charts that obscure the number), or a brief annotated excerpt from a test transcript showing the moment of confusion. |
| **Worked example**      | For the volunteer-app case study's claim that reminder timing caused no-shows, the student doesn't just state the claim — they include a direct quote: 'P3 (missed shift): "I got the text Tuesday but my shift was Thursday, I just forgot by then."' paired with a simple bar chart showing no-show rate by reminder-lead-time (same-day vs. 2-day vs. 5-day), choosing a plain bar chart over a more decorative visualization specifically because the number itself is what needs to be legible at a glance.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** What is the primary criterion this lecture gives for choosing which research evidence to feature in a case study?

\(A\) Whichever piece of evidence is visually the most colorful or decorative

**(B) The single piece that most directly and credibly supports the case study's central claim, presented in a format that preserves rather than obscures it**

\(C\) Whichever piece of evidence was collected most recently in the research timeline

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** From your own research notes, select the single strongest piece of evidence for your case study's central claim and present it as a quote, chart, or annotated excerpt.

**Lecture 601 research evidence**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a compact 'evidence appendix' linking each major claim in a case study to its supporting research artifact, for reviewers who want to verify rigor beyond the main narrative.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | Some reviewers — particularly for research-heavy or senior roles — want to check rigor beyond the polished narrative, so this lecture builds a second artifact: a compact evidence appendix that maps each major claim in the case study ('reminder timing caused no-shows,' 'the confirm/cancel pattern reduced friction') to the specific research artifact backing it (a link to interview notes, a screenshot of raw survey data, a transcript excerpt), without re-narrating the whole study. This is a trust-building artifact aimed at a smaller, more skeptical audience than the main case study, so it should be linked discreetly (an 'evidence' link at the bottom of the page) rather than inserted into the main flow, where it would slow down the broader skimming audience. |
| **Worked example**      | The student builds a one-page evidence appendix for the volunteer-app case study with three rows: Claim 1 ('timing caused no-shows') linked to a screenshot of the raw no-show-by-lead-time data table; Claim 2 ('SMS over push was the right channel') linked to an excerpt of the device-usage survey; Claim 3 ('confirm/cancel reduced friction') linked to two transcript excerpts from usability-test sessions. The link to this appendix sits as a small text link at the very bottom of the case study page, not in the main scroll path.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture recommend linking the evidence appendix discreetly at the bottom of the page rather than placing it in the main case-study flow?

\(A\) Evidence appendices are not permitted to appear anywhere else on a portfolio site for licensing reasons

**(B) It serves a smaller, more skeptical audience checking rigor, and placing it in the main flow would slow down the broader skimming audience**

\(C\) Raw research data must legally be hidden from casual visitors to protect participant privacy

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Build a compact evidence appendix for your case study with at least 3 rows, each mapping one major claim to its specific supporting research artifact.

**Lecture 602 documentation**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Write clear, concise process documentation for a design project — the kind of internal artifact (a decision record, a research summary, a handoff note) that a design team actually relies on day to day, distinct from portfolio narrative.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | Portfolio case studies are written for an external audience with limited time; process documentation is written for an internal audience (teammates, future-you, engineers) who need accurate, retrievable detail rather than a polished story. This lecture covers three common internal documentation formats: a decision record (date, decision, context, alternatives considered, owner — kept short and scannable, not narrative), a research summary (key findings only, with links to raw data, written for someone who wasn't in the room), and a design-to-engineering handoff note (what changed, why, and what needs engineering attention, flagged clearly so it doesn't get missed in a long spec). The skill here is restraint: documentation that tries to read like a case study becomes too long for anyone to actually use. |
| **Worked example**      | For the volunteer-app project, the student writes a decision record: 'Date: March 4. Decision: SMS reminders over push notifications. Context: target users skew low-smartphone-literacy per device-usage survey. Alternatives: push (rejected, requires app open), email (rejected, lower open rates for this demographic). Owner: \[name\].' Four lines, scannable in ten seconds — a format that would be far too terse for a portfolio case study but is exactly right for a teammate checking the record six months later.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** How does internal process documentation differ in purpose and style from a portfolio case study, as described in this lecture?

\(A\) Internal documentation should always be longer and more narrative than a portfolio case study

**(B) Internal documentation is written for teammates needing retrievable accuracy, so it should be short and scannable rather than polished narrative prose**

\(C\) There is no meaningful difference; the same document should serve both audiences

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write one decision record, one research summary, or one handoff note (choose the format that fits a real decision from your project) using the short, scannable style shown.

**Lecture 603 documentation**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Convert internal process documentation into a reusable personal 'design process library' — templates the student can apply to future projects beyond this program.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the run turns the documentation skill into a lasting asset: rather than writing one-off documents, the student extracts reusable templates from the formats practiced in the prior lecture (a blank decision-record template, a blank research-summary template, a blank handoff-note template) and assembles them into a personal process library — a small set of files they can duplicate and fill in for every future project, in a job or freelance work, without re-inventing the format each time. This mirrors a genuinely common practice among senior designers, who often carry a personal template kit from job to job precisely because rebuilding documentation habits from scratch on every new project wastes time that should go to the work itself. |
| **Worked example**      | The student creates three blank template files: decision-record-template.md (fields: date, decision, context, alternatives, owner), research-summary-template.md (fields: question, key findings, raw-data links, confidence level), and handoff-note-template.md (fields: what changed, why, engineering-attention flag, open questions). They save all three in a personal 'process-library' folder they intend to duplicate at the start of every future project, rather than rebuilding the structure from memory each time.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** What is the primary purpose of converting the documentation formats from the prior lecture into a personal template library?

\(A\) Templates are a formal requirement for submitting any portfolio to this program

**(B) It creates a reusable kit the student can duplicate on future projects, avoiding rebuilding documentation habits from scratch each time — a common senior-designer practice**

\(C\) Templates replace the need to ever write a portfolio case study again

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Create your own blank decision-record, research-summary, and handoff-note templates and save them together as the start of your personal process library.

**Lecture 604 Month 35 Examination**

*Year 3 · Month 35 · GitHub + Portfolio Engineering · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Demonstrate mastery of Month 35's portfolio structure, case-study writing, design rationale, prototype presentation, research evidence, and documentation skills by passing a comprehensive review at the program's 80% internal bar.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | This exam reviews Month 35 as a whole, which moved from structural planning into full execution: portfolio structure (sitemap, the hook-proof-path homepage pattern, and a reusable case-study template), case-study writing (problem-decision-impact narrative drafting paired with annotated screens, before/afters, and simplified flow diagrams), design rationale (making evaluation criteria explicit and defending them under mock stakeholder pushback, then compiling a selective rationale appendix), prototypes (matching fidelity to the story and capturing short walkthrough clips for reviewers who won't click through live), research evidence (selecting and presenting the single strongest proof point, plus a discreet evidence appendix for skeptical reviewers), and documentation (internal decision records, research summaries, and handoff notes, converted into a reusable personal template library). As with every month in this program, passing this review requires scoring at or above the 80% internal bar used throughout, and here that bar specifically checks whether the student's portfolio artifacts from this month are genuinely publishable, not just drafted, since Month 36's capstone work will build directly on top of them. |
| **Worked example**      | A student preparing for this exam walks through their own portfolio folder against the month's checklist: sitemap finalized and case studies ordered by strength (589-591), at least one case study fully drafted with alternating text and visuals (592-594), a rationale appendix covering 2-3 genuinely contested decisions that survived mock pushback (595-597), a fidelity-matched prototype with a trimmed walkthrough clip (598-599), a selected evidence quote/chart plus a discreet evidence appendix (600-601), and a personal template library of decision-record, research-summary, and handoff-note files (602-603) — confirming each artifact is publish-ready before sitting the review.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** Which combination of artifacts should a student have ready heading into this Month 35 Examination, consistent with the month's 80% internal passing bar?

\(A\) Only a finished sitemap, since the remaining lectures covered optional enrichment rather than required deliverables

**(B) A finalized sitemap and homepage structure, a fully drafted case study with integrated visuals, a selective rationale appendix, a fidelity-matched prototype clip, selected research evidence, and a reusable documentation template library**

\(C\) A single long video narrating the entire portfolio, replacing the need for written case studies

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Before Month 36 begins, assemble every artifact from this month's checklist into your live or staged portfolio site as the foundation for the final capstone.

**Month 36 Final Professional Product + UX Capstone**

*Allocation: 20 hours \| 20 lectures \| Level: Professional / Job-ready*

**Lecture 605 Full product discovery**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define a capstone product concept and problem statement by scoping a real, specific user problem worth solving across the full remaining month.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | Month 36's capstone is a single, continuous product built across every remaining lecture — discovery through strategy — rather than disconnected exercises, so this first lecture's job is to lock in a scope that's ambitious enough to showcase three years of skills but narrow enough to actually finish in 20 hours. The scoping method: write a one-sentence problem statement naming a specific user, a specific pain, and a specific context (not 'improve productivity' but 'freelance contractors lose track of which clients still owe payment past 30 days'), then stress-test it against a 'can I build and validate this in the time I have' check, deliberately cutting scope (fewer user types, fewer platforms, fewer features) rather than cutting corners on depth. |
| **Worked example**      | A student scopes their capstone as: 'Freelance contractors managing 5-15 concurrent clients lose track of overdue invoices because tracking lives across email, spreadsheets, and memory, leading to delayed follow-ups and lost income.' They explicitly cut scope by deciding the capstone will cover only the invoice-tracking and follow-up-reminder flow, not full invoicing/payment processing, reasoning that a narrow, deep build demonstrates more capability than a broad, shallow one in the time available.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the scoping method in this lecture favor cutting scope (fewer features) over cutting depth when time is limited?

\(A\) Cutting depth is technically impossible once a problem statement has been written

**(B) A narrow but deep build better demonstrates genuine capability than a broad but shallow one, within the fixed time available**

\(C\) Portfolio reviewers specifically penalize any capstone covering more than one feature

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write your capstone's one-sentence problem statement naming a specific user, pain, and context, and list one feature you're deliberately cutting to keep scope achievable.

**Lecture 606 Full product discovery**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Map the capstone product's competitive and adjacent landscape, identifying a specific, defensible point of differentiation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | A capstone that solves a problem no one else addresses is a red flag, not a strength — real products exist in a landscape of alternatives, including non-software ones (the freelancer's current 'solution' might just be a spreadsheet and anxiety), and a credible discovery phase maps that landscape honestly. This lecture's method: list 3-5 real or plausible competitors/alternatives (direct competitors, adjacent tools users might stretch to use instead, and the 'do nothing' baseline), then identify one specific angle where the capstone's approach differs — not a vague 'better UX' claim, but a concrete mechanism (e.g., 'competitors require manual invoice entry; this product parses payment-due dates directly from imported email receipts'). |
| **Worked example**      | For the invoice-tracking capstone, the student maps: direct competitors (two existing freelance-invoicing apps with overdue-tracking as a minor feature), an adjacent tool (a general task manager some freelancers repurpose), and the 'do nothing' baseline (spreadsheet + manual memory). The differentiation claim: 'Existing tools treat overdue tracking as a side feature bolted onto full invoicing; this product's AI-assisted reminder drafting is the primary feature, not an afterthought,' a specific mechanism rather than a vague superiority claim.                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** What specific flaw does this lecture flag as a 'red flag' in capstone discovery, rather than a strength?

\(A\) Choosing a problem that is too narrow for a 20-hour build

**(B) Claiming to solve a problem with no competitors or alternatives at all, since real problems almost always have some existing response**

\(C\) Identifying a 'do nothing' baseline as one of the alternatives

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** List 3-5 real alternatives to your capstone concept (including a 'do nothing' baseline) and write one concrete, mechanism-level differentiation claim.

**Lecture 607 Full product discovery**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
