| **Learning outcome**    | Produce a capstone discovery brief — problem statement, target user, competitive landscape, and success criteria — as the foundational document the rest of the month's work will build on.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the discovery run compiles everything into one discovery brief that functions as the capstone's foundational contract with itself: the problem statement (605), the competitive landscape and differentiation (606), a specific target-user description (not a broad persona, but a tight description of who this is for), and — critically — explicit, checkable success criteria for the finished capstone (e.g., 'a working prototype that lets a user import a sample invoice list and receive one AI-drafted follow-up message'). Writing success criteria now, before any design work starts, prevents the common capstone failure mode of scope creeping upward mid-build with no fixed definition of 'done.' |
| **Worked example**      | The student's discovery brief states: Problem (from 605), Differentiation (from 606), Target user: 'solo freelance designers/developers with 5-15 active clients, moderate but not advanced tech comfort,' and Success criteria: 'a clickable high-fidelity prototype covering the invoice-import, overdue-detection, and AI-drafted-reminder flow, backed by at least one round of usability testing with a real target user.' This document becomes the reference point checked against at the Month 36 Examination.                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture insist on writing explicit success criteria before any design work begins?

\(A\) Success criteria are only useful after the capstone is already finished, as a retrospective exercise

**(B) Fixing a 'definition of done' in advance prevents the common failure mode of scope creeping upward mid-build with no stopping point**

\(C\) Success criteria are a formality with no real effect on how the capstone is built

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write your complete discovery brief: problem statement, differentiation claim, target-user description, and explicit, checkable success criteria for your finished capstone.

**Lecture 608 research**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Plan and conduct a lightweight capstone research round (3-5 target-user conversations) to validate or revise the discovery brief's assumptions before committing design time.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | Discovery brief in hand, the next risk is building on unvalidated assumptions, so this lecture runs a compressed, time-boxed research round appropriate to a 20-hour month: 3-5 short conversations (15-20 minutes each) with people matching the target-user description, structured around a small set of open questions testing the brief's core assumptions directly (not leading questions that just confirm the plan). The discipline that matters: treat every assumption in the discovery brief as a hypothesis to be tested, not a fact to be illustrated, and be genuinely willing to revise the brief if 3-5 conversations surface a pattern the brief didn't anticipate. |
| **Worked example**      | The student interviews 4 freelancers with open questions like 'walk me through the last time you realized a client payment was overdue' rather than 'would you use an app that reminds you about overdue payments?' (a leading question that invites false positives). Two of the four reveal that the real failure point isn't tracking the overdue date — it's forgetting to follow up even when they know — a nuance the original discovery brief didn't capture, prompting a one-line revision to the differentiation claim to emphasize reminder-drafting over detection.                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture specifically warn against questions like 'would you use an app that does X?' in the capstone research round?

\(A\) Such questions take too long to ask within a 15-20 minute conversation window

**(B) Leading questions tend to produce false-positive confirmation rather than testing whether the underlying assumption actually holds**

\(C\) Hypothetical questions about future behavior are prohibited under standard research ethics guidelines

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Conduct (or realistically simulate, if time-boxed) 3 short conversations testing your discovery brief's core assumption, and note whether any response should revise the brief.

**Lecture 609 research**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Synthesize capstone research findings into a short set of concrete design implications, directly linking each finding to a specific decision the design phase must now make.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | Research that doesn't change a design decision wasn't worth doing, so this lecture's method forces that link explicitly: for each notable finding from the prior lecture's conversations, write one sentence stating the specific design implication it produces — not a vague 'users want simplicity' but 'P2 and P3 both said they'd ignore a dashboard they have to remember to check, which means reminders need to be push-based (email/SMS) rather than relying on the user opening the app.' This finding-to-implication mapping becomes the direct input to the UX lectures that follow, so the synthesis step isn't academic — it's load-bearing for everything built next. |
| **Worked example**      | The student's synthesis table: Finding 1 ('2 of 4 forget to follow up even when they know a payment is overdue') -\> Implication ('the product must push a reminder, not just display overdue status passively'); Finding 2 ('freelancers already use email heavily for client communication') -\> Implication ('AI-drafted reminders should be composable as emails, not a separate in-app message type, to fit an existing habit rather than create a new one').                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** What test does this lecture apply to determine whether a research finding was worth collecting?

\(A\) Whether the finding was mentioned by a majority of the 3-5 people interviewed

**(B) Whether the finding produces a specific, stated implication for an upcoming design decision — a finding with no design consequence wasn't worth collecting**

\(C\) Whether the finding can be illustrated with a direct quote from the conversation

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a finding-to-implication table for your capstone research: at least 2 findings, each mapped to one specific, non-vague design implication.

**Lecture 610 research**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Finalize the capstone's research-informed scope by resolving any conflicts between the original discovery brief and the research findings, producing a locked feature list for the design phases ahead.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the research run resolves the tension that real projects always have: research sometimes contradicts the original plan, and a capstone builder has to make an actual call rather than trying to honor both the original brief and every new finding simultaneously. The method: list any point where a research implication (609) conflicts with or extends the discovery brief (607), make an explicit decision on each (revise the brief, or note the finding as a lower-priority future consideration deliberately out of this capstone's scope), and lock a final feature list before design work begins, since re-opening scope mid-design is the most common cause of an unfinished capstone. |
| **Worked example**      | The student resolves one conflict: the original brief emphasized overdue-detection as the core feature, but research showed users already know they're overdue — they forget to act. Decision: the core feature pivots to AI-drafted reminder composition and one-tap send, with passive overdue-status display demoted to a secondary, already-visible element rather than the main value proposition. This decision is locked in a final feature list of exactly 4 items before any wireframing starts.                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture treat re-opening scope mid-design as a significant risk to flag explicitly?

\(A\) Design tools technically prevent any scope changes once wireframing has started

**(B) It is identified as the most common cause of an unfinished capstone, since indecision about scope consumes time that should go to building**

\(C\) Scope changes during design are against this program's academic integrity policy

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Resolve any conflict between your original discovery brief and your research findings with an explicit decision, and write your final locked feature list (aim for 3-5 items) before moving to design.

**Lecture 611 UX**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design the capstone's core user flow as a complete, low-fidelity wireframe sequence covering every screen needed for the locked feature list's primary task.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | With feature list locked, this lecture is where discovery and research turn into the capstone's first tangible design artifact: a full low-fidelity wireframe sequence for the single primary task that proves the value proposition (not every feature — the one flow that, if it doesn't work, the whole capstone fails). The UX discipline being exercised is end-to-end flow thinking: every screen a user would actually pass through, including states easy to skip in a rush (an empty state before any data exists, an error state if an import fails), not just the 'happy path' screens that look good in a presentation. |
| **Worked example**      | For the invoice-reminder capstone, the student wireframes the full primary flow: empty state (no invoices imported yet) -\> import screen -\> parsed-invoice list with overdue items flagged -\> AI-drafted reminder preview screen -\> edit/send confirmation -\> sent-confirmation state -\> an error state specifically for a malformed import file. Six low-fidelity screens total, chosen because skipping the empty and error states would leave two realistic situations completely undesigned.                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture specifically require designing empty and error states alongside the 'happy path' screens?

\(A\) Empty and error states are purely decorative and improve visual variety in a wireframe set

**(B) They cover realistic situations a real user will actually encounter, and skipping them leaves the flow incomplete even if the happy path looks polished**

\(C\) Portfolio reviewers only ever look at empty and error states, never the happy path

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Wireframe your capstone's complete primary flow in low fidelity, including at least one empty state and one error state alongside the happy-path screens.

**Lecture 612 UX**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply information architecture and interaction-design principles from earlier in the program to resolve one genuinely difficult UX decision in the capstone flow, documenting the trade-off.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Every real product flow has at least one decision that doesn't have an obvious right answer, and this lecture's job is to find that decision in the capstone and resolve it deliberately rather than accidentally, pulling directly on IA and interaction-design principles from Year 1 (navigation patterns, progressive disclosure, recognition over recall) rather than treating this capstone as disconnected from everything already learned. The method mirrors design rationale (Month 35): name the genuinely difficult decision, the real options, the criteria, and the resolution — but applied live, in-flow, rather than written up after the fact. |
| **Worked example**      | The student identifies their hardest UX decision: should the AI-drafted reminder be auto-sent after a timeout, or always require explicit user confirmation? Options weighed: auto-send (less friction, matches 'forgetting to follow up' research finding) versus confirm-required (more friction, but avoids an AI-drafted message going out with a wrong tone or error uncorrected). Resolution: confirm-required wins, because research didn't surface trust in unreviewed AI-sent client communication, and sending an embarrassing or wrong message to a paying client is a severity-4-equivalent risk worth the extra tap.                                |

**Knowledge check:** What does this lecture ask students to pull from specifically when resolving the capstone's hardest UX decision?

\(A\) Only material from this current month, treating the capstone as an isolated exercise

**(B) IA and interaction-design principles established earlier in the program, applying them live to a genuinely difficult, undecided flow decision**

\(C\) A randomly assigned design pattern unrelated to the capstone's actual research findings

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Identify the single hardest UX decision in your capstone flow, and resolve it by naming the real options, your criteria, and your final call with justification.

**Lecture 613 UX**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Validate the capstone's wireframed flow with a quick usability check against a real or simulated target user, revising the flow based on observed friction before moving into visual UI design.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the UX run is a checkpoint, not a formality: before investing time in visual polish, the wireframe flow gets tested, even briefly (a single 15-20 minute think-aloud session with one target user, or a careful self-walkthrough treating every click as if it were the first time seeing the screen if a real user genuinely isn't available in the time box). The goal is to catch flow-level confusion now, while it's cheap to fix in wireframes, rather than after UI design has made the flow feel more 'finished' and psychologically harder to change. |
| **Worked example**      | Walking a target user through the wireframes, the student observes the user hesitating for several seconds on the parsed-invoice list screen, unsure which items were actually overdue versus just imported — a flow-level ambiguity, not a visual one. The fix happens in wireframe form: adding a clear overdue/not-overdue grouping to the list screen, tested again informally before any color or typography work begins, since fixing this after visual design would mean redoing polished screens instead of rough ones.                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture insist on validating the wireframe flow before moving into visual UI design, rather than validating the finished UI later?

\(A\) Wireframes are legally required to be tested before any visual design software can be opened

**(B) Flow-level confusion is cheap to fix in rough wireframes, but becomes psychologically and practically harder to revise once screens feel visually finished**

\(C\) Usability testing tools are technically incompatible with high-fidelity visual designs

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Run a 15-20 minute think-aloud (or careful self-walkthrough) of your wireframed flow with a target user, and make at least one flow revision based on observed friction.

**Lecture 614 UI**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply visual design fundamentals and an existing or newly-built mini design system to produce high-fidelity screens for the capstone's validated flow.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | With the flow validated in wireframe form, this lecture moves into visual execution, pulling directly on Year 1-2 visual design and design-systems skills rather than inventing a style from nothing: establishing (or reusing) a small, consistent set of design tokens — a type scale, a restrained color palette with one clear accent color for primary actions, consistent spacing units — and applying them across every screen from the validated flow so the capstone reads as one coherent product rather than a set of disconnected mockups. |
| **Worked example**      | The student defines a mini design system before touching individual screens: a 3-step type scale (body, subhead, heading), a neutral palette plus one accent blue reserved exclusively for primary actions (send reminder, confirm import), and an 8px spacing grid. Every high-fidelity screen from the six-screen flow (611) is then built using only these tokens, so the 'send reminder' button is visually identical in weight and color across every screen it appears on, reinforcing it as the one consistent primary action.                  |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture require defining design tokens (type scale, palette, spacing) before building individual high-fidelity screens?

\(A\) Tokens are only relevant for multi-designer teams and have no effect on a solo capstone project

**(B) Consistent tokens applied across every screen make the capstone read as one coherent product rather than a set of visually disconnected mockups**

\(C\) Design tokens are a legal requirement for any portfolio project built after Month 17

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Define a small mini design system (type scale, palette with one accent color, spacing unit) and apply it consistently across at least 3 high-fidelity screens from your flow.

**Lecture 615 UI**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply visual hierarchy and accessibility principles (contrast, touch-target size, text legibility) to audit and refine the capstone's high-fidelity screens.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | A visually attractive screen that fails basic accessibility or hierarchy checks undermines everything the earlier UX work established, so this lecture is an audit pass specifically on the high-fidelity screens from the prior lecture: checking color contrast ratios on text and the accent-color primary actions (not just eyeballing it — using a contrast checker against WCAG AA minimums), confirming touch targets meet minimum size on any tappable element, and verifying that the single most important action on each screen is visually the most prominent element, not accidentally outcompeted by a secondary element with more visual weight. |
| **Worked example**      | Auditing the AI-drafted reminder preview screen, the student finds the accent-blue 'send' button text fails WCAG AA contrast against its background (3.8:1 against a 4.5:1 minimum) and darkens the blue slightly to pass; separately, they notice the small 'edit' text link is visually louder (larger, higher contrast) than the primary 'send' button due to an earlier styling mistake, and swap their relative visual weight so the primary action is unambiguously the most prominent element on the screen.                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** What specific accessibility check does this lecture require beyond simply 'eyeballing' whether something looks readable?

\(A\) Testing the screen in at least five different browsers for layout bugs

**(B) Measuring color contrast ratios against WCAG AA minimums with a contrast checker, rather than relying on visual impression alone**

\(C\) Running the screen through a spell-checker for every text label

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Audit at least 2 of your high-fidelity screens for contrast ratio (using a contrast-checker tool) and visual hierarchy, and fix any failure you find.

**Lecture 616 UI**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Produce a finished, internally consistent high-fidelity UI set for the entire capstone flow, ready to be turned into an interactive prototype.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the UI run is the consolidation step: every screen from the validated flow now exists in audited, token-consistent, accessible high-fidelity form, and this lecture's job is to review the full set together — not screen by screen in isolation, but side by side — catching the inconsistencies that only become visible at the set level (a spacing unit that drifted on one screen, a button that's slightly the wrong shade of the accent color, an icon style that doesn't match the rest). This full-set review is what the next lecture's interactive prototype will be built directly from. |
| **Worked example**      | Laying all six high-fidelity screens side by side, the student notices the 'confirm send' button on the confirmation screen uses a slightly different corner radius than the 'send reminder' button on the preview screen — an inconsistency invisible when reviewing each screen individually but obvious once placed together. They standardize the corner radius across both before moving to prototyping, since this is the kind of small drift reviewers notice even when they can't articulate why a screen set feels slightly 'off.'                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture review all screens side by side rather than approving each screen individually as it's finished?

\(A\) Side-by-side review is purely a time-saving shortcut with no quality benefit

**(B) Certain inconsistencies (drifted spacing, mismatched corner radii) are only visible when screens are compared together, not when reviewed one at a time**

\(C\) Design software requires all screens to be open simultaneously before export is possible

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Lay out your full high-fidelity screen set side by side and identify at least one cross-screen inconsistency to fix before building your prototype.

**Lecture 617 AI interaction**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design the capstone's core AI-assisted interaction — how a user requests, reviews, edits, and approves an AI-generated output — applying AI UX patterns from earlier in the program.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | The capstone's AI feature (the drafted reminder message) is exactly the kind of AI interaction covered across Months 19-27 of this program, and this lecture requires applying that material specifically rather than bolting on a generic chat box: designing the request moment (what triggers generation — automatic on overdue detection, or user-initiated), the review moment (how the AI output is presented so a user can quickly judge whether it's good, not just displayed as a wall of generated text), and the edit/approve moment (can the user tweak a phrase without regenerating the whole message, and is sending always a deliberate, confirmed action per the UX decision made in lecture 612). |
| **Worked example**      | The student designs the AI reminder interaction in three deliberate moments: generation triggers automatically when an invoice crosses 30 days overdue, but doesn't send automatically; the review screen shows the drafted message with the specific overdue amount and date highlighted inline (not just plain generated text) so the user can fact-check the AI's output at a glance; and the edit interaction allows inline text editing of the draft directly, rather than forcing a full regenerate-from-scratch if only the closing line feels off.                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the review-moment design specifically highlight the AI-generated amount and date inline rather than presenting the draft as plain text?

\(A\) Highlighting specific facts is a decorative choice with no functional purpose

**(B) It lets the user quickly fact-check the AI output's specific claims at a glance, which matters because AI-generated content can be wrong in ways that are costly if sent to a client unreviewed**

\(C\) Plain text rendering is technically unsupported in most prototyping tools

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Design your capstone's AI-interaction sequence as three explicit moments (request/generate, review, edit/approve), and justify one specific design choice in the review moment.

**Lecture 618 AI interaction**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design for AI failure and uncertainty in the capstone's interaction — how the interface communicates low-confidence output, handles a bad generation, and gives the user an easy recovery path.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | An AI feature's UX isn't finished until it accounts for the AI being wrong, since every generative feature produces bad or off-target output some percentage of the time, and a design that only shows the happy-path 'good draft' case will fail in production. This lecture designs specifically for failure: how does the interface signal when a generation is likely low-quality (an unusually short or generic draft, a parsing failure in the source data), what does the interface offer when a user rejects a draft outright (regenerate, or fall back to a blank editable template), and is there always a non-AI path to complete the task so a bad generation never fully blocks the user. |
| **Worked example**      | The student adds a fallback state: if the AI draft comes back unusually short (a heuristic proxy for a likely bad generation) or the user taps 'regenerate' twice without approving, the interface offers a plain editable template with placeholder fields instead of a third AI attempt, ensuring the user can always complete the task by hand even if the AI feature degrades, rather than being stuck in a regenerate loop with no way to just write the reminder themselves.                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture require a non-AI fallback path in the capstone's interaction design?

\(A\) Non-AI fallback paths are required by law for any product using generative AI features

**(B) A generative feature will sometimes produce bad output, so a user must always have a way to complete the task even if the AI path fails or degrades**

\(C\) Fallback paths are only needed if the AI model being used is open-source rather than proprietary

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Design one specific failure-handling element for your capstone's AI interaction (a low-confidence signal, a regenerate limit, or a non-AI fallback), and describe what triggers it.

**Lecture 619 AI interaction**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build an interactive, clickable prototype of the complete capstone flow — including the AI-interaction and failure-handling states — ready for usability testing.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the AI-interaction run turns the full high-fidelity screen set, the AI-interaction design, and the failure-handling states into one connected, clickable prototype — the single artifact the next two lecture runs (testing, then product strategy and the final exam) will all reference. The prototyping discipline: every screen from the UI set needs real click targets wired to its correct destination, including the less-glamorous states (the fallback template, the low-confidence signal) that are easy to forget wiring up because they don't appear on the 'main' happy path a quick demo would show. |
| **Worked example**      | The student wires every screen into one Figma (or equivalent) prototype: the six main-flow screens plus the AI-interaction review/edit screens plus the two failure-handling states (regenerate-limit fallback, low-confidence flag) — eleven total interactive screens, each click target tested to confirm it leads to the correct next state, including deliberately clicking 'regenerate' three times in a row to confirm the fallback-to-template path actually triggers as designed.                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture specifically call out wiring the failure-handling states, not just the main happy-path screens, into the clickable prototype?

\(A\) Failure-handling states are optional in a prototype and can be safely skipped to save time

**(B) They're easy to forget because they don't appear in a quick happy-path demo, but they still need to be testable in the usability session that follows**

\(C\) Prototyping software cannot technically support more than one interaction path per screen

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Build your complete clickable prototype, explicitly confirming that at least one failure-handling or fallback state is wired and reachable, not just the main happy path.

**Lecture 620 testing**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Plan and run a moderated usability test of the capstone prototype with a real or simulated target user, capturing both task-success data and qualitative friction points.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | The capstone prototype now gets tested the way any real product would be before launch: a moderated session (15-25 minutes) with a target user, built around 2-3 realistic tasks derived directly from the primary flow (not 'click around and tell me what you think,' but 'you just noticed a client payment is 35 days late — show me what you'd do'), observing both whether the task completes successfully and where hesitation, confusion, or wrong clicks occur, logged in real time rather than reconstructed from memory afterward. |
| **Worked example**      | The student runs a session with the task prompt 'A client's payment is 35 days overdue — walk me through what you'd do in this app.' The participant completes the import and reminder-review steps smoothly but hesitates for 8 seconds at the edit screen, unsure whether tapping outside the text field would discard their edit — a specific, logged friction point distinct from a general 'it was fine' impression, captured in the moment rather than guessed at afterward.                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture specify realistic task prompts ('show me what you'd do if...') rather than open-ended exploration ('click around and tell me what you think')?

\(A\) Realistic task prompts are faster to write than open-ended prompts

**(B) Realistic tasks mirror actual use and let the moderator observe genuine task-success and friction points, rather than unfocused browsing feedback**

\(C\) Open-ended exploration prompts are not permitted under standard usability-testing ethics guidelines

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Run a moderated usability test of your prototype with 1-2 realistic task prompts, logging at least one specific moment of hesitation, confusion, or error in real time.

**Lecture 621 testing**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Synthesize the capstone usability test findings into prioritized fixes, apply the highest-priority ones to the prototype, and document what was deliberately left unfixed given remaining time.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the testing run mirrors real product work under a deadline: not every finding from a usability test gets fixed before ship, so the skill is honest triage. The method: list every observed friction point, rate each by severity using the same frequency/impact/persistence logic from the heuristic-evaluation lectures (Month 34), fix the highest-severity items that are feasible within remaining time, and explicitly document (not hide) any known issue left unfixed — because a capstone that acknowledges a known limitation with a stated reason reads as more professionally mature than one that pretends everything is perfect. |
| **Worked example**      | From the test, the student rates the edit-screen hesitation a severity 2 (minor, recoverable, user eventually proceeded) and a separate finding — the user missed the overdue flag entirely on first view of the invoice list — a severity 3 (more users likely affected, blocks the core value prop if missed). With limited time left, they fix the severity-3 issue (adding a more visually distinct overdue badge) and explicitly note in their documentation: 'Known issue: edit-screen discard behavior is unclear; deprioritized given limited remaining build time; would address with an explicit "discard changes?" confirmation in a future iteration.'     |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture recommend explicitly documenting a known, unfixed issue rather than leaving it unmentioned?

\(A\) Documentation of unfixed issues is required to avoid academic-integrity violations in this program

**(B) Acknowledging a known limitation with a stated reason reads as more professionally mature than a capstone that implies everything is perfect**

\(C\) Unfixed issues must always be disclosed to comply with accessibility law

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Triage your usability findings by severity, fix at least one high-severity issue in your prototype, and write one sentence documenting a known issue you're deliberately leaving unfixed and why.

**Lecture 622 product strategy**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Define a go-to-market and growth framing for the capstone product, positioning it as a real, launchable product rather than only a design exercise.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | A capstone built purely as a design artifact, with no thought given to how it would actually reach and retain users, misses the product-strategy skills this program built across Years 2-3, so this lecture asks the student to step back from the screens and think like a product manager: who is the first realistic group of users to reach (not 'everyone,' but a specific channel — e.g., freelance-community forums or a specific niche), what's the core retention loop (why would someone keep using this after the novelty wears off), and what's a plausible, honest monetization or sustainability model if this were real (a simple answer like 'free tier covering basic reminders, paid tier for AI-drafted multi-client batch sending' is fine — the point is showing the thinking, not building a full business plan). |
| **Worked example**      | The student frames a brief go-to-market note: initial users reached via freelance-community forums and a niche newsletter sponsorship, not a broad paid-ad campaign; retention loop centers on the product becoming the single place a freelancer checks before any client call, reinforced by the reminder habit itself; monetization framed as a free basic tier (manual reminders) with a paid tier unlocking AI-drafted batch reminders across all clients at once — a simple, plausible model rather than an elaborate projected-revenue spreadsheet.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture ask the student to define a go-to-market and retention framing, rather than stopping at the finished prototype?

\(A\) Go-to-market framing is a legal requirement for any capstone project in this program

**(B) It demonstrates the product-strategy thinking built across Years 2-3, showing the capstone as a realistic product concept rather than only a design artifact**

\(C\) Monetization models are required before a prototype can be legally demonstrated to others

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a short go-to-market note for your capstone: a specific first-user channel, your core retention loop, and a simple, honest monetization framing.

**Lecture 623 product strategy**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a one-page capstone strategy summary — positioning, roadmap-next-steps, and metrics that would indicate success — synthesizing discovery through product-strategy work into a single executive-ready artifact.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the run, and the last lecture before the Month 36 Examination, produces the single document that ties the entire capstone together at the strategic level: a one-page summary covering positioning (the differentiation claim from discovery), a short 'what's next' roadmap (2-3 features deliberately cut from this capstone's scope in lecture 605/610, now framed as a realistic next-iteration plan), and 2-3 specific metrics that would indicate real-world success if this shipped (e.g., 'percentage of flagged overdue invoices where a reminder was sent within 48 hours' — specific and measurable, not a vague 'user satisfaction'). This artifact is what a hiring manager or interviewer would actually want to see to confirm the student can think beyond the screens. |
| **Worked example**      | The student's one-page summary: Positioning ('AI-assisted reminder drafting as the primary feature, not a side function of full invoicing'); Next-iteration roadmap (multi-platform email-client integration, recurring-client auto-scheduling — both explicitly deferred from this capstone's scope); Success metrics ('% of overdue invoices with a reminder sent within 48 hours,' 'reminder edit rate as a proxy for AI-draft quality,' 'week-4 retention among freelancers with 5+ active clients') — each metric specific and measurable rather than a vague satisfaction score.                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture require success metrics to be specific and measurable (e.g., '% reminders sent within 48 hours') rather than general sentiment-based goals?

\(A\) Specific metrics are only useful for consumer products, not freelance productivity tools

**(B) Measurable, specific metrics demonstrate the kind of product thinking that shows the student can reason beyond the screens, which is what a hiring manager wants to see**

\(C\) Vague satisfaction-based goals are prohibited under this program's examination policy

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write your one-page capstone strategy summary: positioning, a 2-3 item next-iteration roadmap of deliberately deferred features, and 2-3 specific, measurable success metrics.

**Lecture 624 Month 36 Examination**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Professional Product + UX Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Complete the 3-year, 624-lecture Product & UX / AI Design Professional Program by presenting the full capstone — discovery through product strategy — and passing the final comprehensive review at the program's 80% internal bar.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | This is the final lecture of the entire three-year program, and the capstone built across lectures 605-623 is the proof of everything those three years were for: Year 1's foundations (visual design, UX research, information architecture, wireframing, interaction design, prototyping) gave the capstone its design bones; Year 2's depth (design systems, product fundamentals, agile planning, roadmaps and metrics, the first wave of AI product work) gave it structure and a product lens; Year 3's advanced work (AI research and evaluation, advanced UX research, accessibility, complex product design, AI design systems, product analytics, and this final trio of months — NN/g-level portfolio rigor, GitHub and portfolio engineering, and this capstone itself) gave it the polish and professional framing to stand as a genuine, job-ready artifact. The final review checks the whole capstone end to end against the same 80% internal bar this program has used in every month since lecture 1: a validated discovery brief, research-informed scope, a tested and iterated UX flow, an accessible and consistent high-fidelity UI, a thoughtfully designed AI interaction with real failure handling, a usability-tested and triaged prototype, and a strategic framing a hiring manager could take seriously — and, having met that bar here, the student has completed the program. |
| **Worked example**      | A student presents their invoice-reminder capstone end to end in roughly 15 minutes: the discovery brief and its research-driven pivot from overdue-detection to reminder-drafting (605-610); the validated UX flow including its hardest resolved decision (611-613); the accessible, token-consistent high-fidelity UI (614-616); the AI-interaction design with its explicit failure-handling fallback (617-619); the usability-test findings and the honestly-documented known issue left unfixed (620-621); and the one-page strategy summary with specific, measurable success metrics (622-623) — tying every stage back to a specific skill first learned somewhere earlier in the three-year program, which is exactly what this final review is checking for.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** What is this final examination of the entire program ultimately checking for, beyond whether the capstone itself meets the 80% internal bar?

\(A\) Whether the student can recite the exact lecture number where every individual skill was first taught

**(B) Whether the finished capstone coherently demonstrates skills drawn from across all three years of the program, not just this final month in isolation**

\(C\) Whether the capstone includes more features than any other student's final project

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Present your complete capstone to a peer, mentor, or mock panel, explicitly naming at least one skill each from Year 1, Year 2, and Year 3 that your finished work draws on — then submit it as your program completion.
